comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I am writing to oppose the proposed elimination of the up-to-60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

I came to the United States in 2010 on an F-1 student visa and have been on H-1B status since 2015. I work in technology. The 60-day period is already very short. Finding a new employer, completing interviews and background checks, receiving an offer, and having a new petition filed takes weeks, even for workers in high demand. Removing the grace period entirely would mean a worker who loses a job through no fault of their own — a layoff, a project ending, or a company restructuring — would fall out of status the next day.

That does not give workers a realistic chance to transfer to a new employer, change to another lawful status, or make orderly arrangements to depart. It would force abrupt departures, disrupt families and children's schooling, and push experienced workers out of the U.S. workforce even when another U.S. employer is ready to hire them.

My family would be affected as well. My wife also works in the United States, and we have two young U.S. citizen children — a 3-year-old and an infant. If I had to leave immediately, we would face an impossible choice: uproot our U.S. citizen children from their home, childcare, and schooling, or separate our family.

I have also built a life here with long-term financial ties that cannot be unwound in a day. I own a home with a mortgage and cars in the United States, and I have a Health Savings Account and retirement accounts here. If I had to leave immediately, I would have no time to sell or rent out my house, sell my cars, or properly handle my HSA and retirement accounts. I would also have no time to close bank accounts, cancel insurance and utilities, or withdraw my children from school. That would mean rushed sales at a loss, missed mortgage payments, and financial harm that follows me even after leaving.

I have paid U.S. federal and state income taxes, as well as Social Security and Medicare taxes, since 2010, starting as an F-1 student working in a dining hall cleaning tables.

It would also harm U.S. employers. Companies invest significant time and resources in recruiting and training skilled workers. A zero-day rule makes it harder to retain that talent and harder to hire from the existing U.S. pool when a position opens.

The current 60-day period is discretionary, capped at 60 days or the end of the authorized stay, whichever is shorter. It is a reasonable bridge, not an open-ended benefit. I urge USCIS to retain it and not finalize this proposal as written. At a minimum, USCIS should retain some grace period or case-by-case discretion, rather than eliminating it entirely.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that removing the grace period harms workers, families, and prevents orderly transitions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I strongly object to the proposed regulation that would remove the current 60-day grace period for H-1B, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, and TN visa holders after job termination. This change would immediately and unfairly harm legal workers and their families. Because layoffs and corporate restructurings happen outside an employee's control, workers would instantly lose their legal status without a chance to find new employment, change their visa status, or make proper arrangements to leave the country. The real human cost affects families who have integrated into U.S. communities by buying homes and paying taxes, leaving them vulnerable to unlawful status and future entry bars. Even though the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) acknowledges these reliance interests in the rule's preamble, moving forward anyway is arbitrary and capricious. Dismissing the grace period as merely "discretionary" and resource-intensive does not justify stripping away a protection that has worked well since 2017 and benefits both workers and the employers who invested in them. Furthermore, eliminating this safety net harms U.S. competitiveness by making the visa process harsher and less predictable, which discourages global talent from coming to the United States. I urge DHS to completely scrap this proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly objects to removing the grace period, arguing it harms workers, families, and U.S. competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Shaibujan Thankappan Kamalamma
comments.commentText:
I am writing with a heavy heart to urge you not to eliminate the 60-day grace period.

I have lived, worked, and paid taxes in the United States on an H-1B visa for over 16 years. When my family first arrived here, my children were practically babies, my eldest was two and a half, and my youngest was just six months old. This country is not just where I happen to work; it is where my children grew up, took their first steps, made their lifelong friends, and built their dreams. America is the only home they have ever known.

Today, my eldest child is navigating his very first semester of college, and my youngest is in the 11th grade, working hard to prepare for university. We own our home, our cars, and have spent nearly two decades investing every bit of our energy and savings into our local community.

Under the proposed rule, if I were to suddenly lose my job tomorrow, through layoffs or circumstances entirely beyond my control, my family and I would be expected to leave the country literally the next day.

How can a family pack up 16 years of an entire life in 24 hours?

How do I look my son in the eye and tell him he must abandon his college education mid-semester? How do I tell my 11th grader that two years before high school graduation, everything they’ve worked for is gone overnight? What happens to our house, our mortgage, our cars, and our belongings? Forcing long-term lawful residents to pack up a lifetime in a single day is not just logistically impossible, it is unnecessarily cruel.

Under the Administrative Procedure Act, agencies are required to account for the serious reliance interests of real people who planned their lives around existing rules. For nearly a decade, the 60-day grace period has provided an orderly, humane window. It gives families time to handle unexpected transitions with dignity, or gives qualified workers the brief breathing room needed to transfer to another employer who wants to hire them.

Taking that safety net away reduces people who have spent 16+ years contributing to this nation down to a disposable commodity. Please do not tear our lives apart overnight.

I strongly urge USCIS to reconsider this proposal and retain the 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly urges the government not to eliminate the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment. I am an H-1B worker and software engineer who has lived and worked in the United States for 12 years. My spouse and I are raising two children here, one in H-4 status and one a U.S. citizen. I respect DHS's responsibility to protect the integrity of the immigration system and the interests of U.S. workers. I respectfully ask DHS to reconsider this proposal and keep the 60-day grace period.

1. The problem this rule solves is unclear. The notice says removal would better align the regulations with the statutory basis for nonimmigrant status, but I could not find data showing the grace period has been misused or has harmed U.S. workers. It came from the 2016 final rule implementing AC21 to help skilled workers change jobs, and it has been in place since 2017. I would be grateful if DHS shared the specific concerns behind this change.

2. Tools to address fraud already exist. I support preventing fraud in the H-1B program. As I understand it, DHS can already deny petitions with false information, revoke approvals when misrepresentation is found, and conduct site visits and investigations. The grace period does not protect fraud. It applies only to people in valid status whose employment ends, often through a layoff. If DHS has particular abuses in mind, I hope they can be addressed directly.

3. A layoff without a grace period is a serious status problem. Even 60 days is tight to find an employer, negotiate an offer, and have a new petition filed. Without it, someone who loses a job through no fault of their own could fall out of status immediately. Layoffs usually come from restructuring or the economy, not performance.

4. Families need time for orderly arrangements. When the main worker loses status, H-4 spouses and children lose theirs too. My family has built our life here over 12 years. Our children attend school here, we pay taxes, and we are part of our community. Even simple steps take longer than a few days:
- Housing: Many landlords require 30 to 60 days of written notice, and arranging movers and shipping belongings often takes weeks.
- Children: Parents need time to gather pediatric records, complete vaccinations, handle school or daycare commitments, and plan safe travel.
- Finances: Paying off or transferring a car loan, selling a vehicle, DMV title transfer, closing utilities, settling medical bills, and moving bank balances all require processing time.
Without a grace period, families would face all of this at once while also searching for a new job. It would affect our U.S.-citizen child as well.

5. Long-term residents who followed the process would be affected. Many H-1B workers wait years in green card backlogs. My employer-sponsored process began in 2016 and my I-140 is approved. A layoff with no grace period could put years of progress at risk, and H-4 children could age out of dependent status while waiting.

6. Employers and communities benefit. Hiring takes time: interviews, an offer, a background review, and filing a new USCIS petition often take several weeks. The grace period lets U.S. employers hire experienced professionals already in the country. Without it, employers could lose qualified candidates in specialized fields, and skilled taxpayers might leave the U.S. labor market.

7. USCIS workload may increase. Without the grace period, I would expect more status gaps, reinstatement requests, and urgent filings.

8. Reliance interests deserve consideration. Workers, families, and employers have made major decisions in reliance on this rule. I respectfully ask DHS to consider these interests, and alternatives such as keeping the grace period or adjusting it with appropriate safeguards.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, or at minimum keep a reasonable grace period. Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter asks DHS to reconsider the proposal and keep the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I believe this proposal lacks sufficient justification. The proposed rule emphasizes maintaining the connection between employment and immigration status and reducing administrative burdens. However, these objectives do not adequately justify eliminating an existing provision that serves an important practical purpose.

The 60-day grace period does not provide unlimited permission to remain in the United States or authorization to work without appropriate approval. Rather, it offers a limited, discretionary period during which individuals can seek new employment, pursue another lawful immigration status, or prepare to depart the country.

The fact that the grace period requires administrative review does not, by itself, establish that eliminating it is necessary. The proposal should provide clearer evidence that the administrative benefits outweigh the economic, professional, and personal consequences for affected workers and employers. Administrative efficiency should not be achieved simply by transferring substantial costs and uncertainty to legally employed professionals and U.S. businesses.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I believe this proposal unnecessarily restricts professional and economic mobility. The elimination of the grace period would create additional barriers to professional advancement and economic mobility for foreign professionals who have already established careers in the United States.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 C.F.R. 214.1(l)(2) and request retention. I am a labor economist with research experience in immigration and human capital, commenting in my personal capacity. The existing period is limited, discretionary, and does not itself authorize unrestricted employment. Its removal requires evidence that the resulting disruption advances a lawful policy objective.

1. Distinguish legal necessity from policy choice.
Employment-based status must remain connected to qualifying activity, but that principle does not independently establish that protection must end immediately upon an unexpected termination. A bounded period to obtain new sponsorship, seek another status, or depart can preserve that connection. DHS should identify any statutory language requiring immediate loss of protection. If elimination is discretionary, assess its advantages and disadvantages as a policy choice and explain why the worker-stability and employer-retention rationale supporting the 2016 rule no longer warrants a transition period.

2. Immediate departure is not operationally realistic.
A worker dismissed without notice may need an international flight, travel documents for a dependent, medical arrangements, housing termination, or coordination with a child's school. A ticket payment cannot ensure immediate departure.

These constraints do not automatically excuse a status violation under existing law; they explain why a practical transition rule matters. DHS should examine actual termination practices and departure logistics, and distinguish failure to maintain status, unlawful presence, removability, and employment authorization. Those concepts do not have identical consequences. Employer return-transportation obligations also have limits and implementation delays.

3. Reduced mobility can undermine labor standards.
The economic effect begins before dismissal. If job loss threatens immediate immigration disruption for a worker and family, the worker may become less willing to negotiate wages, report violations, or leave an unsuitable employer. Formal anti-retaliation protections do not necessarily eliminate that practical pressure.

DHS should assess this mechanism, including bargaining power, wage competition, and enforcement, alongside substitution benefits. Making sponsored workers less mobile can also affect American coworkers' bargaining position. Restrictions on foreign workers should not be assumed to benefit domestic workers without examining these channels.

4. Measure lawful transition time and employer responses.
Recruitment, interviews, internal approval, legal review, and filings take time. The option to seek admission again from abroad is not equivalent to completing a lawful domestic transition. Existing eligibility and portability requirements would still apply if the grace period remains.

Departure does not guarantee domestic replacement. Employers may cancel projects, relocate work, or redistribute tasks. Evaluate vacancies, recruitment costs, complementary jobs, and industry differences.

5. Administrative and utilization claims need better measurement.
Counting filings potentially requiring a grace-period assessment does not measure incremental officer time or net government savings. Officers may still need to determine employment cessation dates and pre-filing status. Assess workload shifted to new processing, departure disputes, enforcement, courts, employers, and families.

Petition withdrawal is not identical to actual unemployment, and subsequent filings do not identify every affected worker or dependent. Low observed utilization does not establish low protective value: an option can provide insurance and bargaining power even when rarely exercised. Distinguish voluntary transfers, involuntary terminations, and repeat observations, and disclose data limitations and sensitivity analyses.

6. Address reliance and compare workable alternatives.
Discretion does not eliminate reliance on a codified transition. DHS v. Regents requires assessment of significant reliance interests, without freezing policy. Evaluate family arrangements, housing, schooling, dependent employment, and existing commitments without double counting.

Please compare retention, clearer cessation definitions, standardized evidence, shorter protected periods, and targeted measures for demonstrated abuse. Include protection for unexpected dismissal, retaliation, medical constraints, and disrupted travel. Explain why these alternatives cannot meet the agency's objectives with fewer costs.

Please withdraw the proposal. Otherwise, substantiate net benefits and provide transition protections and clear guidance for existing cases.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the grace period and argues for its retention.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ed Juan
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). H-1B specialty occupation workers drive critical research and engineering across American artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced manufacturing. When workforce reductions occur, they are driven by macroeconomic headwinds, interest rate shifts, and corporate restructuring—not an individual lack of talent or productivity. Abruptly terminating lawful status penalizes top contributors for broader economic cycles outside their control.

Forcing laid-off workers to immediately leave the country inflicts severe, avoidable economic damage on American enterprise. Years of institutional knowledge, specialized domain expertise, and technical training acquired inside U.S. firms are permanently erased. When the market rebounds or hiring needs shift, American businesses are forced to spend tens of thousands of dollars per hire to recruit, onboard, and sponsor entirely new foreign workers—paying substantial legal fees, statutory USCIS surcharges, and training expenses, all while navigating annual lottery caps. This duplicative process creates substantial deadweight loss, raises operating costs for U.S. employers, and ultimately burdens American consumers and the broader economy with higher prices and slowed innovation.

Retaining this talent directly advances U.S. national security and economic interests in an era of intense global technological competition. During recent tech restructurings, the 60-day window allowed experienced engineers to quickly transition into early-stage domestic startups and strategic U.S. industries that previously could not compete with Big Tech's compensation packages. Eliminating this buffer hands an unearned advantage to strategic competitors. When Canada launched an expedited work permit targeting laid-off U.S. H-1B holders in 2023, its 10,000-applicant cap was exhausted in less than 48 hours. Without a viable transition window, the United States will actively export high-skilled talent, intellectual property, and tax revenue to competing foreign economies.

Furthermore, removing the grace period ignores standard federal immigration timelines. Sponsoring a transferring H-1B worker requires an approved Labor Condition Application (LCA) from the Department of Labor, which takes 7 to 10 business days to certify before an employer can legally submit Form I-129 to USCIS. Without a grace period, completing an orderly transfer between sudden job loss and petition filing is procedurally impossible. Rather than reducing administrative burdens, this rule will overwhelm USCIS with defensive Form I-539 change-of-status filings as workers seek bridge visitor status, worsening agency backlogs.

The 60-day grace period is already strictly limited, non-renewable, and discretionary, without granting unauthorized employment. It serves as an indispensable economic stabilizer that protects American investments in skilled human capital. DHS and USCIS should withdraw this proposed rule.

I understand DHS’s responsibility to ensure that individuals comply with the conditions of their immigration status and that employment-based classifications serve their intended purposes. Clear rules and effective oversight benefit workers, employers, and the public.

I hope DHS will reconsider eliminating the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days, taking into account its practical value for lawful transitions, American businesses, and affected families.

Employment can end unexpectedly because of restructuring, budget reductions, or a business closure, even when a worker has followed all applicable rules. A limited grace period gives that person time to understand their options, seek another qualifying position, prepare an appropriate application, or arrange an orderly departure. It does not guarantee another job or a future immigration benefit.

Complying with immigration requirements after an unexpected job loss involves practical steps. Preparing an appropriate application or arranging departure requires time to obtain advice, gather documents, and coordinate necessary arrangements. A clearly defined transition period helps people carry out these responsibilities in an orderly manner while remaining subject to DHS oversight.

The grace period also serves a practical purpose for U.S. employers. Hiring involves interviews, assessment of qualifications, internal approvals, and immigration-related paperwork. An employer may identify a suitable candidate but need time to complete these steps. Preserving a limited transition period allows businesses to make considered hiring decisions while meeting applicable requirements.

The potential loss to the United States extends beyond an individual worker’s job search. Someone whose position ends may still have skills and experience that could contribute to another American team. If that person cannot make a lawful transition within a reasonable period, U.S. organizations may lose the opportunity to benefit from those capabilities. The experience a person develops in one workplace can remain valuable even after that particular employment relationship ends.

I am also concerned about the pressure that removing the grace period could place on workers in problematic employment situations. A worker who fears having almost no time to make alternative arrangements may be more reluctant to leave an abusive employer or report workplace concerns. A limited transition period can support workers’ ability to raise concerns and seek lawful alternatives.

Dependents may also need time to address housing, children’s schooling, and travel arrangements. Allowing a brief, defined period to manage these responsibilities supports orderly transitions and departures.

I recognize that administering a discretionary provision requires government resources. I respectfully ask DHS to weigh those costs against the disruption that eliminating the provision could create for workers, families, and employers. Because the existing grace period is limited and discretionary, DHS retains the ability to address individual circumstances and concerns about misuse.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposal and retain the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Preserving this reasonable transition period would support compliance while allowing the United States to continue benefiting from lawful professional contributions.

Re: Opposition to Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (Docket USCIS-2026-0364)

I respectfully oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I urge DHS to retain this limited but vital protection for lawfully employed nonimmigrant workers and their families.

I have lived and worked legally in the United States for many years. My family and I have established roots here, purchased a home, and made long-term financial commitments. Our children attend American schools, have friendships and activities here, and consider this country their home.

The existing 60-day grace period provides a limited but essential opportunity to navigate these transitions responsibly and lawfully.

Second, the proposal would harm U.S. businesses and undermine America’s ability to attract and retain global talent and fill the positions where American citizens are less willing to work for. Many employment-based visa holders work in specialized fields, including technology, healthcare, engineering, research, and some jobs that U.S. citizens are not so willing to work for such as poultry processing, fish processing and trimming, etc. Eliminating the grace period would make it significantly more difficult for American employers to recruit experienced foreign professionals who have already established careers in the United States. It could also force qualified workers to leave the country even when other U.S. employers are willing to hire them. This creates unnecessary recruitment costs, disrupts workforce continuity, and risks losing valuable human capital to competing economies.

Third, eliminating the grace period would create an unhealthy imbalance of power between employers and foreign workers. When a worker’s ability to remain in the United States depends almost entirely on continuous employment with a particular employer, the threat of immediate immigration consequences can discourage employees from reporting workplace harassment, discrimination, wage violations, or other unlawful practices. The existing grace period provides a modest but important safeguard, allowing workers some opportunity to seek alternative employment rather than remain in potentially exploitative circumstances. Removing this protection could weaken worker mobility and undermine labor standards.

Fourth, the proposal would impose disproportionate hardship on families and established communities. Many visa holders have spent years building their lives in the United States, contributing to local economies, paying taxes, signing leases or purchasing homes, and raising children. Requiring families to leave immediately after an unexpected job loss could disrupt children’s education, interrupt medical care, create substantial financial losses, and separate families from their established communities. These consequences are disproportionate to the proposed administrative benefits.

I also question whether the proposed rule would meaningfully reduce administrative burdens. Eliminating an established transition mechanism could instead increase immigration-related complications, disrupt employer hiring processes, and create additional uncertainty for workers seeking to maintain lawful status. DHS should provide stronger evidence that the anticipated administrative savings outweigh these economic and human costs.

The existing 60-day grace period is already limited and discretionary. It does not provide indefinite permission to remain in the United States or unrestricted employment authorization. Rather, it offers a reasonable transition mechanism that balances immigration compliance with the practical realities of employment changes.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to withdraw the proposed rule and retain the existing 60-day discretionary grace period. Preserving this protection would support American businesses, promote fair labor practices, protect families, and maintain the United States’ competitiveness in attracting highly skilled professionals.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Dear USCIS and Department of Homeland Security,

As an American citizen, I strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for foreign workers who lose their jobs. I find this proposal unnecessarily harsh, economically shortsighted, and frankly contrary to the values that America is supposed to stand for.

First, I think we Americans sometimes forget just how much our country depends on foreign workers. And I’m not just talking about scientists, engineers, or highly paid professionals. I’m talking about the people who process our food, work in factories, and take on physically demanding jobs that are often difficult to fill. Anyone who has seen what it’s like to work long hours in a poultry processing plant or a seafood processing facility knows these are not easy jobs. They can be physically exhausting and mentally stressful. While those particular workers often fall under different visa programs, they remind us of something important: foreign workers contribute to this country in all kinds of ways, and their work deserves respect.

Second, foreign workers are not simply taking from the American system. They contribute to it. Many pay federal and state income taxes, Social Security taxes, and Medicare taxes, just like American citizens do. Some may never stay in this country long enough to qualify for the retirement benefits they helped fund. They also pay rent, buy groceries, support local businesses, and help keep our economy running. I don’t understand why we would want to make life harder for people who are working legally, following our laws, and contributing to our communities.

Third, I find it deeply troubling that someone could lose their job through absolutely no fault of their own and then be expected to uproot their entire life immediately. Layoffs happen every day in America. Companies restructure, budgets get cut, and businesses shut down. American citizens know how stressful and devastating losing a job can be. Now imagine dealing with that while also having to worry about packing up your home, pulling your children out of school, making arrangements for your family, and potentially leaving the country you’ve lived in for years. Is giving someone up to 60 days to figure things out really too much to ask?

To me, this is a matter of basic human decency. You don’t have to be an immigrant or have a foreign-born family member to recognize that. America has always taken pride in being a country that values hard work, opportunity, and fairness. I don’t think telling someone who has worked hard, paid their taxes, and followed the rules that they must leave immediately after an unexpected layoff reflects those values.

Fourth, this proposal doesn’t make much economic sense either. American businesses benefit when they can hire qualified workers who are already here. Eliminating the grace period would make it harder for those businesses to recruit people who unexpectedly become available for employment. Why should an American company lose the opportunity to hire someone simply because the government won’t allow a reasonable transition period? This creates unnecessary problems for businesses without a clear benefit to American workers.

I understand the importance of enforcing immigration laws and maintaining an orderly immigration system. But enforcement and compassion are not mutually exclusive. The existing grace period is already limited to a maximum of 60 days and is subject to government discretion. It isn’t an invitation to stay indefinitely. It’s a modest allowance for people to make arrangements, find another qualifying job, or prepare to leave in an orderly manner.

I believe America is a better country when we recognize the contributions of people who work hard here, regardless of where they were born. Not even allowing someone a reasonable period to get their affairs in order after losing a job is, in my opinion, a disgrace to the American spirit of fairness and decency.

I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing 60-day grace period.

Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule under Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, which seeks to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for certain nonimmigrant workers, including H-1B visa holders.
As an H-1B professional currently contributing to the U.S. economy, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. Eliminating the grace period is a regressive step that undermines the U.S. immigration system, harms American employers, and creates severe, unnecessary hardships for high-skilled legal immigrants. My opposition is based on the following critical grounds:
1. Contradiction of Congressional Intent Under AC21
The American Competitiveness in the Twenty-First Century Act (AC21) explicitly introduced visa portability to allow high-skilled foreign workers to transition between employers in response to market demands. The 60-day grace period is the operational mechanism that makes this law functional. Eliminating it entirely strips workers of their statutory right to portability, effectively locking them into their current employment and subverting Congress's intent to foster a dynamic, mobile, and competitive workforce.
2. Ambiguity and Complexities of Employment Termination
Modern corporate separation processes are rarely instantaneous or straightforward. Defining the exact "end of employment" is highly complex, often involving garden leave, severance pay structures, and the exhaustion of accrued paid time off (PTO). By enforcing a zero-day grace period, the rule creates immediate compliance traps. Well-intentioned, law-abiding professionals could be placed in unlawful status overnight simply due to payroll processing delays or corporate administrative timelines.
3. Severe Humanitarian Burden on Families and Children
An abrupt, immediate termination of status ignores the human reality of living in the United States. For H-1B holders with families, an unexpected layoff would require them to break housing leases, liquidate assets, pull H-4 dependent children out of school, and arrange international travel within 24 hours. Forcing legal residents into such extreme personal and financial chaos is inhumane and disregards the dignity of professionals who have followed every rule to immigrate legally.
4. Flawed Justification of "Reducing Administrative Burdens"
DHS argues that eliminating the grace period simplifies the system. In reality, it does the exact opposite. Without a grace period, thousands of suddenly laid-off professionals will be forced to flood USCIS with applications for a Change of Status (COS) to B-1/B-2 visitor visas to avoid unlawful presence. This will create a massive, unnecessary backlog of paperwork for USCIS officers, shifting the administrative burden rather than reducing it, while overwhelming immigration courts and enforcement agencies with technical violations.
5. Long-term Damage to U.S. Economic Competitiveness
The 60-day grace period acts as a vital safety net that keeps elite global talent within the U.S. ecosystem. If a company downsizes, another American employer can quickly hire that pre-vetted talent via a transfer. Eliminating this window deprives American companies of an immediate, local talent pool during market fluctuations. Furthermore, introducing such extreme instability will deter top international students and experts from choosing the United States, ultimately driving global innovation to competing nations like Canada, the UK, or Germany.
Conclusion
The current 60-day grace period is a fair, balanced, and orderly policy that protects both the integrity of the immigration system and the rights of legal workers. Eliminating it would cause widespread operational chaos, administrative backlogs, and immense personal distress. I strongly urge the Department to reject this proposed rule and maintain the 60-day grace period.

Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Opposition to Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

To U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services:

I strongly oppose the proposed rule eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers and their families.

1. Job loss should not immediately become an immigration crisis.

Layoffs frequently occur for reasons entirely outside an employee’s control, including corporate restructuring, economic downturns, and budget reductions. It is unreasonable to require a legally employed individual to leave the United States immediately after losing a job, potentially disrupting their housing, finances, family life, and future employment.

Sixty days is already a limited period in which to find a new employer, complete interviews, negotiate an offer, and coordinate an immigration petition. Eliminating this protection entirely is disproportionate to the government’s stated administrative objectives.

2. The proposal would undermine American economic competitiveness.

The United States benefits from attracting and retaining highly skilled international professionals, particularly in engineering, artificial intelligence, scientific research, and other innovative industries.

Forcing experienced professionals to leave immediately after a layoff would make it harder for American companies to recruit qualified workers already living in the United States. It could also discourage talented international graduates from building their careers here.

DHS’s own analysis in the proposed rule recognizes that approximately 3,795 workers annually had new employment petitions filed within the existing grace period, based on its historical data. These cases illustrate the practical value of allowing qualified workers to transition between employers without unnecessary international relocation.

3. Eliminating the grace period would weaken employee mobility and bargaining power.

When a worker’s ability to remain in the country depends entirely on continued employment, the threat of immediate departure creates an extreme imbalance of power.

The existing grace period provides a modest safeguard, allowing workers to pursue alternative employment rather than remain with an unsuitable employer solely out of fear of losing immigration status.

Removing this safeguard risks making workers more vulnerable to exploitation and reducing healthy competition among American employers.

4. The proposed administrative benefits do not justify the human and economic costs.

DHS argues that eliminating the grace period would simplify immigration adjudications. However, the proposal does not establish that these administrative savings outweigh the substantial costs imposed on workers, families, and employers.

DHS acknowledges that it cannot reliably quantify some of the affected populations and economic consequences. Administrative convenience alone is not a sufficient reason to eliminate an important protection that has existed for approximately a decade.

Furthermore, the existing grace period does not generally authorize employment without separate work authorization. It simply provides limited time for individuals to pursue lawful immigration options.

5. DHS should preserve the existing rule rather than eliminate it.

The 60-day grace period promotes orderly immigration compliance, supports lawful transitions between employers, and reduces unnecessary disruption to American businesses and communities.

If DHS believes the current system creates administrative challenges, it should consider improving documentation requirements and adjudication procedures rather than eliminating the grace period itself.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and retain the existing protections under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.commentText: I oppose the proposed elimination of the up-to-60-day discretionary grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). The grace period is already narrow, discretionary, limited to once per validity period, and does not confer work authorization; USCIS retains authority to shorten or deny it in individual cases. Determining its applicability is ordinarily straightforward (the day after the last day of paid employment), and removing it is likely to increase, not decrease, agency workload through more emergency change-of-status filings, consular processing, and status-violation adjudications. More importantly, the proposal undermines the job-portability goals Congress advanced in the American Competitiveness in the 21st Century Act and that the 2016 final rule sought to implement. Corporate hiring timelines—interviews, offer negotiation, LCA certification, and petition preparation—routinely exceed zero days. Forcing workers and their families out of status the day after a layoff (often for reasons beyond their control) creates unnecessary hardship, reduces labor-market flexibility for U.S. employers, and ignores nearly a decade of reliance interests built around the existing rule. DHS has not demonstrated meaningful fraud or abuse uniquely enabled by the current provision. The proposal should be withdrawn.

comments.commentText:
To those supporting this proposal because of fraud: how much fraud is actually caused by the 60-day grace period? How much happens because these 60 days are available, and would not happen without them? If you have data showing that connection, please share it. You cannot simply point to fraud somewhere in the program and assume that taking these 60 days away from everyone will fix it.

Now weigh that against what you are asking families who follow the rules to go through. Do you honestly expect someone who gets laid off to pack up their family and leave the country the next day? Their children still have school. Their spouse may be receiving medical treatment. Even if they fully intend to leave, they need time to arrange it. What measurable reduction in fraud justifies putting them through that? These are real people losing their jobs, not people caught doing something wrong. Is giving them a little time to leave with dignity really too much to ask?

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: A Human Appeal to Preserve the H-1B 60-Day Grace Period

I am writing as an H-1B employee to respectfully request that the Department of Homeland Security reconsider its proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period.

I wish that policymakers could see this issue through the eyes of the families who would be affected, rather than looking at it only as an immigration regulation.

For many of us, the United States is where we have built our lives. We came here to work, grow professionally, contribute to the economy, and create a better future for our families. We have spent years paying taxes, buying homes, raising children, supporting local businesses, and becoming part of our communities.

Our children go to school here. They have friends, teachers, routines, and dreams. Some families are preparing to welcome a new baby. Some are going through pregnancy, medical treatments, or ongoing healthcare needs. Others have mortgages, car payments, and responsibilities that cannot be abandoned overnight.

Now imagine a family receiving unexpected news that their employment has ended due to a corporate layoff. Within an extremely short period, they may have to worry not only about finding another job but also about their children’s future, medical care, housing, finances, and potentially leaving the country they have called home for years.

Layoffs are happening across industries, and they are often beyond an employee’s control. Losing a job should not suddenly erase years of contributions or make an entire family’s life uncertain overnight.

We understand that immigration comes with rules and responsibilities. We are not asking for unlimited time or permission to work without authorization. We are simply asking to retain a reasonable transition period that allows families to find another sponsoring employer or make responsible arrangements if they must leave.

Please remember that behind every H-1B petition is a person, and behind that person may be a spouse, children, an expecting mother, or someone receiving essential medical care. These are real families, not just immigration case numbers.

The 60-day grace period offers a small but meaningful amount of security during one of life’s most difficult and unexpected situations. Removing it could create hardship far beyond the individual employee.

I respectfully ask DHS to preserve this protection and consider the human consequences of eliminating it.

We have invested our time, skills, hard work, and lives in contributing to this country. All we ask is to be treated with dignity and given a reasonable opportunity to navigate circumstances that are often beyond our control.

Thank you for listening to the voices of H-1B workers and their families.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly requests DHS to preserve the 60-day grace period and highlights the negative impact on families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Serena Liang
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders.

The 60-day grace period is an essential protection that allows highly skilled foreign workers to navigate unexpected employment changes, including layoffs, company restructuring, and other circumstances beyond their control. Eliminating this protection would create unnecessary uncertainty and hardship for thousands of workers and their families who have built their lives in the United States.

Losing a job should not automatically put someone’s entire immigration status, career, and family stability at risk. Finding a new employer, completing interviews, negotiating offers, and transferring H-1B sponsorship takes time. Even highly qualified professionals may need several weeks to secure another position, particularly during economic downturns when layoffs are widespread.

Furthermore, eliminating the grace period would hurt American employers by making it more difficult to recruit and retain international talent. It would discourage skilled professionals from coming to or remaining in the United States, ultimately undermining the country’s competitiveness in the global economy.

The existing 60-day grace period does not authorize individuals to work without proper authorization. It simply provides a reasonable transition period to find new employment, change immigration status, or make necessary arrangements to leave the country.

I urge DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period. It is a reasonable, humane, and practical safeguard that balances immigration enforcement with the realities of the modern workforce. Please do not take away this essential protection from hardworking individuals and their families.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing hardship and instability for workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Aakash Hongal
comments.commentText:
To: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I oppose eliminating the up to 60-day grace period in 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I ask DHS to retain it.

I have lived in the United States for many years, own a home, and am a parent. If I unexpectedly lost my job, I would need time to assess lawful immigration options while caring for my family. If departure became necessary, I would need to arrange housing, a vehicle, belongings, finances, and travel. Families with children in school face further disruption. Requiring departure immediately upon job loss gives families no practical opportunity to make those arrangements responsibly.

The grace period also serves U.S. employers. DHS’s Table 3 reports that in FY2025, a new employer filed a Form I-129 petition for 5,178 workers within 60 days of withdrawal of a prior approved petition. Another 2,733 workers filed Form I-539 to seek an extension or change of status. DHS estimates an annual average of 3,795 new employer petitions in this window across FY2021–FY2025; it says approximately 99.2% of that group were H‑1B workers. For the FY2025 H‑1B workers who obtained a new petition in the window, DHS reports a median offered annual wage of $131,000.

I understand that petition withdrawals are an imperfect proxy: these numbers do not prove that every worker needed all 60 days or that every job offer would be lost under the proposal. They do establish that thousands of workers and prospective employers take action during the period DHS proposes to remove. DHS should estimate how many of those transitions would instead require departure and reentry, be delayed, or fail to occur.

The proposal assumes employers may fill positions with equally qualified U.S. workers, sponsor another worker, or reassign the work. It also acknowledges that employers may lose productivity. How many additional U.S. workers does DHS estimate would actually be hired because this grace period is eliminated? How does that estimate compare with lost productivity, delayed hiring, and the costs of departure and possible reentry? The rule should not treat a possible replacement hire as an established benefit without measuring it.

DHS also acknowledges that affected families may have purchased homes, paid taxes, and invested in their communities. Yet it says it cannot reliably estimate affected dependents and concludes that the rule would not negatively affect family well-being. I ask DHS to reconsider that conclusion and assess the effects of immediate departure on spouses, children, housing, and employers of working dependents.

Finally, DHS cites administrative burden but says it cannot estimate the time that grace-period analysis adds to each adjudication. Before eliminating a longstanding period that allows lawful job transitions or orderly departure, DHS should quantify the expected savings and compare them with these costs. The current period is limited to up to 60 days, does not itself authorize continued work, and may already be shortened or eliminated by DHS in an individual case.

Please retain the up to 60-day grace period.

References: 91 Fed. Reg. 57807 (Sept. 11, 2026), Sections IV.C–D and V.A, Table 3 and Family Assessment; 81 Fed. Reg. 82398 (Nov. 18, 2016), discussion of the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the grace period and asks DHS to retain it.

comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Beyond its impact on individual workers, this proposal overlooks the broader consequences for families, employers, and communities that have made long-term commitments based on the existing regulation.

The consequences of job loss extend far beyond the primary visa holder. Spouses and children in dependent status may be forced to leave the United States immediately, disrupting children's education, family stability, housing arrangements, and spouses' professional lives. It is unreasonable to impose such widespread consequences on entire families because of an employment change that may be entirely outside the worker's control.

The 60-day grace period has been part of the immigration regulatory framework since 2016. Over nearly a decade, workers, employers, and families have made significant professional, financial, and personal commitments based on this established policy. DHS itself acknowledges that affected individuals may have purchased homes, paid taxes, and invested in their local communities in reliance on their ability to remain in the United States. Eliminating this protection would undermine reasonable expectations and create significant uncertainty for people who have built their lives around existing regulations.
Foreign professionals contribute to the U.S. economy through income taxes, consumer spending, specialized expertise, and years of professional experience. Forcing them to depart immediately following job termination could result in the loss of valuable talent, reduced consumer spending, and disruption to businesses that have invested in their training and development. The proposal also risks shifting administrative costs rather than eliminating them, as DHS acknowledges that it may increase referrals to immigration courts and create additional workloads for DOJ and ICE.

I urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and retain the discretionary 60-day grace period. Immigration regulations should account not only for statutory requirements but also for the substantial reliance interests, family consequences, and economic contributions of affected individuals. A limited transition period is a reasonable safeguard that benefits workers, employers, families, and the broader U.S. community.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (91 FR 57807)

I am writing in strong opposition to this proposed rule as someone whose lawful status in the United States depends directly on it. I am in E-3 status in Washington. I have lived in the United States for 1 year. I work in Geotechnical Engineering.

I want to address the administrative burden rationale directly, because the rule appears to produce the opposite of what DHS predicts. Today a worker whose job ends is covered by a grace period that requires no application and no adjudication. Under this proposal, remaining lawfully requires a filing: Form I-129 from a new employer, or Form I-539 from the worker to change to another status, and a separate Form I-539 from every dependent whose status falls with theirs. DHS's own figures describe roughly 65,752 affected workers a year and more than 208,000 dependents. Form I-539 receipts already exceed 400,000 annually, with published processing times averaging nine to twelve months and backlogs reaching eighteen at some service centers, and since the Edakunni settlement expired on January 18, 2025, USCIS is no longer obliged to adjudicate dependent applications alongside the principal's petition. Adding tens of thousands of filings a year to that queue is not a reduction in agency workload, and the proposal neither estimates the increase nor explains why it is outweighed.

DHS characterizes this as restoring a prior policy, but that framing skips the most important question: what has been built in the years since. Nearly a decade of workers, employers, landlords and schools have arranged their affairs around a predictable 60-day window. Those reliance interests are legally relevant, and the proposal neither identifies nor weighs them. DHS should address this before it goes any further.

DHS estimates that an average of 65,752 workers covered by this grace period lost a job or changed employers each year between 2021 and 2025, and that more than 208,000 dependents hold status tied to those workers. Having established a population that large, the agency then assessed the impact only qualitatively. That is not an adequate basis for a rule of this consequence. DHS should quantify the costs it is imposing: lost wages, broken leases and mortgages, relocation costs, forgone tax revenue, and the cost to employers of vacancies they cannot fill. It should then weigh those against the benefit, which it has described only as reduced administrative burden and has not quantified at all.

To put a concrete case behind that, here is my own situation:

I moved here in September 2025. If I were laid off on Monday, it would be devastating to be considered an illegal immigrant by Wednesday. I simply do not have the ability to leave the country within 24 hours.

Even though I do not have a spouse or children, there are numerous logistical challenges that cannot be resolved in a single day. These include selling my car, terminating my lease, finding a replacement tenant, saying goodbye to friends, organizing a farewell gathering, closing bank accounts, and transferring or liquidating investment accounts.

I cannot imagine how much more difficult this would be for visa holders who have spouses and children and would be expected to leave almost immediately.

The proposed change is not only inhumane, but also counterproductive. By creating an unrealistic timeline for compliance, it could encourage people to remain in the country out of necessity rather than depart through lawful channels, which appears contrary to the stated goals of DHS.

I urge DHS not to finalize this rule and to retain the existing grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). The record as it stands does not support the change: the benefits are asserted rather than measured, the costs fall on tens of thousands of families a year, and less drastic alternatives have not been addressed. Thank you for taking this comment into account.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they are in strong opposition to the proposed rule eliminating the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Mike Spencer
comments.commentText:
Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364-0001 / RIN 1615-AD22)

To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B and other employment-based nonimmigrant visa holders following the termination of their employment.
Since its implementation, the 60-day grace period has served as a vital lifeline and a matter of basic human dignity for high-skilled foreign professionals in the United States. Eliminating this buffer period will introduce extreme, undue hardship for legal immigrants and systematically destabilize the American talent pipeline.

The current 60-day grace period is a critical mechanism for the following reasons:
1. Mitigation of Sudden Financial and Personal Hardship
Job loss is inherently stressful, but for an H-1B worker, it immediately threatens their entire life in the United States. Forcing highly skilled professionals—many of whom have established families, bought homes, and enrolled children in American schools—to abruptly depart the country without any transition window is inhumane. The 60-day period provides necessary time to handle personal affairs, pack households, and manage a dignified departure if necessary, rather than facing instant unlawful status.

2. Preservation of Job Portability and Career Continuity
The grace period was originally designed to enhance job portability. It allows terminated workers the necessary time to interview, secure new employment, and have a new sponsoring employer file an H-1B petition. Without this window, an unexpected layoff turns into an immediate immigration crisis, preventing qualified workers from filling other critical vacancies in the U.S. economy.

3. Protection of U.S. Economic Interests and Competitiveness
The United States relies heavily on high-skilled nonimmigrants to fuel innovation in technology, engineering, healthcare, and research. Forcing these individuals out of the country the moment a layoff occurs strips American industries of a readily available talent pool and drives top global professionals to more stable immigrant-welcoming nations like Canada, the UK, or Australia.

4. Administrative Fairness
Unexpected layoffs are completely outside the control of the employee. Punishing legal, tax-paying nonimmigrant workers for business decisions made by their employers undermines the fairness and predictability of the U.S. legal immigration system.

The 60-day grace period is not a loophole; it is a pragmatic, compassionate, and economically sound policy that protects vulnerable workers while keeping top talent within our borders. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal and maintain the 60-day grace period as a valid, permanent rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly expresses strong opposition to the proposed rule to eliminate the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders would create significant hardship for thousands of skilled professionals and their families who have built their lives in the United States.

The 60-day grace period is not simply an employment-related benefit. It provides a critical transition period for families to manage unexpected job losses, search for new employment, transfer immigration sponsorship, and make important decisions about their future.

The impact of eliminating this period goes far beyond the individual H-1B worker.

1. Impact on Children and Their Education

Many H-1B families have children attending high schools, colleges, and universities in the United States. Their education, academic schedules, college admissions, examinations, and graduation plans cannot simply be interrupted overnight.

Imagine a high school student preparing for final examinations or a university student halfway through a semester suddenly being forced to leave the country because a parent lost their job. Such a disruption could affect years of educational progress and the future these children have worked hard to build.

2. Impact on Families and Dependents

H-1B workers often have spouses and children whose immigration status depends on the primary visa holder. An unexpected job loss could put the entire family’s immigration status at risk, creating tremendous uncertainty and emotional stress.

Families should not have to make life-changing decisions within just a few days.

3. Financial and Housing Commitments

These families have established permanent lives in their communities. They have mortgages, rent payments, car loans, insurance, utility bills, school expenses, and other financial obligations.

Many have purchased homes, financed vehicles, and made long-term financial commitments based on their employment and lawful immigration status.

Eliminating the grace period would leave families with little time to manage these responsibilities, potentially resulting in financial losses, disrupted housing arrangements, and significant hardship.

4. Time Needed to Find New Employment

Finding a new employer willing to sponsor an H-1B transfer is not an overnight process. Interviews, background checks, offer negotiations, immigration documentation, and legal processing all take time.

The 60-day grace period provides a reasonable opportunity to secure another job and maintain continuity in lawful immigration status, subject to applicable immigration requirements.

Removing this safeguard could force highly skilled professionals to leave the country even when they have the qualifications, experience, and willingness to continue contributing to the U.S. economy.

5. Impact on the U.S. Economy and Communities

H-1B professionals contribute to American businesses, technology, healthcare, research, education, and many other industries. Their families are also active members of local communities.

Sudden departures can disrupt employers, schools, universities, housing arrangements, and local economies.

Our Request

We respectfully request that policymakers reconsider any proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders.

The grace period is an important safety net that provides families with time, stability, and dignity during an unexpected employment transition.

We understand the importance of immigration compliance and protecting the integrity of the immigration system. However, immigration policies should also consider the real-life consequences for innocent family members, especially children pursuing their education in the United States.

A job loss should not automatically put an entire family’s future, children’s education, home, financial stability, and years of hard work at risk.

Please preserve the 60-day grace period and consider the human impact of such a policy change before making decisions that could affect thousands of families.

Behind every H-1B visa is not just an employee, but often a family, children with dreams, a home, financial responsibilities, and a future they have worked hard to build in America.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that eliminating the 60-day grace period creates hardship and disrupts families and education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Digvijay Kanuri
comments.commentText:
There are economic consequences as well. H-1B professionals are homeowners, taxpayers, consumers, parents, and contributors to local communities. We pay federal, state, and property taxes, support local businesses, purchase homes, and participate in the American economy.

Forcing experienced professionals and their families to leave can mean lost tax revenue, disrupted projects, additional recruitment costs for employers, and reduced spending in local communities. DHS’s own economic analysis recognizes potential wage losses for affected workers, including an estimated loss of approximately $21,877 for some individuals.

I also ask DHS to consider people who have spent years navigating the employment-based green card process.. An approved I-140 does not independently guarantee permanent residence or authorization to remain, but it represents years of professional commitment, employer sponsorship, and compliance with immigration requirements. It is deeply concerning that an unexpected layoff could force someone so far into this process to abandon the life they have built without a meaningful opportunity to continue working.

I understand that H-1B status is employment-based. I am not asking the government to guarantee anyone a job or allow indefinite unemployment. I am asking for a reasonable opportunity to find another employer when circumstances beyond our control result in job loss.

If DHS has concerns about misuse of the grace period, those concerns could be addressed through clearer documentation and eligibility requirements rather than eliminating this protection altogether.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing 60-day grace period.

A job can disappear overnight. A home, a child’s education, years of savings, and a family’s stability cannot simply be packed up and relocated overnight.

We are not just immigration petition numbers. We are parents, spouses, homeowners, taxpayers, colleagues, and members of American communities. We came here to work hard, contribute, and build a future for our families.

Please do not turn an unexpected employment setback into a situation where an entire family loses the home and future they have worked so hard to build.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues for keeping the grace period to allow laid-off workers a reasonable opportunity to find new employment.

If the grace period were eliminated or significantly shortened, a company that needs those skills later might have to recruit another worker from outside the U.S. That can mean additional immigration/legal costs, relocation, onboarding, and training, even though there may already be an experienced worker in the U.S. who can fill the role.

The 60-day period also creates a reasonable opportunity for the labor market to determine someone's value. If an H-1B worker can find another qualifying job during a difficult hiring market, that is evidence that the worker's skills are actually needed by U.S. employers.

So, from my perspective, the grace period isn't simply a benefit for H-1B workers. It gives U.S. companies a chance to retain experienced talent, reduces unnecessary replacement costs, and allows the labor market to make the decision about who remains employed.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Rui Liu
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period"

I am an H-1B software engineer living in California, and I am writing to oppose this proposed rule and ask DHS to withdraw it.

I came to the United States for my master's degree and have worked here legally on H-1B since. My entire life is built here — my job, my apartment lease, my taxes, my community. I have not been laid off, but like every H-1B worker, I know that a layoff can come with a single email on a Friday afternoon. If this rule takes effect, that email would not just end my job. It would end my legal status the next day.

People misunderstand what the 60 days are for. They are not a vacation and not a loophole. A new employer cannot file a transfer petition overnight — the LCA alone takes about a week, and that is after interviews, an offer, and the company's lawyers preparing the filing. Sixty days is already tight for a worker who does everything right and immediately starts looking. And even for someone who decides to leave, 60 days is barely enough to break a lease, sell or ship a household, and book a flight home. Zero days is not a policy; it is chaos imposed on people who followed every rule.

DHS states in the proposal that it did not estimate the costs of this rule. Those costs are real and they fall entirely on compliant workers and their families: lease-termination penalties, forced moves, spouses and children uprooted overnight. If the concern is fraud, fraud is already illegal and already enforceable against the people who commit it. Removing the grace period does not catch a single fraudster — it only removes the bridge that law-abiding workers rely on.

The 60-day grace period is a narrow, reasonable safeguard that has worked since 2017. Please keep it.

Rui Liu
H-1B worker, California

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period." I strongly oppose this rule.

I am a Senior Data Engineer with nearly two decades of experience in financial services. I hold a Master's in Computer Science, which I completed while working full-time. I have lived and worked lawfully in the United States for many years as an H-1B professional. My wife and I own our home in North Carolina, and we have two sons who are U.S. citizens. They were born here, go to school here, and know no other home. I pay federal, state, and property taxes, and I build systems that U.S. financial institutions rely on every day.

I ask DHS to withdraw this rule, for these reasons.

1. It would punish workers for decisions they do not control. Layoffs are made by employers, often across whole teams, with no regard to individual performance. Under this rule, a worker hired because the country needed their skills would be out of status the day after a layoff. That worker would have no chance to find another employer that needs those same skills. A rule that keeps the benefit of a worker's skills but takes away all protection the moment the employer no longer wants them is fundamentally unfair.

2. It would harm U.S. citizen children. My sons are American citizens. If I lost my job and had no grace period, my family would have to leave almost immediately. My children would be pulled out of school in the middle of the year and separated from their friends, their activities, and the only country they have known. DHS should not adopt a rule that so directly harms American children without serious analysis of the impact on them. The proposal gives that impact no meaningful weight.

3. The financial harm is severe and unavoidable. Like many H-1B families, we have built a stable life here, including a mortgage and car loans. With zero days to act, a family cannot sell a house, end a lease, sell vehicles, or close accounts in an orderly way. Families would be forced into distressed sales, defaults, and heavy losses. That harm reaches lenders, neighbors, and local communities too. The proposal itself acknowledges that affected workers may have bought homes and paid taxes in their communities, yet it still concludes the grace period's harms outweigh its benefits. DHS has not justified that conclusion.

4. Sixty days is already too short in this job market. Hiring for senior technical roles often takes two to three months of interviews. After that, the new employer must still prepare and file a petition. Many qualified workers cannot finish this within 60 days even today. Removing the window entirely would make a job change after a layoff nearly impossible. In practice, it would turn every layoff into a removal.

5. DHS's own numbers show how many people would be harmed. DHS estimates that a yearly average of 65,752 workers covered by the grace period experienced a job loss or changed employers between 2021 and 2025. Counting spouses and children, this rule would disrupt well over a hundred thousand people every year. Many of those children are U.S. citizens like mine.

6. The stated justification does not hold up. DHS says it wants to reduce administrative burden. Without a grace period, workers will rush to file change-of-status and visitor applications just to remain lawfully present while they settle their affairs. That would increase USCIS's workload, not reduce it. The grace period is already discretionary, so DHS can deny it in individual cases of abuse. Eliminating it for everyone is not a measured response to any identified problem.

7. It would weaken U.S. competitiveness. Since 2017, the grace period has helped U.S. employers keep skilled workers who are already in the country, already trained, and already contributing. Removing it tells highly skilled professionals that years of lawful work, taxes, and community ties can be erased overnight. That will push talent toward other countries.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and keep the 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). If DHS revises the rule in any way, it should extend the grace period rather than eliminate it, and it should specifically protect families with U.S. citizen children.

comments.commentText:
**Re: Public Comment Opposing Proposed Rule "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period"**
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule that seeks to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers (including H-1B, L-1, O-1, and TN visa holders).
The 60-day grace period is a vital safety net for both high-skilled foreign talent and American employers. Eliminating this grace period creates severe disruptions for several reasons:
1. **Economic & Labor Market Instability:** Sudden job departures or unforeseen layoffs occur in every industry. A 60-day window allows specialized professionals to transfer their skills to new domestic employers without unnecessary disruption, keeping valuable talent within the U.S. economy rather than forcing an immediate departure.
2. **Unrealistic Administrative Deadlines:** Processing immigration paperwork, employer petitions, and background checks inherently takes time. Requiring an immediate change of status or departure upon termination creates an impossible administrative burden for both workers and USCIS adjudicators.
3. **Severe Human Impact:** Foreign workers in nonimmigrant status build lives, lease homes, enroll children in schools, and contribute to local communities. Removing the grace period forces families to uproot their entire lives abruptly without sufficient time to wrap up personal affairs or secure legal alternatives.
Maintaining the discretionary 60-day grace period ensures fairness, supports economic agility, and protects skilled workers from sudden distress. I urge USCIS to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the 60-day grace period.
### Key points to keep in mind before submitting:
* **Personalize it:** Adding 1–2 sentences about your perspective (e.g., as an employer, high-skilled worker, student, or concerned community member) makes federal public comments significantly more impactful.
* **Avoid Personally Identifiable Information (PII):** Do not include sensitive information like your Social Security number, passport number, or address in the comment text itself, as public comments on Regulations.gov become part of the public record.
-Naresh Vadla

Ending it turns a layoff into immediate unlawful presence, a possible 3- or 10-year bar, and a forced exit with no time to end a lease, move a child out of school, or finish a job search. Employers lose trained workers they could have kept, and the US loses talent to other countries. We are writing to express our strong opposition to the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for high-skilled nonimmigrant workers under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
