comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This comment is submitted in opposition to the proposal to eliminate the up to 60-day grace period, and in support of retaining it.

A job loss does not end a life in one day. Many H-1B workers have families in the United States, children in school mid-year, apartment leases, car loans or leases, and other obligations that cannot be unwound overnight. Requiring a worker and dependents to fall out of status the day after employment ends, with an expectation to depart immediately, is inhumane in practice even if framed as a return to prior policy. Sixty days is already a short window to make an orderly decision about a job, a move, or a change of status. Zero days leaves no window at all.

Many H-1B workers chose this path in part because Congress designed H-1B as a dual intent visa. H-1B workers are expressly permitted to work temporarily while also pursuing permanent residence. For many workers, that green card process can take many years because of backlogs. Eliminating the grace period does not formally repeal dual intent, but it undermines it in practice. A single layoff would end status before a worker with a pending or approved immigrant petition can use portability or seek a new sponsor.

That risk is greater now, not smaller. Finding a new H-1B sponsor already takes weeks: an offer, a certified Labor Condition Application, and a new petition filing. With AI disruption, hiring freezes, and a difficult job market, 60 days is already tight. With zero days, portability becomes almost impossible to use, because a new petition must be filed while status is still valid. The result will be forced departures and large, avoidable financial losses for workers who did nothing wrong except lose a job.

Fairness on Social Security should also be considered. H-1B workers pay Social Security and Medicare taxes from the first paycheck, just like U.S. workers. Many workers from countries without a totalization agreement with the United States will never reach the 40 credits needed for a benefit, and those contributions are not refunded if they leave early. Other countries, for example Germany, return the employee share of pension contributions to non-EU workers who leave permanently. If the United States is going to make it harder for temporary workers to stay and complete the path to permanence, the government should at least address the contributions they will never benefit from.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and retain the 60-day grace period. At a minimum, if any change is made, the grace period should be preserved for workers with an approved I-140 or pending adjustment application, and a transition period should be provided for workers already in the United States in reliance on the current rule.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period and argues that removing it harms workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers, including H-1B and O-1 visa holders.

The existing 60-day grace period provides an essential safeguard for skilled workers who have built their careers and lives in the United States while complying with immigration laws.

First, job loss is often beyond an employee's control. Layoffs, reorganizations, and business closures can affect even highly qualified and productive employees. Eliminating the grace period would impose severe immigration consequences on individuals who have done nothing wrong.

Second, the grace period supports the American economy. Hiring skilled workers involves interviews, background checks, immigration paperwork, and government processing. Even highly qualified candidates may need several weeks to secure a new position. Removing this flexibility could force talented professionals to leave the country before American employers have a reasonable opportunity to hire them.

Third, eliminating the grace period would create unnecessary instability for workers and their families. Many nonimmigrant workers have lived in the United States for years, paid taxes, contributed to American businesses, and established deep community ties. A sudden job loss should not immediately jeopardize their ability to remain in the country lawfully while arranging their next steps.

Finally, the grace period helps the United States retain global talent. Skilled immigrants contribute to technological innovation, economic growth, and American competitiveness. Policies that create unnecessary uncertainty may discourage talented professionals from building long-term careers in the United States.

I respectfully urge DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period. Maintaining this limited transition period would provide reasonable flexibility without eliminating the government's authority to enforce immigration requirements.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposal because it can make compliance impossible and does not demonstrate a workable or more efficient enforcement system.

1. The rule can create unavoidable status violations.

Consider an H-1B employee notified at 5 p.m. on a Friday that employment ends immediately. Assume the employee has no independent authorization to remain and no available flight that would permit departure that day. The employee books the earliest available itinerary and departs the next morning. Under Section IV.D and footnote 32, the employee would nevertheless fail to maintain status despite taking the earliest physically available departure.

Diligence cannot create a flight or reverse a cancellation. An alternative destination works only if the person can lawfully enter it and reach it in time. Dependents may face additional travel-document or medical constraints.

DHS should explain exactly how this person can comply. The proposal provides no defined departure window or express protection for documented inability to depart immediately. A rule that can place a willing, previously compliant person in violation before compliance becomes physically possible is not a workable compliance standard. This objection concerns failure to maintain status; it does not assume that every such person immediately accrues unlawful presence.

2. Enforcement discretion cannot substitute for an achievable rule.

If DHS intends to excuse unavoidable delays, it should specify the protection in the regulation, including the applicable deadline, acceptable evidence, and consequences for subsequent benefit applications. A possibility that an officer might decline enforcement does not itself preserve status or resolve eligibility for a later application.

An excessively strict rule can produce widespread, involuntary noncompliance and then leave selective enforcement to determine who suffers the consequences. If ordinary logistical barriers make technical violations routine, enforcement discretion becomes the practical rule. Similarly situated people may face different outcomes based on whether and how their cases attract enforcement attention. This invites arbitrary outcomes and undermines predictability and public confidence in the rule of law.

Officers would also need to assess flight availability, cancellations, medical constraints, and efforts to depart. DHS should explain how it would prevent inconsistent treatment and why creating these new factual inquiries is preferable to preserving a clear compliance window.

3. Employment cessation dates still require verification.

Section IV.C identifies difficulties establishing employment cessation dates. Those dates remain essential under the proposed rule: they determine when a person allegedly failed to maintain status and whether a subsequent filing was timely.

DHS should distinguish work that actually disappears from work that merely moves to status determinations, requests for evidence, denials, or enforcement proceedings. Removing a grace-period calculation does not resolve ambiguous payroll records or disputed termination dates. The agency should provide evidence of net time savings rather than equating the number of potentially reviewed cases with avoidable workload.

4. The enforcement forecast relies on the wrong baseline population.

Section V.A.3.b cites 37 FY2025 Notices to Appear involving H-1B beneficiaries who exceeded the existing grace period. That observation does not establish that eliminating the grace period would cause only a small increase in enforcement cases.

The existing rule allows people to resolve their situation during the intervening 60 days. Removing it exposes a different population, including people who would previously have secured new employment, pursued another eligible status, or departed within that period. DHS should model that newly exposed population and the resulting workload for USCIS, ICE, and immigration courts. Transferring work between agencies is not necessarily an efficiency gain.

5. DHS should retain an administrable path to compliance.

I request withdrawal of the proposal and retention of the existing grace period. If DHS proceeds, it should first evaluate standardized employment-cessation documentation and clearer filing instructions as ways to reduce adjudicative burden.

At a minimum, any replacement must provide a realistic departure period, explicit protection for documented inability to depart, and clear transition provisions. DHS should explain how an unexpectedly terminated worker can actually comply, assess the additional case-by-case inquiries its approach would create, and demonstrate net administrative savings across affected agencies. Predictable status violations caused by impossible timing requirements should not be treated as evidence of an effective immigration system.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the rule makes compliance impossible and harms workers by eliminating necessary departure time.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
USCIS should not adopt an immediate-departure requirement without explaining how people can comply when no same-day departure is available.

Consider an H-1B employee who receives an unexpected termination notice late in the afternoon, effective immediately. The employee has no independent authorization to remain. There are no available flights or other feasible means of leaving the United States that day. The employee immediately books the earliest available flight for the following morning and goes to the airport the next day to leave.

There is no deliberate delay or refusal to comply. The employee simply cannot depart on a flight that does not exist.

Under Section IV.D and footnote 32, however, the employee would fail to maintain status the following day unless another applicable protection intervened. By the time the employee arrives at the airport to take the earliest available flight, the proposed rule would already treat the person as having failed to maintain status.

That creates a troubling possibility: if ICE encounters the employee at the airport, the person could face civil immigration arrest and detention, subject to the applicable legal requirements, while actively attempting to leave. A ticket for the earliest available departure does not itself preserve immigration status or establish immunity from enforcement. DHS should explain what protection would prevent this outcome.

The contradiction is practical and serious. The government would demand immediate departure, provide no time in which departure is physically possible, and potentially subject the person to detention at the very place they must go to leave. Detention could then prevent the departure the rule ostensibly seeks to achieve.

What should this employee have done differently? The worker cannot dictate when an employer announces a termination, require an airline to operate another flight, or assume a right to enter an arbitrary third country. A requirement to leave immediately does not create an available route out of the country.

This is an ordinary scheduling problem, not an exceptional edge case that requires an unlikely chain of disasters. Employment can end without advance notice. International departures operate on schedules. For someone notified after the last feasible departure, even the fastest possible response may require remaining overnight.

The proposal's exception for people otherwise authorized to remain does not answer this concern. Eligibility for another immigration benefit is not universal. A person receiving an unexpected termination notice may have only hours to obtain advice, establish eligibility, collect documents, and prepare an appropriate filing. DHS should identify a concrete protection that applies to this example, rather than assume that another immigration option will always be available in time.

Nor would an assurance that officers may exercise discretion adequately resolve the problem. A decision not to arrest someone does not itself establish that the person maintained status. The same interruption could matter in a subsequent immigration application. DHS should explain both the immediate enforcement consequences and the potential consequences for future benefit eligibility.

An excessively strict deadline can make involuntary noncompliance routine and leave selective enforcement to determine who bears the consequences. Two workers who receive identical notice and book the earliest available flights could face different outcomes depending on whether they encounter immigration officers. That uncertainty is created by the rule's design, not by a difference in their willingness to comply.

If DHS intends to protect people who depart at the earliest reasonable opportunity, that protection should appear in the regulation. It should specify how status is treated during the departure interval and what evidence establishes compliance. People should not have to rely on an officer overlooking a violation that the regulation makes unavoidable.

Individualized judgments about travel logistics also create administrative costs. Officers may need to reconstruct flight availability, booking times, airport access, and alternative routes. Arrest, detention, and removal proceedings would consume additional resources where they occur. DHS should assess those costs before asserting that elimination will simplify administration.

I request that DHS retain the existing 60-day grace period. If it proceeds with a replacement, it must provide a realistic departure window and a clear regulatory safeguard for people making timely, good-faith efforts to leave.

Someone who books the earliest available flight and arrives at the airport to take it should have a clear path to compliance, not an avoidable exposure to arrest and detention. DHS should resolve this foreseeable consequence before finalizing the proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the rule is impractical and harms workers by removing the grace period without feasible departure options.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to this proposed rule, as a skilled foreign worker, I believe that removing 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) would inflict severe harm on American innovation, impose undue burdens on U.S. employers, and unnecessarily jeopardize the legal status of highly skilled foreign professionals.
I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule based on the following critical points:
1. Severe Harm to U.S. Businesses and Economic Competitiveness
The existing 60-day grace period provides U.S. employers with the vital flexibility needed to recruit experienced, high-skilled international talent already in the country. If an employee is laid off, the 60-day window allows other U.S. companies to conduct thorough hiring processes and submit H-1B transfer petitions. Eliminating this period will create artificial labor market friction, forcing qualified workers out of the country before U.S. companies can onboard them, ultimately weakening American economic competitiveness.
2. Unreasonable Administrative and Personal Disruption
The job search, interview, background check, and USCIS petition preparation processes inherently take several weeks. Expecting nonimmigrant workers—who have legally lived, paid taxes, and contributed to their local U.S. communities—to wrap up their entire personal and professional lives immediately upon cessation of employment is inhumane and impractical. It disrupts housing leases, children's schooling, financial obligations, and ongoing medical care.
3. Increased Burden on USCIS and U.S. Immigration System
The grace period actually reduces administrative overhead by giving workers an orderly, standardized mechanism to either secure new employment, change status (such as to B-1/B-2), or prepare for a timely departure. Removing the 60-day grace period will lead to a spike in emergency change-of-status filings, litigations, and chaotic compliance issues, creating more paperwork and backlogs for USCIS.
4. Disincentivizing Global Top Talent from Choosing the United States
Global talent has options. Providing zero flexibility during involuntary job loss projects instability and hostility toward foreign scholars, engineers, researchers, and specialists. Top STEM talent may choose other nations with more predictable and compassionate immigration frameworks, leading to a permanent "brain drain" from the U.S. tech and research sectors.
Conclusion
The 60-day grace period introduced in 2017 was a practical, sensible, and humane legal policy that benefits both U.S. industry and legal visa holders. Removing it does not solve any legitimate administrative burden, but rather creates instability and unnecessary hardship.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

Losing a job is already one of the most stressful experiences a person can face. For foreign professionals legally working in the United States, that stress is compounded by immigration restrictions that directly tie their ability to remain in the country to their employment. The current 60-day grace period provides a reasonable and necessary buffer for people who unexpectedly lose their jobs through no fault of their own. Removing this protection would turn an ordinary employment setback into a potentially life-altering immigration crisis.

The modern American labor market is unpredictable. Even highly qualified and productive employees can be laid off because of corporate restructuring, budget reductions, mergers, or shifting business priorities. These events are often entirely outside an employee's control. It is fundamentally unreasonable to expect someone who has followed immigration laws, worked legally, and contributed to the American economy to immediately face the possibility of leaving the country simply because their employer eliminated their position.

Finding another job is not an instantaneous process. American companies routinely require multiple rounds of interviews, background checks, internal approvals, and immigration paperwork before onboarding a new employee. Even a highly qualified candidate may need several weeks or months to secure a new position. Eliminating the grace period would create a serious mismatch between the realities of American hiring practices and the immigration system's expectations.

This proposal would also harm American employers. Companies invest significant resources in recruiting and training skilled professionals, and many depend on the ability to hire experienced workers already residing in the United States. Making employment transitions unnecessarily difficult would shrink the available talent pool, increase hiring costs, and make it harder for American businesses to compete internationally. The United States should be encouraging talented professionals to contribute to its economy, not creating additional barriers that push them toward other countries.

I am also concerned that removing the grace period would give employers disproportionate power over foreign workers. When losing a job can immediately threaten someone's immigration status and family stability, workers become more vulnerable to exploitation and less willing to report unfair treatment or seek better opportunities. A healthy labor market depends on reasonable worker mobility, and immigration policy should not create unnecessary conditions of dependency.

Beyond employment, this proposal overlooks the lives and families that foreign professionals have built in the United States. Many have lived here for years, paid taxes, purchased homes, established community relationships, and made long-term financial commitments. Their spouses may also have careers, and their children may attend American schools. Forcing these families into immediate uncertainty after a layoff would impose significant emotional and financial burdens while providing little apparent benefit to the broader public.

The existing 60-day grace period is already limited and conditional. It does not provide indefinite immigration status, unrestricted employment authorization, or an exemption from immigration laws. It simply recognizes that people need a reasonable amount of time to manage an unexpected transition. Preserving this modest protection is entirely consistent with maintaining a lawful and orderly immigration system.

Administrative efficiency is a legitimate policy goal, but it should not come at the expense of fairness, economic competitiveness, and the stability of law-abiding families. If DHS believes the existing system creates administrative challenges, it should address those challenges through clearer guidance and more efficient processing rather than eliminating the grace period altogether.

The United States has long benefited from attracting ambitious, highly educated, and hardworking people from around the world. Policies that introduce unnecessary insecurity for legally employed professionals risk undermining that advantage. A country that wants to remain a global leader in innovation should recognize that skilled workers are human beings with families, responsibilities, and lives extending well beyond their employment contracts.

I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to withdraw this proposed rule and retain the existing 60-day grace period. Doing so would support American employers, protect reasonable expectations for lawful workers and their families, and preserve a more practical and competitive immigration system.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, arguing it creates an unfair immigration crisis.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To USCIS:
Docket USCIS-2026-0364

I oppose eliminating the 60-day grace period because weakening H-1B workers' bargaining power could also harm American workers' wages and employment opportunities.

The effect begins before anyone loses a job. When termination can require immediate departure, negotiating pay or challenging unreasonable conditions becomes substantially riskier. Workers may accept lower compensation, forgo raises, or tolerate unfavorable treatment to avoid abruptly disrupting their lives and families. The ability to search for another job while employed does not protect against an unexpected termination before a new petition is filed.

This vulnerability can distort competition with American workers. Some employers may find an employee's dependence on continued sponsorship attractive because it reduces pressure to raise wages or improve conditions. American applicants could then compete against workers whose willingness to accept an offer reflects immigration-related pressure rather than the job's market value. Making foreign workers easier to pressure does not necessarily make Americans easier to hire.

Existing wage requirements do not eliminate this concern. Under 20 CFR 655.731, employers generally must pay the higher of the applicable prevailing wage or the actual wage for similarly employed workers. However, meeting that requirement does not establish that compensation matches what a worker could negotiate in a more competitive market. Reduced bargaining power can suppress compensation above the required wage and weaken pressure for workplace-wide increases.

The proposal could also discourage reporting of wage violations. Legal protection against retaliation is less effective when workers fear that losing their jobs could immediately jeopardize their ability to remain in the country. Employers violating labor standards could gain an advantage over compliant employers, harming both immigrant and American workers. DHS itself recognized the grace period's relevance to workers facing retaliation in its 2016 final rule, 81 FR 82398, 82454.

The net labor-market effect requires analysis. Departures could reduce labor supply, but greater employer leverage over workers who remain could weaken wage competition. DHS should examine both effects rather than assume that reduced protection for foreign workers benefits Americans.

I request retention of the 60-day grace period and a joint assessment with the Department of Labor of the proposal's effects on bargaining power, wages, retaliation reporting, and American workers' hiring opportunities. Immigration rules should encourage employers to compete through better compensation and conditions, not through greater control over workers who fear immediate departure.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the grace period due to negative impacts on worker bargaining power.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed removal of 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and urge DHS to withdraw this rule.

The fundamental problem with this proposal is that it punishes lawful workers for circumstances beyond their control. Layoffs, corporate restructuring, and business closures can affect even highly qualified employees. Eliminating the 60-day grace period would leave affected nonimmigrant workers and their dependents facing immediate immigration uncertainty, potentially jeopardizing their ability to maintain status, change employers, or pursue other lawful options. Losing a job should not automatically become an immigration crisis.

The proposal would also undermine the practical effectiveness of H-1B portability. Although eligible H-1B workers may begin new employment upon the proper filing of a qualifying petition, finding a new employer, completing interviews, obtaining an offer, and preparing immigration paperwork takes time. The grace period provides a reasonable opportunity to complete these steps. Removing it would create unnecessary barriers to employment transitions and deprive American businesses of experienced workers already living in the United States.

The economic consequences extend beyond individual workers. The United States competes globally for engineers, scientists, researchers, and entrepreneurs. Increasing immigration uncertainty following involuntary job loss would make the country less attractive to international talent, increase recruitment costs, and weaken American innovation. It could also give employers disproportionate leverage over foreign workers, discouraging legitimate job mobility and potentially making workers more vulnerable to exploitation.

The proposal also fails to adequately account for established reliance interests. For nearly a decade, workers and families have made major life decisions under the existing framework, including purchasing homes, raising children, and building careers. In DHS v. Regents of the University of California (2020) and Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm (1983), the Supreme Court emphasized the importance of reasoned agency decision-making, including appropriate consideration of reliance interests and alternatives. DHS should meaningfully evaluate these consequences before reversing an established policy.

Administrative efficiency alone does not justify eliminating this protection. Removing the grace period could simply shift administrative burdens toward additional change-of-status filings, status disputes, enforcement proceedings, and litigation. DHS should evaluate these downstream costs alongside the potential financial and operational harm to American employers and families.

Less disruptive alternatives exist. DHS could retain the current grace period while improving documentation requirements, clarifying eligibility standards, or implementing targeted safeguards against misuse. Although the proposal discusses alternatives, it does not adequately establish why these narrower approaches would be insufficient.

The 60-day grace period is limited, conditional, and consistent with lawful immigration enforcement. It provides neither indefinite residence nor unrestricted employment authorization. Instead, it offers a practical transition mechanism that benefits workers, families, and American businesses.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and preserve the existing 60-day grace period. Maintaining this protection would better support fairness, economic competitiveness, and a stable, predictable immigration system.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that removing the grace period creates unfair immigration crises for laid-off workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose eliminating the 60-day grace period because it could undermine American workers' wages and employment opportunities.

Requiring immediate departure after job loss would give employers greater leverage over H-1B workers. Americans should not have to compete against workers pressured to accept worse terms by the threat of having to leave the country.

I recognize that this proposal could reduce the number of H-1B workers in the United States. Some would leave after losing employment, and others might decide against working here. That could reduce competition for some positions and potentially create opportunities for American workers.

But the number of H-1B workers is only part of the equation. The workers who remain could become substantially more dependent on their employers and more willing to accept lower compensation than they could otherwise negotiate. A smaller workforce with much weaker bargaining power could still put significant pressure on American wages and hiring opportunities. Those effects could offset, or potentially outweigh, the benefits Americans receive from reduced labor supply. DHS should investigate that possibility rather than assume that fewer H-1B workers necessarily means better outcomes for Americans.

A hiring manager could see an advantage in employing someone who has more to lose by challenging management or walking away. That advantage would have nothing to do with qualifications or productivity. It would come from having less bargaining power.

Americans cannot compete on that basis, and public policy should not encourage employers to value it. If a company can retain workers without offering competitive raises because leaving is unusually risky, other employees lose some of the pressure that would otherwise push compensation upward. An American applicant seeking better pay may also become less attractive relative to an applicant under greater pressure to accept the employer's terms.

The legal wage requirement does not settle the issue. Employers must generally pay H-1B workers the higher of the applicable prevailing wage or the actual wage for similarly employed workers. But Americans benefit from competition that pushes pay above required levels. A wage floor is not a substitute for employees having a credible ability to reject an offer or leave.

The relevant question is whether this proposal improves American workers' actual wages and employment prospects, after accounting for both departures and increased employer leverage over those who remain. Counting departures alone cannot answer that question.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the 60-day grace period. Any reconsideration should include a credible assessment with the Department of Labor of these risks to American workers. Employers should win employees by offering a better job, not because immigration rules make those employees harder to lose.

comments.commentText:
Please withdraw this proposal. Its discussion of family impacts leaves out a distinction that matters enormously in ordinary life: losing a job is one disruption; being required to immediately uproot a household is another.

Imagine a parent who loses a job but finds another qualifying position several weeks later. With the existing grace period, the family may be able to remain at home while the parent completes the necessary employment transition. The children can continue attending school, and the household can avoid an international move.

Now consider the same family experiencing the same layoff under the proposed rule, without another basis to remain. They may have to leave first, interrupt their arrangements, and then attempt to return. The job loss is identical. The additional disruption comes from changing the rule.

Section V.F largely attributes financial harm to unemployment and the obligation to depart. That does not explain away the difference between these two outcomes. DHS should ask what the family loses because the grace period disappears, beyond what it would already have lost because of the layoff.

Even a family that ultimately leaves benefits from time to organize its departure. Giving notice on housing, obtaining school records, arranging transportation, and coordinating medical care all take time. Doing those things in an orderly way can cost less than doing them under immediate pressure. The fact that a move might eventually occur does not make its timing irrelevant.

There is also a question of reasonable expectations. Families do not need to believe that a policy will last forever to make decisions around the rules currently in place. A conditional grace period is still a meaningful part of that framework. Its discretionary nature does not make every decision made in reliance on its availability unreasonable.

DHS can reconsider policy. But it should explain how it has weighed those existing commitments and whether a transition could prevent unnecessary harm. The Supreme Court's decision in DHS v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), underscores the importance of assessing serious reliance interests when changing policy; it does not require that every existing policy remain permanent.

The agency should clearly explain what would happen to people already in a grace period, pending applications, and arrangements begun under the current rules. This is a request for clear transition provisions, not an assumption that the proposal would operate retroactively.

I ask DHS to retain the grace period. At minimum, it should reassess family impacts against the actual alternative of keeping the existing rule and meaningfully evaluate transition protections.

A layoff does not make every subsequent loss inevitable. When a regulatory change adds disruption that a family could otherwise avoid, that additional harm deserves to be counted and explained.

I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

As a software engineer working in the United States, I believe this proposal would significantly harm American innovation, economic competitiveness, and the ability of U.S. companies to attract and retain highly skilled talent.

First, eliminating the grace period would give employers disproportionate power over foreign workers. Without a reasonable transition period, losing a job could immediately jeopardize a worker’s immigration status. This creates an unhealthy imbalance of power, potentially discouraging workers from reporting workplace misconduct, negotiating fair compensation, or leaving exploitative employment situations. A policy that makes workers excessively dependent on individual employers is harmful to the broader American labor market.

Second, the proposal would undermine America’s competitiveness in attracting global talent. Highly skilled immigrants contribute to American technological leadership, entrepreneurship, and economic growth. These professionals often invest years building their careers and lives in the United States. Requiring them to leave immediately after an unexpected layoff would introduce unnecessary uncertainty and make competing countries more attractive destinations for global talent. At a time when the United States faces intense international competition in artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies, driving away experienced professionals would be counterproductive.

Third, job loss is not always a reflection of individual performance or qualifications. Having worked in the U.S. technology industry, I have witnessed how layoffs can affect talented and hardworking professionals through no fault of their own. Immigration policy should not turn an ordinary employment transition into an immediate personal and family crisis.

Even highly capable employees can be affected by corporate restructuring, economic downturns, or mass layoffs. Punishing workers with immediate immigration consequences for circumstances outside their control is neither reasonable nor economically productive. Sixty days is already a relatively short period to find a new employer, complete interviews, and coordinate immigration filings.

Fourth, eliminating the grace period would impose substantial costs on workers, families, and businesses without demonstrating corresponding public benefits. Workers may have housing leases, financial obligations, and family members whose lives would be abruptly disrupted. Employers seeking to hire displaced workers would also face unnecessary immigration and recruitment obstacles. The proposal should not proceed without a rigorous assessment of these economic and social costs.

Finally, the existing 60-day grace period is not an unlimited immigration benefit. It is a narrowly defined, temporary transition mechanism that supports lawful compliance with immigration requirements while allowing workers and employers to manage unexpected employment changes responsibly.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the existing 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Maintaining this reasonable safeguard would better serve American workers, businesses, economic competitiveness, and the integrity of the immigration system.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services
Docket USCIS-2026-0364

I oppose finalizing the proposal without correcting the population estimate used in its impact analysis. The principal concerns are coverage, timing, and the unsupported characterization of an estimate as an upper bound.

1. The upper-bound claim is not established.

Section V.A.3.a characterizes 3,795 people annually as an upper-bound estimate of the population potentially incurring the relevant costs. Footnote 49 acknowledges that the underlying withdrawal data do not capture all potential grace-period users.

Possible overcounting elsewhere does not establish that omissions are offset. Without estimating the direction and magnitude of these errors, DHS cannot demonstrate that the figure is conservative. It should either substantiate the bound or label the figure as a proxy with unresolved uncertainty.

2. The measurement window requires validation.

Employment cessation, submission of a withdrawal, and recorded revocation are distinct events. DHS should identify the date used to anchor its 60-day window and validate it against actual employment cessation.

For illustration, a worker could lose employment on day 0, have a new petition filed on day 20, and have the former employer submit a withdrawal on day 40. A query limited to petitions filed after withdrawal could omit this genuine period between jobs. The frequency of such cases requires investigation; it cannot be assumed to be zero.

3. The cost-bearing population needs a precise definition.

Workers obtaining a new employer's petition are not the only people potentially affected. Individuals arranging departure, pursuing other eligible immigration options, and dependent family members may also incur incremental costs.

DHS should define separate populations, account for overlap, and clarify whether 3,795 is intended to bound a narrow subgroup or the broader affected population. Those are materially different claims.

4. Uncertainty must carry through to the conclusions.

The analysis should test plausible assumptions about missing records, reporting delays, and household effects. Where reliable probabilities are unavailable, transparent scenarios would still show whether the conclusions depend on optimistic assumptions.

Requested revisions:

- Publish the relevant population definitions, date fields, and matching criteria.
- Validate the method against a sample of case files.
- Estimate or bound coverage and timing errors.
- Present sensitivity analyses for the resulting costs.
- Provide an opportunity for public comment on materially revised analysis.

I request retention of the existing grace period while these deficiencies are addressed. Perfect data are not required, but the strength of the conclusion must match the strength of the evidence. An incomplete administrative dataset does not, by itself, establish an upper bound.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule and ask DHS to withdraw it.

I am an H-1B worker who has lived and worked lawfully in the United States for more than 8 years. I work as a Software Engineer in New Hampshire. My employer has filed an immigrant petition (Form I-140) on my behalf, which has been approved. However, because of the green card backlog, I remain in a long-term waiting pattern and expect to wait more than 10 years before being able to complete my permanent residency process.

I live with my spouse, who is on a dependent visa, and we rent our home under a residential lease agreement. If I were laid off on a Friday, this rule would make my whole household out of status by Saturday. We could not terminate our lease, settle our financial affairs including incurring approximately $6,000 in lease-break penalties or find a new job in one day. In my field, it typically takes six weeks to find a new employer, complete interviews, fulfill other formalities, and transfer H-1B. Under this proposed rule, I would have had zero days.

Why the Rule Should Be Reconsidered and Withdrawn:
1. The rule undermines Congressional intent for worker mobility under H-1B portability (INA § 214(n)) and green card flexibility (INA § 204(j)). Without the 60-day grace period, workers risk immediately falling out of status. In my field, securing a new offer, obtaining LCA certification, and filing an H-1B petition takes roughly 6 weeks under ideal conditions leaving zero room for delay.

2. DHS improperly dismisses the removal of the 60-day grace period reference in 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i) as a mere "technical revision," ignoring its real-world impact. Currently, workers with approved I-140 petitions can apply for a compelling circumstances EAD during the grace period. Facing a total backlog of over 10 years myself, an abrupt job loss without a grace period would prevent me from paying rent and leave me without enough time to manage moving and relocation. DHS must retain this regulatory protection to prevent severe hardship for backlogged workers.

3. DHS fails to adequately weigh the substantial reliance interests built over nearly a decade. Since 2017, workers and employers have relied on the 60-day grace period to make critical life decisions. Having lived in the U.S. for years under this framework, I have made long-term financial and personal commitments including a housing lease, household establishment, and active credit lines with the expectation of this safety net. Labeling the protection as "discretionary" does not excuse DHS from ignoring the severe financial and personal disruption caused by eliminating it.

4. Eliminating the grace period turns minor administrative uncertainties into major status violations. Because the legal end date of employment is often unclear due to advance notice periods, severance pay, administrative delays, or furloughs removing the 60-day buffer leaves workers vulnerable to accidental out-of-status determinations

5. DHS improperly dismisses significant economic impacts merely because they are difficult to quantify. In reality, eliminating the 60-day grace period creates severe financial burdens on families and businesses. In my case, an abrupt forced departure would result in immediate emergency moving, travel, and relocation costs exceeding $10,000, on top of lost wages and broken lease obligations. DHS should fully evaluate these real financial harms before eliminating a longstanding protection.

6. DHS fails to justify why its legal interpretation suddenly requires eliminating a reasonable transition period after maintaining it for nearly a decade. The fact that nonimmigrant status is tied to employment does not strip DHS of its authority to grant a reasonable wind-down window when job loss occurs unexpectedly. DHS adopted this rule in 2016 to foster worker mobility, family stability, and employer retention; it must fully explain why those statutory objectives are no longer valid today.

7. Eliminating the grace period is an overreaction to a manageable administrative issue. Instead of abolishing an essential protection, DHS could easily streamline review by updating Forms I-129 and I-539 to require self-reporting of grace period reliance, or by making the 60-day period automatic. DHS must evaluate these practical alternatives before taking away a vital safety net for workers.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues against removing the grace period because it harms workers and families facing layoffs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I believe one of the fundamental goals of U.S. immigration policy should be to strengthen American businesses, attract highly skilled professionals, and maintain the country's global leadership in innovation and technology.

The United States has built a world-class education and research ecosystem that attracts talented individuals from around the world. Many of these professionals complete master's and Ph.D. programs at American universities, contribute to research and technological development, pay taxes, and build their careers, families, and lives in the United States.

Unexpected layoffs and organizational restructuring are normal realities of a dynamic economy. Losing a job does not diminish an individual's skills, qualifications, or potential contributions to American businesses.

In today's globally connected economy, multinational companies can hire these same professionals through overseas offices and global capability centers. This creates a risk that valuable expertise, innovation, and future employment opportunities will move outside the United States rather than remain within American businesses.

A reasonable grace period strengthens America's ability to attract and retain global talent, encourages long-term investment in the U.S. economy, and supports American innovation, entrepreneurship, and competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I would like to vote against thus proposed rule stating my reasons below-

1. Economic and Innovation Disruption (U.S. Competitiveness)
Brain Drain and Loss of Top Talent: High-skilled visa holders are critical drivers in technology, research, healthcare, and engineering. Forcing immediate departure upon job loss leaves zero runway for these professionals to find alternative employment within the U.S., driving valuable talent directly to competitors in countries like Canada, the UK, or the EU.

Friction for U.S. Employers: Employers frequently face sudden market shifts, reorganizations, or layoffs. The 60-day grace period acts as an essential "buffer" allowing companies to quickly onboard specialized talent already in the United States without having to navigate lengthy, expensive overseas consular processing. Eliminating it increases hiring friction and costs for American businesses.

2. Practical Impossibility of Immediate Transition or Departure
Logistical Chaos: Packing up an entire life, breaking apartment leases, pulling children out of mid-semester schools, selling vehicles, and transferring bank accounts within days (or hours) of a layoff is practically unfeasible.

Disruption of Legal Transition Pathways: Under current law, nonimmigrants are permitted to use the 60-day window to file for a change of status (e.g., switching to a B-2 visitor visa, a dependent visa, or a student F-1 visa) or to secure a new employer sponsor. Eliminating this grace period creates an abrupt "trapdoor," forcing individuals into immediate unlawful presence through no fault of their own, even when they are actively and legally attempting to adjust their status.

3. Disproportionate and Punitive Impact on Workers
Arbitrary Hardship: Sudden layoffs are already stressful; layering the immediate threat of deportation compounds this anxiety. It strips workers of basic stability, making them hyper-vulnerable to workplace exploitation because they cannot risk even a brief gap in employment to advocate for better working conditions.

Erosion of Reliance Interests: Many workers and families made significant financial and life decisions moving to the United States relying on the stability afforded by the 60-day grace period (which was originally codified to provide reasonable transition equity). Stripping it away disrupts these long-standing reliance interests.

4. Administrative Inefficiency for USCIS
Increased Backlog: Paradoxically, rather than reducing administrative burdens (a common stated goal of such rules), eliminating the grace period will likely increase pressure on U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). Workers who would have cleanly transitioned to a new employer within 60 days will now be forced to file emergency bridge petitions, extension-of-stay applications, or change-of-status requests just to avoid accruing unlawful presence, flooding the agency with additional paperwork.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule and urge DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period.

I have lived lawfully in the United States for approximately 11 years. I originally came here for higher education, earned a master's degree from a U.S. university, and received a merit-based scholarship. After graduation, I remained lawfully and built my professional career here as a software engineer.

I am also the beneficiary of an approved I-140 immigrant petition. Because of the employment-based visa backlog, I may still wait approximately another decade before permanent residence becomes available to me.

During these 11 years, I have built my education and career while maintaining lawful immigration status. I also have the ordinary financial & practical obligations that come with living and working here.

I understand that H-1B status is temporary & tied to qualifying employment. I'm not asking for an indefinite right to remain after employment ends. I am requesting DHS to preserve a reasonable transition period after an unexpected job loss.

1. The grace period makes H-1B portability workable.

Changing employers takes time. A worker must find a position, complete interviews, receive an offer, allow the employer to complete immigration review, obtain a certified Labor Condition Application, & prepare and file the H-1B petition. I have changed H-1B employers before and know from experience that these steps cannot realistically be completed immediately after an unexpected termination. Without a transition period, H-1B portability may exist in law while becoming much harder to use in practice.

2. Long-term workers have reasonably relied on a transition period.

The 60-day grace period has existed since 2017. For workers like me, it is not a loophole or permission to remain unemployed indefinitely. It provides limited time to find another sponsoring employer, pursue another lawful status, or prepare to depart. I have followed the employment-based immigration process and obtained an approved I-140, yet visa backlogs may leave me dependent on temporary status for many more years.

3. Immediate consequences would cause serious practical disruption.

Unexpected job loss does not make existing obligations disappear. After living and working here for many years, I have ordinary housing, financial, insurance, and practical obligations that cannot all be resolved immediately. If I were unable to obtain another lawful status and ultimately had to leave, I would need time to address my home and belongings, existing obligations, international travel, and relocation.The issue is not whether departure may eventually be required. The issue is whether a worker receives reasonable time to pursue a lawful alternative or arrange an orderly departure.

4. Eliminating the grace period would increase dependence on employers.

H-1B workers already depend heavily on employer sponsorship. Without a transition period, a worker experiencing discrimination, unpaid wages, unsafe conditions, or another serious workplace issue could reasonably fear that termination would immediately threaten immigration status. A brief grace period gives workers an opportunity to seek another employer or lawful option without changing the requirement that H-1B status be based on qualifying employment.

5. U.S. employers would also be affected.

Hiring experienced professionals takes time. Employers must interview candidates, obtain approvals, prepare offers, and complete immigration procedures. A U.S. employer may be willing to hire an H-1B worker but unable to complete these steps immediately after the worker's previous employment ends. Eliminating the grace period could cause employers to lose qualified candidates who could otherwise lawfully transition to new employment.

6. Administrative burden can be addressed without eliminating the grace period.

If DHS is concerned about determining whether applicants rely on the grace period, it could require applicants to identify this directly on Forms I-129 or I-539 and provide the date qualifying employment ended. Administrative efficiency should not require eliminating the transition period when less disruptive alternatives are available.

Conclusion

I have lived lawfully in the United States for approximately 11 years. I received my graduate education here, earned a merit-based scholarship, built my professional career here, and obtained an approved employment-based immigrant petition. The 60-day grace period provides something modest but important: time to find another employer, pursue another lawful immigration option, or, if no alternative exists, arrange an orderly departure. It does not guarantee continued employment or permanent residence. It simply recognizes that employment changes, immigration filings, and international relocation cannot happen overnight.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and retain the existing 60-day grace period.

Subject: Strong Opposition to Eliminating the 60-Day H-1B Grace Period – Protect Families and Long-Term, Law-Abiding Workers

I strongly oppose any proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period currently available to H-1B workers following the termination of their employment.

I came to the United States nearly 20 years ago. During these two decades, I have worked hard, followed immigration laws, paid taxes, contributed to the economy, and built a life here. The United States is not simply a temporary workplace for my family anymore. It is our home.

My children are growing up here. They are U.S. citizens and are attending American schools, one in high school and the other in middle school. We own a home, have established financial responsibilities, and have built our family, professional, and social lives here.

Consider what happens if someone like me suddenly loses a job and is not given even 60 days to manage the transition.

What happens to the mortgage and the house we have spent years building our lives in? What happens to our cars, financial obligations, and other commitments? What happens to children who are in the middle of an academic year? Should parents be expected to uproot their children from their schools, friends, education, and familiar surroundings and move them to another country on extremely short notice?

These are not just immigration paperwork issues. These are real families, real children, and real lives.

There is another important aspect of the H-1B immigration system that must be considered. Employment-based green card backlogs for nationals of countries such as India and China can extend for decades. Many skilled professionals have been waiting for permanent residency for 10, 15, or even 20 years despite maintaining lawful status, continuing employment, and complying with every immigration requirement.

The system itself requires many of these individuals to keep renewing their H-1B status year after year while they wait for their green cards. They have followed the rules and built their lives around the immigration framework established by the United States.

If the government requires people to remain on temporary work visas for decades because of green card backlogs, it should also recognize the human consequences of that arrangement.

The 60-day grace period is not an unreasonable benefit or an opportunity to bypass immigration requirements. It is a basic safeguard that provides a limited amount of time for workers and their families to respond to an unexpected loss of employment.

Even in a challenging job market, finding a new employer, completing interviews, negotiating an offer, and having a new employer file an H-1B petition can take time. Sixty days is already a relatively short period to accomplish all of this while simultaneously managing family responsibilities.

For someone who has spent 20 years contributing to this country, 60 days is the bare minimum of time needed to make responsible decisions about their family’s future.

Eliminating this grace period would create enormous uncertainty and hardship for thousands of law-abiding professionals and their families. It could force families to make life-changing decisions under extreme time pressure, disrupt children’s education, and cause significant financial losses.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to retain the existing 60-day H-1B grace period.

Immigration policy should consider not only employers and employment relationships but also the human beings and families affected by these policies. People who have spent decades working, paying taxes, raising children, and contributing to American communities deserve a reasonable opportunity to transition when circumstances beyond their control result in job loss.

A country that has allowed families to build their lives over decades should not force them to dismantle those lives overnight. Sixty days is not too much to ask. It is a reasonable and humane minimum.

Thank you for considering the real-life impact of this proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364; RIN 1615-AD22
"Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period," 91 Fed. Reg. 57,807 (Sept. 11, 2026)

Dear Sir or Madam:

I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule. I am an H-1B nonimmigrant worker employed as a software engineer in California. I earned my master's degree at a U.S. university, worked in the United States under F-1 status, and changed to H-1B status on October 1, 2026. I pay federal and state income taxes, including FICA taxes, and I have complied with every condition of my status. The proposed rule would not affect only future applicants; it would strip a protection that workers like me rely on today.

1. The grace period is the only realistic bridge between employers. If my employment ends, finding a new job and having a new employer prepare and file an H-1B petition takes weeks — recruiting, interviews, an offer, a labor condition application, and petition preparation cannot be completed overnight. The 60-day period is what makes a lawful transfer possible. Without it, a layoff — a decision entirely outside the worker's control — would make the worker out of status the next day and force an immediate departure from the country, abandoning a lease, a home, and a life built here over years. Sixty days is already short; zero days is not a policy, it is a trapdoor.

2. The proposal also quietly removes another protection. Footnote 19 of the notice would delete the reference to the grace period in 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i), which allows workers with an approved I-140 petition to seek a compelling-circumstances employment authorization document during the grace period. DHS calls this a "technical revision," but its effect is substantive: workers who have already been approved for the first step of the green-card process would lose a lawful way to keep working while they wait. A change of that significance should be proposed and justified on its own, not buried in a footnote.

3. DHS has not shown that the grace period is being abused. The grace period has been in place since January 2017, and DHS adopted it precisely because the absence of any transition period caused unnecessary disruption for workers and employers alike. The notice rests largely on the observation that the grace period is discretionary rather than required by statute — but discretion is a reason to exercise judgment, not to eliminate a working policy. The notice identifies no data showing that workers use the period to remain in the United States without working, or that it harms American workers.

4. The rule harms American employers and the American economy. U.S. employers recruit globally because the skills are scarce. Forcing experienced, tax-paying, law-abiding workers to leave the country within a day of a layoff does not create a single American job; it hands trained talent to competitors abroad and discourages the next generation of international students from studying and working here at all. Many of us were educated at American universities at our own expense; the United States benefits when we stay and contribute.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If the Department has specific concerns about how the grace period is used, it should address those concerns with targeted conditions — not by eliminating the only transition period these workers have.

Respectfully submitted,
comments.reason: The commenter argues against removing the grace period, stating it is essential for lawful job transfers after a layoff.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Comment on Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I oppose removing the up-to-60-day grace period in 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), and I ask DHS to address the reliance interests workers, families, and employers have built on it since 2017.

The grace period is not a loophole; it is the minimum time the government's own processes require. A new employer cannot file a portability petition instantly: a certified Labor Condition Application alone takes about seven working days at the Department of Labor, before petition preparation, filing, and receipt. If status ends the day after employment, H-1B portability becomes unusable in practice — the petition cannot be received while the worker is still in status, no matter how quickly both sides act. The rule would therefore not speed departures of people who have left the workforce; it would block job-to-job transfers of people employers are actively trying to hire.

The reliance interests are concrete. Workers sign leases, keep children in school, and hold approved immigrant petitions built over years, all in reliance on an orderly 60-day bridge after an involuntary job loss. Employers in shortage fields rely on that bridge to backfill critical roles. Removing it converts every layoff into an immediate family departure, including for workers with U.S.-citizen children, without any showing that the grace period has been abused.

At minimum, if DHS proceeds, it should retain a shorter grace period long enough for an LCA to certify and a petition to be received, and should grandfather workers whose employment ended before the final rule's effective date.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes removing the grace period, citing reliance interests and practical difficulties.

Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period," 91 Fed. Reg. 57,807 (Sept. 11, 2026)
I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule and ask DHS to withdraw it.
Who I am. I am an H-1B worker and automotive controls and simulation engineer in Michigan, with more than 11 years of engineering experience. I have lived and worked in the United States on H-1B status for 11 years. My wife works as a paraprofessional in a public school, and our son, a U.S. citizen, is under two years old. We rent our home for $1,460 a month.
What this rule would mean for my family. If my employment ended, this proposal would make my whole family out of status the very next day. We could not end a lease, arrange an international move with a toddler, or withdraw from the life we have built here in one day. Finding a new employer willing to sponsor an H-1B petition — then obtaining a certified Labor Condition Application and having the petition filed — takes weeks at minimum. In my own job search this year, hiring processes with U.S. employers have lasted two months or more. Sixty days is already tight; zero days is not a transition period at all, it is an eviction notice.
Why the rule should be withdrawn.
It undermines the portability Congress created. Congress enacted H-1B portability (INA §214(n)) so a worker could start with a new employer upon the filing of a qualifying petition. That only works if the worker has time to find the employer and get the petition filed. Eliminating the grace period strands workers who have a willing new employer but no time to complete the filing — the exact situation portability was written for.
Families and children should not be expected to leave immediately. DHS's own figures show an average of more than 208,000 dependent approvals a year in the affected classifications, yet DHS calls the effect on family well-being negligible. For a family with a U.S.-citizen toddler in Michigan, the effect is not negligible: a job loss on a Friday would mean unlawful presence by Saturday, with no time to sell, move, or arrange schooling and care. Other categories get transition time — F-1 students generally receive 60 days after completing a program, J-1 visitors 30 days. Workers who have lived here for years deserve no less.
Workers and employers have relied on this rule for nearly a decade. The 60-day grace period has been in the regulations since January 2017, and USCIS has published guidance telling workers how to use it. Families have signed leases, enrolled children, and made career decisions around it. DHS acknowledges these reliance interests but does not adequately weigh the disruption of removing them overnight.

The proposal also removes, in a footnote, the regulatory language that lets workers with approved I-140 petitions apply for a compelling-circumstances Employment Authorization Document during the grace period. DHS calls this a "technical revision," but it removes a safety net for workers stuck in the green-card backlog. That protection should be retained regardless of what DHS decides about the grace period.
DHS also states it did not estimate the monetized costs of this rule — no count of lease-break fees, forced home sales, lost spousal wages, or the cost of visa appointments abroad. My family's costs are real even if DHS did not count them: a broken lease, a move across the world with a toddler, and months of lost income while a new petition is prepared from outside the country.
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and retain the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As you are aware, many employees on H-1B and other employment-based visas have lived and worked in the United States for more than a decade. Over time, these individuals establish deep personal, financial, and community ties. Eliminating the 60-day grace period would create significant hardship for workers and their families who are already navigating the uncertainty of a job loss.

Some of the key impacts are outlined below:

1. Children's Education

One of the most significant concerns is the disruption to children's education. The current 60-day grace period provides families with time to search for new employment, either locally or in another state, while minimizing interruptions to their children's schooling. Even if a family ultimately decides to return to their home country, they need adequate time to research schools, complete enrollment requirements, and ensure a smooth educational transition for their children.

2. Mortgage and Housing Obligations

Many long-term visa holders own homes and maintain mortgage obligations. The grace period allows families to make responsible decisions regarding their property, including selling their home, arranging for rental management, or establishing a power of attorney if they must leave the country. Eliminating the grace period could force individuals to leave before addressing these important financial commitments.

3. Financial Assets, Retirement Accounts, and Insurance

Over the years, visa holders accumulate financial assets, including savings accounts, investment accounts, retirement plans such as 401(k)s, and various insurance policies. An immediate requirement to depart the country following job loss would leave little time to evaluate financial options, complete necessary paperwork, seek tax guidance, or make informed decisions regarding investments and benefits. This could result in substantial financial losses and administrative challenges.

4. Dependents and Dual-Income Families

Many spouses of H-1B visa holders are employed under H-4 EAD authorization. The current grace period provides these individuals an opportunity to provide notice to their employers, transition responsibilities, and make arrangements for their own careers. Eliminating the grace period would negatively affect not only the primary visa holder but also dependent family members who have established professional and financial commitments in the United States.

5. Pets and Animal Welfare

For many families, pets are beloved family members. Transporting pets internationally often requires extensive planning, including vaccinations, health certifications, import permits, airline arrangements, and compliance with destination-country regulations. The 60-day grace period provides families sufficient time to complete these requirements responsibly. Without such a period, some families may face extremely difficult circumstances despite their commitment to caring for their animals.

Conclusion

The 60-day grace period serves as a reasonable and compassionate safeguard for individuals and families experiencing an unexpected job loss. It provides time to secure new employment, manage financial obligations, protect children's education, support dependents, and make orderly transition plans. Maintaining this provision helps ensure that law-abiding visa holders who have contributed to the U.S. economy and their communities for many years are treated fairly during periods of professional transition.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that eliminating the grace period causes severe hardships for workers and their families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose DHS’s proposal to end the grace period in 8 C.F.R. § 214.1(l)(2). If it moves forward, it should consider less harmful options and give workers and families time to adjust.

The grace period is limited and optional. It lasts up to 60 days, or until the worker’s authorized stay ends, whichever comes first. DHS can shorten or deny it. This short window gives workers who lose their jobs time to find a new employer or prepare to leave the country. Without it, losing a job could quickly become an immigration emergency.

DHS can set rules for nonimmigrant status under INA § 214(a), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a). But it should explain why ending this limited protection is better than less harmful options. In 2016, DHS adopted the grace period to help skilled workers change jobs after sudden job loss. Under the Administrative Procedure Act, DHS should explain why it is changing course, address the facts behind the 2016 rule, and consider how workers and families have relied on it.

Ending the grace period could also hurt U.S. employers and innovation. A short transition window lets a new U.S. employer keep a skilled worker by filing a petition. Without it, employers may lose qualified workers because leaving the country and returning later takes time and creates uncertainty—even when a suitable job is available. If skilled workers and their families must leave after a layoff, other countries may become more attractive places to work. The United States could lose their skills, research, and business ideas. Over time, this could weaken U.S. companies’ ability to innovate and compete, and encourage more investment and technical work to move abroad. DHS should study these effects before ending a rule designed to help skilled workers change jobs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose DHS’s proposal to eliminate the current discretionary 60-day grace period for certain employment-based nonimmigrant workers. I urge DHS to retain the existing rule because the grace period provides important flexibility not only for workers, but also for U.S. employers and the broader American economy.

Eliminating the grace period would increase unnecessary loss of skilled workers from the U.S. labor market. Many employment-based nonimmigrant workers have specialized technical, scientific, engineering, or business expertise that U.S. companies have already invested significant resources to recruit and develop. When employment ends because of a layoff, restructuring, project cancellation, or other business decision, a reasonable transition period allows these workers to seek another U.S. employer that needs their skills. Requiring substantially faster departure would increase the likelihood that experienced workers leave the United States entirely, taking their knowledge and productive capacity to competing economies.

The current grace period reduces recruiting, onboarding, and replacement costs for U.S. businesses. Hiring specialized employees can involve lengthy searches, interviews, immigration filings, relocation, training, and integration into complex teams. If qualified workers already present in the United States have a practical opportunity to transfer to another employer, American companies can fill vacancies more efficiently. Eliminating that transition period would make otherwise viable employment matches harder to complete and could force employers to restart expensive domestic or international recruitment processes.

A 60-day transition period also helps reduce project disruption and improves labor-market mobility. Modern technology, engineering, healthcare, research, and other specialized industries frequently depend on employees with highly specific knowledge. Abrupt departures can delay product development, customer commitments, research efforts, and knowledge transfer. At the same time, reasonable employee mobility helps talent move from companies experiencing layoffs to companies that are expanding. That reallocation of skilled labor is economically productive and should not be unnecessarily constrained by an immigration deadline that is shorter than normal professional recruiting and petition-processing timelines.

Retaining the current rule supports U.S. competitiveness without eliminating immigration enforcement. The existing grace period is limited in duration and does not create permanent immigration status or unrestricted employment authorization. It simply provides a defined window for an eligible worker to obtain another qualifying status, change status, or depart. Preserving this framework gives U.S. businesses reasonable access to talent already contributing to the American economy while maintaining clear immigration requirements. For these reasons, I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period and retain the current regulation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Michael Jose
comments.commentText:
I support this new rule that would eliminate the 60-day grace period for aliens in non-immigrant employment-related visa categories to find a new job. The entire point of such visas is to provide labor that is not available in the native population and as such the presence of the alien ought to dependent on the specific need for which he or she was admitted. Allowing the visa-holder time to find a new job undermines the entire stated purpose of these visas. The jobs they officially came here to do become a pretext to import foreign labor generally rather than addressing specific needs. This must end.
