comments.title: Comment Submitted by Siddharth S
comments.commentText:
Strongly oppose the rule eliminating the 60-day grace period.

1. It Counterintuitively Increases Administrative and Economic Burdens

The agency’s stated intent in removing the grace period is to reduce the administrative burden on [USCIS] resources used to track or process discretionary extensions. However, eliminating this window will likely increase the systemic administrative burden on both the agency and U.S. employers.
• The Real-World Impact: Rather than allowing a worker to seamlessly port their existing visa status to a new employer during a 60-day grace period, the rule will force an influx of immediate, frantic filings. Laid-off workers will have no choice but to immediately file hasty, last-minute applications for a change of status to B-1/B-2 visitor visas or dependent visas just to avoid falling out of status overnight. [USCIS] will then be forced to adjudicate a massive wave of these temporary, stop-gap visa modifications, vastly multiplying their paperwork and processing queues.

2. It Punishes Sudden, Unpredictable Corporate Layoffs

Tech and corporate sectors go through rapid restructuring, unexpected budget cuts, and sudden layoffs. Under the current rule, if an engineer or analyst is laid off overnight, they have up to 60 days to find a new employer to sponsor them, file for a change of status, or wind up their affairs and pack up a life they built.
• The Real-World Impact: Imagine an H-1B software developer at a mid-sized firm who receives a Friday afternoon pink slip due to a sudden corporate downsizing. Without the 60-day window, they would fall out of legal status immediately at midnight. They cannot even stay to finish logging out of company systems, sell their car, break their apartment lease responsibly, or conduct a standard job interview.

3. It Destroys Families and Upends Children’s Lives

Many high-skilled workers are not single; they live in the U.S. with spouses on H-4 visas and children who are enrolled in local schools, play in neighborhood sports teams, and only know the United States as home.
• The Real-World Impact: Forcing an immediate departure means pulling a child out of school mid-semester without warning, selling a family home or breaking a lease with massive financial penalties, and uprooting spouses who may have work authorization or ongoing career paths of their own. It transforms an administrative job separation into an immediate, chaotic displacement for entire households.

4. It Disrupts Years of Pending Green Card Investments

Many H-1B and specialized workers have spent five, seven, or ten years in the legal immigration queue with pending PERM (Labor Certification) or I-140 petitions.
• The Real-World Impact: If an employee is laid off while waiting for a green card backlog to clear, the 60-day grace period is what allows them to hustle and find a new employer who can port or salvage their multi-year permanent residency filing. Eliminating the window destroys years of legal and financial progress in a single instant, discouraging top global talent from building roots or contributing to the U.S. economy.

5. It Harms U.S. Employers and Innovation

DHS claims the rule reduces administrative burdens, but the reality is more destructive to American businesses. Navigating H-1B sponsorships is already expensive and slow. If a sudden layoff means the candidate vanishes from the country by the next morning, U.S. companies lose the ability to quickly hire vetted, specialized, high-demand talent already living locally.
• The Real-World Impact: Startups and tech firms trying to fill critical engineering or research roles will find it far riskier to hire foreign-born talent, pushing investment, research, and high-paying jobs overseas where immigration policies are more predictable.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear uscis,

I am a law abiding immigrant who loved, worked and built family in usa since more than a decade . ​I am writing to formally oppose the proposed changes affecting the 60-day grace period for H-1B nonimmigrant workers following the cessation of employment (8 CFR 214.1(l)(2)). Eliminating or restricting this vital transition period contradicts the spirit of congressional law, ignores deep reliance interests, and will inflict severe economic and humanitarian harm on law-abiding families, U.S. citizen children, and local communities.
​Alignment with Congressional Intent and Statutory Spirit
​The 60-day grace period was established in the true spirit of the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-First Century Act (AC21) and related statutory frameworks passed by Congress. Congress explicitly recognized that high-skilled workers need job portability and reasonable flexibility to transition between employers without immediately falling into unlawful status. In a dynamic economy where corporate restructurings, mergers, and layoffs happen without warning, a 60-day buffer is the bare minimum required for a skilled professional to secure a new petitioning employer, wrap up affairs, or change status lawfully.
​Overnight Loss of Status for Law-Abiding Contributors
​Rescinding this grace period means that hardworking employees who have followed every rule, paid hundreds of thousands of dollars in federal and state taxes, and contributed enormously to American innovation and economic growth will become unlawfully present overnight through no fault of their own. A sudden corporate layoff should not immediately strip legal status from individuals who have spent years—and often over a decade due to green card backlogs—building their lives and careers in the United States.
​Irreparable Harm to U.S. Citizen Children
​Tens of thousands of H-1B professionals are parents to U.S. citizen children who were born and raised in the United States. Forcing parents to depart the country immediately upon job loss effectively deports U.S. citizen children, uprooting them mid-school year from their classrooms, healthcare providers, communities, and the only country and way of life they have ever known. The psychological, educational, and developmental disruption to these American children is irreparable and wholly unjustified.
​Catastrophic Financial Distress and Housing Market Disruption
​Long-term H-1B residents have legitimately relied on existing regulations to purchase homes, take on mortgages, and invest in their neighborhoods. Eliminating the 60-day grace period leaves laid-off workers unable to legally remain in the country to live in their homes, transition to new employment to pay their monthly mortgage installments, or manage an orderly sale of their property. It is legally and logistically impossible to sell a home at fair market value or settle leases, vehicles, and bank accounts within twenty-four hours. Forcing families into sudden departure will trigger a wave of distressed fire sales, defaults, and foreclosures, wiping out families' life savings while destabilizing local housing markets and U.S. lending institutions.
​Conclusion and Request
​Federal agencies must account for serious reliance interests and the economic repercussions of regulatory changes. The 60-day grace period serves as an essential, common-sense safeguard for both American employers seeking domestic talent and legal immigrants navigating sudden employment shifts. I urge the agency to withdraw any proposal that eliminates or shortens the 60-day grace period and to preserve this critical protection in full.
​Respectfully submitted,

I respectfully oppose removing the up-to-60-day discretionary grace period.

I am an H-1B manufacturing engineering professional with extensive experience in regulated medical-device manufacturing, including process validation, supplier coordination, production improvement, and technical project leadership. Hiring in my field can involve recruiter screening, several technical and management interviews, reference checks, compensation approval, and immigration counsel review. A prospective employer also needs time to prepare the required immigration filings. These steps cannot realistically be completed immediately after an unexpected termination.

I respectfully request that DHS:
1. Retain the existing up-to-60-day discretionary grace period.
2. Evaluate the combined effects on workers, dependent spouses, and prospective U.S. employers.
3. Assess whether elimination would increase emergency filings, departures, and subsequent reentry-related processing.
4. If DHS proceeds, provide a meaningful transition period, clear prospective applicability rules, and a workable opportunity to pursue qualifying filings or orderly departure.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I am writing to strongly oppose this proposed rule, as someone whose ability to remain and work lawfully in the United States depends on the existing protections. I have lived and worked in New York for two years in E-3 status, having moved here to take up a role in the entertainment industry that my organisation had struggled to fill with suitably qualified US citizens. My wife moved here with me and is here on dependent status, with her employment and ability to work tied to my immigration status. We have established our lives here, and an unexpected loss of employment would have consequences for both of us.

Administrative burden:

I believe this proposal is likely to increase, rather than reduce, the administrative burden on USCIS.

Under the current system, someone who loses their job has a 60-day grace period without needing to submit an application or wait for approval. Under the proposed rule, remaining in lawful status would require a new filing, either a Form I-129 from a new employer or a Form I-539 to change status. Each dependent would also need to submit a separate Form I-539.

DHS estimates that around 65,752 workers and more than 208,000 dependents could be affected annually. Form I-539 receipts already exceed 400,000 a year, with processing times averaging nine to twelve months and backlogs reaching eighteen months at some service centres. Since the Edakunni settlement expired in January 2025, USCIS is no longer required to process dependent applications alongside the principal applicant’s petition.

Adding tens of thousands of applications to an already stretched system hardly seems like a reduction in workload. The proposal does not quantify this additional burden or explain why the claimed administrative savings would outweigh it.

Impact on families and employers:

A spouse or child has no control over whether the principal visa holder loses their job, yet under this proposal their lawful status would also be affected. Spouses could immediately lose their work authorisation, while children could be forced to leave school part-way through an academic year. Many of these households also include US-citizen children.

In my own case, if I were made redundant, my wife would also have to stop working. Her employer would immediately lose an employee despite her having done nothing wrong and her employment having no connection to my redundancy. This would apply to thousands of other families too, meaning American businesses could lose perfectly good employees because of someone else’s employment circumstances.

There is also a wider impact on recruitment. The existing grace period allows employers to recruit talented people who have been let go by another company. Without it, the timing can make this practically impossible. A Labor Condition Application can take around a week before a new petition can be filed. By then, the individual may already have fallen out of lawful status. This makes it harder for American businesses to recruit people with skills they need.

Reliance and alternatives:

DHS describes this as a return to an earlier policy, but overlooks the fact that workers, employers, landlords and schools have relied on the 60-day grace period for nearly a decade. People have built their lives around having a reasonable window to deal with unexpected job loss. These reliance interests deserve proper consideration, but the proposal does not adequately address them.

If the concern is the administrative difficulty of assessing eligibility for a discretionary grace period, there are less disruptive alternatives. DHS could make the period fixed and non-discretionary, require workers or employers to notify USCIS when employment ends, or shorten the period rather than eliminate it. The proposal does not adequately explain why these alternatives have not been adopted.

There are also practical financial consequences to consider. Having to leave the country at short notice would mean disrupting established lives, breaking rental arrangements and potentially leaving US landlords facing financial difficulties. The effects extend well beyond the individual visa holder.

I urge DHS not to proceed with this proposed rule and to retain the existing 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

The proposal does not make a convincing case for such a significant change. The administrative benefits have not been properly quantified, the consequences for workers, families and American businesses have not been adequately assessed, and less disruptive alternatives have not been given sufficient consideration.

Thank you for taking the time to consider my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yinzhe Lu
comments.commentText:
Re: Comment on Proposed Rule, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period," 91 FR 57807 (Sept. 11, 2026); DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364; RIN 1615-AD22

I'm an H-1B worker in a specialty occupation. I'm asking the Department to withdraw the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period in 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). At a minimum, it should do the quantitative and alternatives analysis the Administrative Procedure Act requires before finalizing anything. My concerns are practical, not abstract. As written, the proposal would turn an ordinary layoff, something the current job market makes increasingly common, into an immediate loss of lawful status, with consequences the proposal never measures.

1. The proposal measures the wrong people, so its central number can't support the rule.
The impact analysis gets its affected population, 3,795 people a year, 99.2% H-1B, from beneficiaries of revoked I-129 petitions followed by a new change-of-employer filing within 60 days. 91 FR at 57821. But the Department concedes it "cannot distinguish" voluntary job changes from workers laid off involuntarily.

2. The cost-benefit analysis is qualitative where it matters and quantitative only where it helps the Department.
The OMB A-4 accounting statement lists monetized costs and benefits as "Not Estimated." 91 FR at 57817-18. The proposal computes an upper-bound individual loss ($21,877 = $131,000 median wage x 2/12, 91 FR at 57822-23) yet never does the multiplication its own numbers invite: $21,877 x 3,795 is about $83 million a year in lost worker income at the upper bound. That is before counting family disruption or employer replacement costs, none of which are estimated.

3. The reliance analysis is a citation, not an analysis.
The proposal dismisses reliance interests as "misplaced" because the grace period is discretionary, citing Wages & White Lion Investments, 604 U.S. 542, 585 (2025). 91 FR at 57816. But Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California requires assessment of the nature and extent of reliance, its weight, and alternatives that preserve it.

4. The alternatives considered are only flavors of elimination.
The proposal's alternatives, eliminate for some classifications, shorten the period, impose stringent evidentiary requirements, are variants of the same outcome. 91 FR at 57816. Never considered: an automatic (non-discretionary) grace period, self-certification of the cessation date with adjudicator review limited to fraud or security flags, or keeping the period for H-1B workers covered by Congress's statutory portability provision.

5. The rule creates the enforcement problem it claims to solve, and undermines the portability Congress created.
In FY2025, only 37 Notices to Appear were issued to H-1B workers for failure to maintain status beyond the grace period. 91 FR at 57823-24. That tiny figure is evidence the grace period works.

6. Family effects are asserted without data, and the combined burden of simultaneous H-1B actions is never analyzed.
The proposal's family assessment concludes the rule "would not negatively affect family well-being" and that financial effects are "incidental to the alien's obligation to depart." 91 FR at 57827. H-4 spouses and children lose status simultaneously with the principal, and H-4 employment authorization is tied to the principal's status. Yet the proposal contains zero data on how many of the 3,795 workers have dependents.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask the Department to withdraw the proposal. If it does not, I ask at minimum for: (a) a supplemental quantitative regulatory impact analysis with a disaggregated involuntary-layoff population estimate; (b) analysis of a true less-burdensome alternative; (c) transition provisions protecting reliance interests; and (d) a cumulative-impact analysis, each published for public comment before any final rule.
comments.reason: The commenter asks the Department to withdraw the proposal to eliminate the grace period.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the end of the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders, drawing from my own experience and observation of the current landscape.

The 60-day window is a critical buffer for skilled workers and their families, and removing it would have severe consequences for several reasons:

- Impact on Families and Children: For foreign national families, an abrupt departure severely disrupts children currently enrolled in school. Families need adequate time to plan transitions thoughtfully so that their children’s education and well-being are not compromised.
- Medical and Caregiving Needs: An abrupt end to the grace period leaves families vulnerable during critical health situations, such as when a spouse is pregnant or undergoing medical treatment, leaving them affected without proper support or continuity of care.
- Financial and Logistical Realities: Many H-1B workers have invested deeply in their communities, including purchasing homes. Wrapping up financial obligations, managing personal assets, or selling a property cannot realistically be handled overnight.
- Humane Considerations: Allowing workers who have contributed significantly to the economy a reasonable amount of time to settle their affairs or secure new employment aligns with American values of fairness, compassion, and respect.
- Evolving Market Dynamics: In today's economy, many highly skilled H-1B professionals are facing job disruptions not due to a lack of skill, but because of rapid technological shifts, including the widespread advancement of AI and automation. However, their skills may still be applicable to other industries and save time for start-ups looking to utilize their expertise.

Ending the grace period creates unnecessary hardship for law-abiding, highly skilled immigrants who simply ask for a fair and humane transition timeline. I strongly urge a reconsideration of this policy to ensure that H-1B workers and their families are treated with the dignity they deserve.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes ending the 60-day grace period, citing impacts on families, health, and finances.

I oppose the proposed rule, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period," and ask DHS to withdraw it.

I am an H-1B software quality engineer living in Texas. I have lived in the United States for 14 years. I was born in India and have an approved I-140 with a December 2016 priority date. I am still waiting for my green card. My wife is on H-4, and our two children attend public school, one in 12th grade and the other in 7th grade.

Under the proposed rule, if I lose my job, my entire family would be out of status the same day. This does not give a laid-off worker a reasonable chance to find another employer and continue working legally. A new employer cannot file an H-1B petition until the Department of Labor certifies the Labor Condition Application, which can take up to seven working days. Finding a new job takes much longer. Removing the grace period would make H-1B portability practically impossible for workers who lose their jobs.

The impact on families would be severe. A family cannot arrange international travel and leave the country in one day. My child is in the junior year of high school, and an unexpected departure would seriously disrupt their education. Leaving the United States also does not guarantee a quick return. H-1B and H-4 visa interviews in India have been delayed by months since December 2025.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this rule. If DHS decides to proceed, I request that it preserve the 60-day grace period for workers with approved I-140 petitions and their families. Any changes should apply only to employment ending after a delayed effective date, giving affected workers and families reasonable time to prepare.

Thank you.
Anonymous
H-1B software engineer, Texas

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
MEMORANDUM OF PUBLIC COMMENT
TO: USCIS, Department of Homeland Security (DHS)
RE: NPRM: Elimination of the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period for Nonimmigrant Workers
POSITION: Strongly Opposed

I. INTRODUCTION

This comment strongly opposes the proposal to eliminate the up to 60-day grace period for high-skilled nonimmigrant professionals (H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN). Removing this critical buffer will trigger immediate, severe macroeconomic, regional, and corporate contractions across the United States.

II. MACROECONOMIC IMPACTS: EROSION OF TAX REVENUE AND INFRASTRUCTURE CAPITAL

Forcing immediate departure upon employment termination removes highly productive capital and tax revenue from the U.S. economy:
• Disproportionate Fiscal Yields: According to the Economic Innovation Group (EIG), an H-1B household generates $30,050 in net positive fiscal balance annually—2.6 times higher than the average U.S. household baseline. Annually, H-1B professionals contribute $24 billion in federal taxes and $11 billion in state/local revenues. Immediate deportation destroys this high-bracket tax base with no replacement.
• Asset Liquidation: High-skilled visa holders are active investors in American equities and employer-sponsored 401(k) plans. Denying a transition window forces premature asset liquidations and immediate capital flight out of U.S. financial networks.
• Freezing EB-5 Rural Investments: Many high-earning nonimmigrants utilize their capital to pursue permanent residency via the EB-5 program, injecting vital funding into EB-5 rural infrastructure projects in targeted employment areas (TEAs). Eliminating the grace period chokes this critical pipeline of private domestic infrastructure capital, leaving high-value rural developments stranded.

III. DESTABILIZATION OF REGIONAL REAL ESTATE MARKETS

The housing markets of rapidly expanding tech corridors across the American South and Southeast rely heavily on the purchasing power of international professionals:
• The North Texas Corridor: Suburbs north of Dallas (Frisco, Celina, Prosper, Melissa) have experienced immense real estate expansions driven by corporate relocations and H-1B professionals. In peak growth periods, homebuilders in markets like Celina reported that 70% to 75% of new home sales were executed by international buyers and H-1B holders. Policy disruptions in 2026 already drove down Collin County home prices by nearly 9% year-over-year. Eliminating the grace period will turn market corrections into rapid foreclosures as families are forced to abruptly abandon active mortgages and properties.
• The Southeast Corridor (North Carolina): Similar contractions will damage the Research Triangle and Charlotte. Removing the transition window will strand builders with unsold inventory and severely erode municipal property tax bases, directly defunding local public schools and infrastructure.

IV. CORPORATE CORROSION AND GLOBAL REVERSE BRAIN DRAIN

By transforming the U.S. into a volatile environment for global talent, this rule accelerates a massive "reverse brain drain" directly undermining American innovation:
• Decimating Core Technical Competencies: Flagship enterprises like Google, Nvidia, and Microsoft rely on specialized global technical talent. H-1B employees command a median wage of $108,000—double the national median—reflecting their irreplaceable value. Stripping away a survival buffer during cyclical corporate restructurings ensures this elite talent leaves the country entirely.
• Subsidizing Competitors via Global Capability Centers (GCCs): Displaced talent will return to home countries or relocate to expanding GCCs in India, or tech ecosystems in Taiwan, South Korea, Singapore, and China.
• Historical Precedent of Tech Flight: Restrictive domestic policies consistently birth competing global empires. The iconic Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) was catalyzed by Morris Chang and a cohort of U.S.-educated immigrant engineers who returned to Taiwan to pioneer the global semiconductor foundation. Similar talent returns accelerated the growth of India’s enterprise tech sector and China's domestic AI industries. A zero-tolerance policy actively subsidizes foreign competition with talent trained within the United States.

V. CONCLUSION

The elimination of the 60-day grace period is economically short-sighted. It threatens federal tax yields, destabilizes regional housing markets, and acts as an outsourced talent recruitment mechanism for foreign tech sectors. DHS should withdraw this proposal and preserve the 60-day grace period to protect the U.S. economy.
Respectfully submitted,

References and Economic Data Sources:

comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day discretionary grace period for nonimmigrant workers following job termination. As an H-1B visa holder who has lived, worked, and contributed to the United States for many years while waiting in the green card backlog, I urge USCIS to retain this essential protection.

In today’s technology sector, corporate restructurings and layoffs are frequent and unpredictable. Even for highly skilled professionals, securing a new role, completing interviews, and having a new employer file an H-1B transfer petition takes several weeks. Removing the 60-day grace period leaves zero buffer for law-abiding workers to transition smoothly between jobs without immediately falling out of status.
Eliminating this grace period would create impossible logistical barriers and cause severe disruption to established families:

1. Impact on U.S.-Raised Children: I have a 17-year-old child who is currently applying to U.S. colleges. He has attended school exclusively in the United States since kindergarten. America is the only home and education system he knows. Forcing our family to abruptly uproot and leave the country due to a sudden layoff during his critical college application and transition period would be devastating to his education and future.

2. Homeownership and Financial Commitments: Like many long-term visa holders waiting for permanent residency, I own a home in the United States and carry an active mortgage. Being forced to leave the country immediately upon an unannounced job loss makes it impossible to responsibly sell a home, settle financial obligations, or wind down years of community ties.

3. Impossibility of Immediate Departure After Sudden Layoffs: Employers do not always provide advance notice of a layoff, meaning an employee can lose their job on the spot without warning. Practically and logistically, it is impossible for an individual—let alone a family—to pack up a household, book international travel, and leave the country the very same day.

The 60-day grace period is not a loophole; it is a practical, humane safeguard that provides basic logistical feasibility and stability for tax-paying workers and their families while allowing U.S. employers to retain experienced talent. I respectfully request that USCIS withdraw this proposal and preserve the 60-day grace period.
Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Anonymous H-1B Visa Holder
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing negative impacts on families and workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposed rule to eliminate or drastically reduce the H-1B 60-day grace period is a short-sighted measure that will cause profound, unnecessary trauma to high-skilled families and inflict severe damage on American communities. Beyond its economic flaws, this policy enforces fundamentally inhumane practices that reduce dedicated professional families to numbers on a page, ignoring the deep human and social roots they have planted in the United States.
Consider the devastating disruption this policy inflicts on a typical high-earning H-1B household—such as a family with a $500,000 household income, consisting of executive-level professionals, a dependent spouse, and U.S. citizen school-aged children. Under the current 60-day grace period, a sudden, unexpected layoff is a highly stressful professional hurdle; under the proposed elimination, it instantly becomes a terrifying, chaotic humanitarian crisis.
Forcing an established family to uproot their entire existence overnight is fundamentally cruel. It gives parents virtually no time to responsibly wind down a life, let alone manage the fragile emotional well-being of their children. U.S. citizen children, who have known no other home but America, will be abruptly pulled out of their classrooms, separated from their friends, and stripped of their support systems mid-school-year. The emotional trauma of forcing parents to look into their children's eyes and explain that they must leave their home, their school, and their country in a matter of days—solely due to corporate restructuring—is a form of structural cruelty that no civilized society should tolerate.
Furthermore, the immediate forced departure of high-earning households triggers a destructive economic domino effect within local neighborhoods and communities. A family earning $500,000 annually is a vital pillar of the local economy. They are homeowners who pay substantial property taxes that directly fund public schools, parks, and first responders. They are active consumers who sustain local small businesses, high-end retail, tutoring centers, youth sports leagues, and neighborhood services.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Acting Director and Regulatory Policy Division,

I am writing to formally oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period" (91 Fed. Reg. 57807, published September 11, 2026). Eliminating 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) is arbitrary, capricious, and ignores the operational realities of the U.S. labor market and statutory compliance timelines. 

I am currently working in the United States as an H-1B professional in the technology company. I have lawfully lived, worked, and paid taxes in the U.S. for 11 years. Having built my life here—including signing a long-term residential lease and integrating into my local community—this rule directly threatens my ability to maintain lawful status during unforeseen economic shifts.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule based on the following substantive flaws:

1. Statutory Compliance Makes Same-Day Job Transitions Impossible
Under the proposed rule, a nonimmigrant worker falls out of status the very day after employment ends. However, even if a laid-off H-1B worker secures a new job offer immediately, the new U.S. employer cannot file Form I-129 the next day. Department of Labor (DOL) regulations mandate a 10-business-day posting period and certification for a Labor Condition Application (LCA), which routinely takes 7 to 14 days before an H-1B transfer petition can even be submitted. Eliminating the 60-day grace period effectively nullifies H-1B portability under AC21 during involuntary terminations. 

2. Failure to Quantify Severe Economic and Familial Costs
In the NPRM, DHS admits it did not estimate the monetized costs of this rule and concludes that the impact on family well-being would be "negligible". For thousands of tax-paying families, the consequences of having zero days to wrap up their affairs are catastrophic. It is logistically impossible to break a lease, sell a home or vehicle, pull children out of U.S. schools, close bank accounts, and book international flights within 24 hours of a sudden corporate layoff. By failing to quantify lease-termination penalties, distressed asset sales, lost spousal wages (such as H-4 EAD holders), and sudden recruitment losses for U.S. employers, DHS has failed to conduct a valid cost-benefit analysis under Executive Order 12866.

3. Unjustifiable Disregard for Reliance Interests
Since the 60-day grace period was codified in 2017, hundreds of thousands of skilled workers and U.S. employers have relied on 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) when making long-term housing, financial, and family decisions (91 Fed. Reg. 57815–57816). Abruptly stripping away this protection traps workers in abusive or exploitative employment conditions, as employees will fear immediate unlawful status if they report workplace violations or face retaliation. Furthermore, removing the grace period reference from 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i) (91 Fed. Reg. at 57812 n.19) strips away the realistic window to apply for a Compelling Circumstances EAD.

4. Increased Administrative Burden on USCIS and DOS
DHS claims this rule will reduce adjudication burdens. In reality, forcing workers to file frivolous defensive change-of-status applications (e.g., Form I-539 to B-2) or depart the country to undergo redundant consular processing at already backlogged U.S. embassies will drastically increase the administrative workload for both USCIS and the Department of State. 

Rather than eliminating the 60-day grace period entirely, DHS should preserve 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) to protect U.S. economic competitiveness and prevent extreme humanitarian disruption. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers. While DHS attempts in the preamble to address reliance interests, economic impacts, and family well-being, its conclusions are legally flawed, commercially detached from reality, and vulnerable under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

Specifically:
1. The Preamble's Analysis of Logistical Costs Mischaracterizes Physical Reality (Section V.A.3.a)
In Section V.A.3.a, DHS acknowledges that departing nonimmigrants incur lease termination penalties, travel costs, and lost time, but summarily dismisses these hardships by asserting that the rule "only accelerate the time in which such beneficiaries would incur these costs." This assertion defies the basic mechanics of tenancy and commerce:

Compelled Default vs. Orderly Wind-Down: Standard residential leases in the United States contractually require 30 to 60 days of written notice to vacate. Forcing an individual into unlawful status immediately upon cessation of employment makes compliance with local tenancy laws physically impossible, exposing lawful residents to forfeitures of security deposits and rent acceleration penalties, while inflicting unrecoverable bad debt onto U.S. landlords.

Predatory Travel Costs: Booking international transit on 24 hours' notice during peak travel periods costs several times more than planned travel. Compelling abrupt departures does not merely "accelerate" expenditures; it inflates them punitively.

2. Flawed "Family Assessment" and Unconsidered Medical Catastrophes (Section V.F)
Under Section V.F (Family Assessment), DHS concludes that the rule would not negatively impact family well-being, claiming that any financial loss stems from the underlying job termination rather than the rule. This reasoning is legally deficient:

Mid-Semester Academic Disruption: Employment loss causes unemployment; DHS's zero-day policy causes immediate educational exile. The rule forces dependent children (H-4, L-2, E-2) to be ripped from schools mid-semester without standard transfer protocols.

Failure to Consider Medical Emergencies: DHS completely failed to evaluate how an immediate loss of status affects family members undergoing active cancer chemotherapy, prenatal care, or post-operative rehabilitation. Terminating status with zero transition time endangers human lives when patients cannot medically clear international air travel. Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, failing to consider this vital dimension renders the rule arbitrary and capricious.

3. Economic Misconceptions Regarding Talent Retention (Section IV.D & V.B.3)
In Table 3 and Section V.B.3, DHS notes that an average of 3,795 individuals annually transition to new employers within the 60-day window, dismissing this pool by suggesting U.S. employers can simply hire domestic workers or re-import these individuals later via consular processing:

Market-Vetted Assets: A professional capable of securing a certified LCA, completing corporate interviews, and filing a new Form I-129 within a contracted 60-day economic downturn represents top-tier, battle-tested talent.

Severe Re-Hiring Deadweight Loss: Offshore re-hiring entails consular delays, visa backlogs, international relocation costs, and substantial onboarding overhead. Suggesting that American enterprises simply "re-import" departed talent months later ignores operational continuity, driving unnecessary labor friction into the U.S. economy.

4. Unlawful Dismissal of Reliance Interests (Section IV.D)
DHS dismisses the established reliance of workers, homeowners, and employers by asserting that "any reliance on the existing up to 60-day discretionary grace period would be misplaced" because the benefit is discretionary.

This directly contradicts established Supreme Court precedent (DHS v. Regents of the University of California, 140 S. Ct. 1891). An agency cannot brush aside a decade of deep economic and personal reliance—home purchases, multi-year leases, tax contributions, and business pipelines—merely because the underlying regulatory mechanism involves agency discretion.

5. Counterproductive Administrative Outcomes (Section IV.C)
DHS cites eliminating adjudicative burden on 1.9 million historical filings as its primary motivation. However, eliminating the safe harbor of 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) will incentivize tens of thousands of abruptly terminated workers to file precautionary Form I-539 Change of Status applications (e.g., to B-1/B-2 visitor status) solely to maintain authorized stay while winding down their lives. Far from relieving administrative friction, this proposal will flood USCIS lockboxes with low-priority, temporary filings.

DHS's rationales fail to justify the substantial disruption, commercial penalties, and humanitarian risks generated by this proposed rule. DHS should withdraw this NPRM and retain 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) in its entirety.
Looking forward to the considerations. Thanks!

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule eliminating the 60-day grace period for certain nonimmigrant workers following the loss of employment. I believe this proposal is deeply inhumane, unnecessarily harsh, and fails to recognize the real-life challenges faced by individuals and families during one of the most difficult periods of their lives.

Losing a job is already an incredibly stressful and painful experience. It means suddenly losing financial security, facing uncertainty about the future, and dealing with the emotional burden of unemployment. For nonimmigrant workers, these challenges are even greater because their ability to remain legally in the United States is often tied to their employment. Eliminating the 60-day grace period would turn an already devastating personal setback into an immediate immigration crisis.

Sixty days is not an unreasonable privilege. It is a basic and necessary period of time for people to regain stability after an unexpected life disruption.

People need time to search for new employment, evaluate their financial situation, manage housing and other obligations, and make important decisions about their future. They also need time to support their spouses, children, and other family members who may be directly affected by the sudden loss of income and stability. These responsibilities cannot simply disappear overnight because someone has lost a job.

Nonimmigrant workers are not merely visa holders or immigration case numbers. They are human beings who have built lives, careers, families, and communities in the United States. They work hard, pay federal, state, and local taxes as applicable, contribute to the American economy, and support American businesses and communities. Their contributions deserve recognition, and they deserve to be treated with basic fairness, dignity, and compassion.

While paying taxes does not automatically confer immigration status, it is entirely reasonable to expect a government that benefits from these workers' contributions to adopt policies that recognize their humanity and provide reasonable protections during unexpected hardships.

No one should have to face the possibility of abruptly uprooting their entire life and family simply because they lost their job.

The impact on families is particularly concerning. A spouse may also lose immigration stability, children may face disruptions to their education, and families may be forced to make life-changing decisions under extreme emotional and financial pressure. The proposed rule would punish not only workers who have lost their jobs through no fault of their own, but also their loved ones.

I also strongly disagree with the idea that reducing administrative burdens justifies eliminating this important protection. Government efficiency should not come at the expense of human dignity and family stability. The administrative convenience of an agency should not outweigh the very real suffering that this policy could impose on thousands of individuals and families.

The existing 60-day grace period represents a reasonable balance between immigration enforcement and basic human compassion. It does not guarantee permanent residence, nor does it eliminate immigration requirements. It simply gives people a limited opportunity to recover from an unexpected employment disruption and make responsible decisions about their next steps.

Losing a job should not mean immediately losing the ability to maintain a stable life. Unemployment is already a hardship. Government policy should not deliberately make that hardship worse.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security and USCIS to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the existing 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

A fair and humane immigration system should recognize that people are more than their employment status. Compassion, dignity, and basic fairness should remain fundamental principles of American immigration policy.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
**Re: Opposition to Proposed Rule USCIS-2026-0364 — Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period**

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers.

As an international researcher working in artificial intelligence in the United States, I am deeply concerned about the consequences this proposal would have for highly skilled professionals, American employers, and the country's ability to attract and retain global talent.

**1. The 60-day grace period provides essential protection against circumstances beyond workers' control.**

Employment termination is not always voluntary or related to an employee's performance. Layoffs, corporate restructuring, funding changes, and unexpected business decisions can affect even highly qualified workers. Eliminating the grace period would expose lawfully employed individuals to immediate immigration uncertainty following a job loss, despite their full compliance with immigration laws.

A reasonable transition period is not an immigration loophole. It is a practical safeguard that allows individuals to respond to unexpected employment changes while maintaining lawful status.

**2. Eliminating the grace period would undermine American competitiveness and innovation.**

The United States depends on international talent in critical fields such as artificial intelligence, semiconductor technology, biotechnology, and advanced engineering. Many international researchers spend years studying at American universities before contributing their expertise to American companies.

If an unexpected layoff could immediately jeopardize their immigration status, talented professionals would face strong incentives to pursue careers in countries offering greater stability. This would ultimately harm American innovation, economic growth, and technological leadership.

**3. The proposal would create unnecessary obstacles for American employers.**

Hiring highly skilled workers involves interviews, internal approvals, immigration petitions, and sometimes extensive background checks. These processes routinely take weeks or months, even when employers and candidates act promptly.

Without a reasonable transition period, American companies could lose qualified candidates simply because immigration paperwork cannot be completed immediately following a previous employment termination.

This would reduce labor market flexibility and impose additional administrative burdens on employers without a clear corresponding public benefit.

**4. The grace period supports compliance with immigration law rather than undermining it.**

The existing 60-day grace period provides a structured and limited opportunity for affected workers to seek new employment, apply for an appropriate change of status, or arrange departure from the United States.

Removing this mechanism would not eliminate the practical need for these transitions. Instead, it would create greater uncertainty and increase the risk of unintended status violations among individuals who have consistently attempted to comply with immigration requirements.

**5. A more proportionate approach would preserve the existing grace period.**

If DHS has concerns about misuse of the current provision, those concerns should be addressed through targeted safeguards and enforcement rather than eliminating a protection relied upon by law-abiding workers and American employers.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period and retain the existing regulatory framework.

America's ability to lead in science and technology depends not only on attracting exceptional talent but also on providing a predictable and reasonable immigration system that allows that talent to contribute productively.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sandy Burnett
comments.commentText:
DHS should not eliminate the existing grace period without clearly defining the event that triggers the alleged immediate cessation of status. The proposed rule repeatedly relies on the concept of “cessation of employment” or cessation of the activity underlying a nonimmigrant classification, but employment relationships do not always end through a single, objectively identifiable event.

For example, an employer may notify a worker of termination on one date, place the worker on paid notice or garden leave, discontinue active duties on another date, continue salary or severance payments for a further period, and formally terminate the employment relationship on a later date. Different employers may also use different payroll, benefits, and separation practices. In corporate restructurings, mergers, reductions in force, and disputed terminations, the date on which employment legally or practically ends may be unclear.

These distinctions are not merely administrative. Under DHS's proposal, the relevant date could determine whether an individual is maintaining nonimmigrant status, whether a subsequent petition or change-of-status filing is timely, and whether the individual and derivative family members must depart. A rule that attaches immediate immigration consequences to an undefined event creates substantial uncertainty for workers, employers, petitioners, and adjudicators.

The NPRM itself recognizes that determining the start and end dates of the existing grace period requires additional adjudicative work. See 91 FR 57807. But DHS does not adequately explain how eliminating the grace period resolves the underlying factual problem of identifying when employment has actually ceased. Instead, the proposal risks making the consequences of an uncertain employment date more severe.

DHS should explain, with concrete examples, how it would treat at least the following situations:

1. An employee remains on payroll and receives regular wages after being relieved of active duties.
2. An employee is placed on paid garden leave during a contractual notice period.
3. An employee receives severance payments after the employment relationship has ended.
4. An employee is subject to a termination date that is later corrected or disputed by the employer.
5. An employee's work authorization, employer sponsorship, payroll status, and formal employment relationship end on different dates.

DHS must also clarify whether the relevant event is the last day of productive work, the date the employer-employee relationship legally ends, the last day of paid employment, or another objectively verifiable event. These concepts are not interchangeable.

Under the Administrative Procedure Act, DHS must consider important aspects of the problem and provide a reasoned explanation for its regulatory choice. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). A rule imposing immediate and potentially severe immigration consequences cannot reasonably depend on an undefined factual trigger without explaining how that trigger will be identified and applied consistently.

At minimum, DHS should retain a transition period while it establishes a clear, prospective, and administrable definition of employment cessation. If DHS proceeds with the proposal, it should expressly provide that a worker will not be treated as having violated status based on a good-faith, objectively reasonable understanding of the employment end date where the employer's own records or actions create ambiguity.

DHS should not shift the consequences of inconsistent employer practices and ambiguous termination records entirely onto nonimmigrant workers and their families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Daniel Hutchinson
comments.commentText:
DHS's conclusion that the proposed rule would not negatively affect family well-being is inadequately reasoned. The Department acknowledges that termination of employment may affect a family's disposable income, but dismisses that impact as incidental to an existing obligation to depart after a worker no longer maintains nonimmigrant status. See 91 FR 57807.

That reasoning is circular. The question is not whether an employment termination may occur independently of this rulemaking. The question is whether eliminating the existing discretionary grace period materially changes the consequences of that termination for the worker and the worker's family.

Under the current regulation, eligible workers may receive up to 60 days, subject to DHS discretion, to pursue another qualifying employment opportunity, seek a change of status, apply for adjustment of status where eligible, or prepare for departure. The proposed rule would remove that limited period. The resulting loss of time and options is a direct consequence of the regulatory change, even if the underlying employment termination is not.

DHS's analysis also appears to equate the existence of a legal obligation to depart with the absence of a meaningful regulatory impact. That is a false equivalence. A regulation can materially change the timing, feasibility, and cost of complying with an existing legal obligation. Eliminating a limited transition period may force a family to make immediate decisions concerning housing, schooling, childcare, medical care, relocation, and the disposition of property, while simultaneously disrupting the principal worker's ability to secure a new qualifying position or pursue another lawful immigration option.

The impact is not limited to the principal worker. The NPRM expressly covers derivative family members. A spouse may have employment or other commitments, and children may be enrolled in school or receiving ongoing educational services. A family may have entered into leases, mortgages, childcare arrangements, or other contractual obligations in reasonable reliance on the regulatory framework that DHS is now proposing to eliminate.

DHS should not dismiss these consequences merely because the family may ultimately be required to depart. The relevant regulatory question is whether the proposed rule makes the consequences more abrupt, costly, or difficult to manage than under the existing framework.

DHS should provide a meaningful analysis of the effects on family well-being, including the practical consequences for derivative spouses and children, and explain why those consequences are justified. It should also explain why less disruptive alternatives—such as a shorter transition period, a defined period for pending filings, or a limited exception for involuntary employment termination—would not adequately address the Department's stated objectives.

A conclusion that the rule has no negative family-well-being impact cannot substitute for an analysis of the consequences created by removing the existing transition mechanism. DHS should revise its analysis and explain its conclusion based on the actual incremental effects of the proposed rule, rather than attributing those effects to employment termination alone.
comments.reason: The commenter argues against eliminating the grace period because doing so negatively impacts workers and their families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Peter Braun
comments.commentText:
DHS should explain how the proposed elimination of the discretionary grace period will operate when an affected individual has timely pursued an alternative lawful immigration option but cannot obtain an adjudication before the employment-based status underlying the individual's admission or stay ceases.

The NPRM identifies several alternatives that may be available to affected individuals, including filing a change-of-status application, an adjustment-of-status application, or an application for employment authorization based on compelling circumstances. However, the practical availability and legal effect of these options differ substantially. Some require a qualifying underlying petition or other statutory eligibility conditions. Others may not provide immediate employment authorization or an immediate determination that the applicant may remain in the United States.

The proposed rule does not adequately explain how DHS expects individuals to navigate these alternatives when the time available to act may be effectively eliminated.

For example, an individual may have a qualifying basis to pursue adjustment of status but may not yet have a current priority date. Another individual may be eligible to request a change of status but may need additional time to obtain documents, secure a new school admission, or prepare a complete filing. A worker may also have a new employer willing to file a petition, but the employer may require time to complete the petition and supporting documentation.

These are not necessarily situations involving noncompliance or disregard of immigration law. They may involve individuals actively attempting to comply with the law while navigating procedures that require documentation, employer cooperation, agency filing systems, and adjudication time.

DHS should distinguish between an individual who takes no steps to maintain or obtain lawful status and an individual who timely pursues an available statutory or regulatory option but faces unavoidable processing or preparation delays. The proposed rule's categorical approach does not adequately address this distinction.

DHS should specifically explain:

1. Whether and under what circumstances a timely filed Form I-539, Form I-485, or Form I-765 provides a basis for the individual to remain in the United States after the underlying employment ends.
2. How the proposed rule interacts with pending petitions and applications that have not yet been adjudicated.
3. Whether DHS has considered the time required for employers and applicants to prepare and submit complete filings.
4. How the Department will prevent individuals from being penalized for agency processing delays or other circumstances beyond their reasonable control.
5. Whether DHS will provide a defined transition mechanism for individuals who have already begun pursuing an alternative lawful immigration option before the effective date.

DHS cannot simply list alternative immigration benefits in the NPRM without analyzing whether those alternatives are realistically accessible within the time available under the proposed rule. The existence of a theoretical filing option does not establish that the option provides a practical or legally sufficient substitute for the existing grace period.

Under the APA, DHS must consider important aspects of the problem and provide a reasoned explanation for its chosen approach. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). DHS should therefore explain how the proposed rule accounts for government processing delays, employer-dependent filing procedures, and the practical time required to pursue alternative lawful immigration options.

At minimum, DHS should adopt a transition provision protecting individuals who, before the effective date, have already taken documented steps to pursue another lawful immigration classification or benefit. It should also explain the legal treatment of pending applications and petitions rather than leaving these questions to uncertain future adjudications.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the rule creates practical difficulties and fails to account for delays in alternative status applications.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Josie Ford
comments.commentText:
DHS's central statutory justification for this proposal is insufficiently developed. The Department repeatedly invokes INA § 214(a), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a), as authority to establish the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission and argues that individuals must depart upon cessation of the employment or activity underlying their classification.

However, the existence of broad authority to prescribe conditions of admission does not, by itself, establish that Congress expressly required the immediate termination of every affected individual's authorized stay upon cessation of employment, regardless of the circumstances or the remaining period of admission.

Section 214(a)(1) authorizes the Secretary to prescribe regulations governing the time and conditions of admission of nonimmigrants. It does not expressly state that every cessation of employment must result in immediate departure, nor does it expressly prohibit DHS from establishing a limited, discretionary transition period during which an individual may pursue another lawful immigration option.

DHS therefore must distinguish between two separate propositions:

First, the underlying nonimmigrant classifications generally require qualifying employment or activity.

Second, Congress has required DHS to eliminate any limited regulatory period during which an individual may pursue another lawful immigration option after that employment or activity ceases.

The first proposition does not automatically establish the second.

The current regulation does not provide an unconditional right to remain for 60 days. It provides a limited period, subject to DHS discretion, and does not independently authorize employment. The Department must explain why this carefully limited mechanism is incompatible with the statutory scheme rather than merely asserting that it creates a disconnect between status and employment.

DHS's reasoning also risks conflating the termination of the underlying employment relationship, the maintenance of nonimmigrant status, the expiration of an authorized period of stay, and the commencement of unlawful presence. These are distinct legal concepts. The Department should identify the specific statutory and regulatory provisions governing each consequence and explain how its proposed interpretation follows from those provisions.

If Congress intended employment termination itself to require immediate departure in every affected classification, DHS should identify the statutory language establishing that result. A general delegation of authority to regulate admission conditions should not be treated as though it were an express congressional command to adopt the most restrictive regulatory approach available.

The Department should also explain how its interpretation accounts for INA § 214(n), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(n), which separately establishes portability provisions for qualifying H-1B workers. Although section 214(n) does not guarantee portability to every worker or resolve every scenario addressed by this rulemaking, its existence demonstrates that Congress has expressly addressed certain circumstances involving changes in H-1B employment. DHS should explain how its proposed interpretation of section 214(a) operates consistently with that statutory framework.

Under the APA, DHS must provide a reasoned explanation for its interpretation of the governing statute and may not substitute a conclusory assertion of broad authority for analysis of the statutory text and structure. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), (C).

DHS should therefore revise the NPRM to distinguish what the statute actually requires from what the Department independently prefers as a matter of policy. If the Department's objective is to eliminate the grace period as a policy choice, it should say so directly and provide a reasoned explanation for that choice, rather than implying that Congress has already mandated immediate departure in all covered circumstances.
comments.reason: The commenter challenges DHS's legal justification for eliminating the discretionary grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Pranshu S
comments.commentText: This rule would be very disruptive for any workers on H-1b, and their families. If they have US born children, their education would be disrupted and property sales would be difficult to manage too. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Elly Hart
comments.commentText:
DHS relies heavily on the assertion that, from October 1, 2017, through May 20, 2026, USCIS received more than 1.9 million petitions or applications on which adjudicators potentially had to perform an initial assessment concerning the discretionary grace period.

This figure does not, by itself, establish the actual administrative burden attributable to the grace period. The NPRM distinguishes between the broad population of filings that might require an initial screening and the smaller subset of cases in which a further grace-period analysis was actually required. DHS also estimates that approximately 3,795 new employer-filed Form I-129 petitions annually involve workers who may have been within the grace period.

These figures measure different things. The number of filings that potentially trigger an initial screening is not equivalent to the number of cases requiring a substantive grace-period determination, the number of cases in which the grace period was granted, or the number of additional adjudicator hours actually spent administering the provision.

DHS must therefore avoid treating the 1.9 million figure as though it represented 1.9 million substantive grace-period adjudications. Such a characterization would materially overstate the burden if most filings required only a brief threshold review or did not ultimately require a detailed determination.

The NPRM does not provide sufficiently granular information about the actual time and resources consumed by these different stages of review. In particular, it does not adequately disclose:

1. The percentage of the 1.9 million filings that required only an initial screening.
2. The percentage that required a detailed factual determination concerning employment cessation and the beneficiary's subsequent activities.
3. The average adjudicator time attributable specifically to the grace-period inquiry.
4. The number of cases in which the grace period was shortened or denied.
5. Whether the same information was already being reviewed as part of the underlying petition or application.
6. The methodology used to extrapolate the claimed administrative burden from the number of potentially affected filings.

DHS should also explain how it distinguishes the cost of identifying a potentially relevant case from the incremental cost of actually administering the grace period. These are not necessarily equivalent costs. A threshold screening process may be substantially less burdensome than the comprehensive individualized analysis described in the NPRM.

The Department's own estimate of approximately 3,795 annual new employer-filed petitions involving potentially affected workers further demonstrates why the broader screening population should not be used as a substitute for a more precise workload analysis.

Under the APA, an agency must examine relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation showing a rational connection between the facts found and the regulatory choice made. State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43. A broad count of potentially screened filings, without a sufficiently transparent estimate of actual incremental adjudication time and cost, does not establish that eliminating the entire grace period is a reasonable response.

DHS should publish or explain its underlying workload methodology and quantify the actual incremental burden attributable to the grace period. Until it does so, the Department has not adequately demonstrated that the asserted administrative burden justifies eliminating this limited discretionary mechanism for all covered classifications.
comments.reason: The comment only critiques the administrative burden data without stating a clear stance on eliminating the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anson Zhang
comments.commentText:
Dear USCIS and Department of Homeland Security,

I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B and other employment-based visa holders. I urge DHS to retain this policy, not merely for the benefit of foreign workers, but more importantly for American employers, the U.S. labor market, and America's economic competitiveness.

**1. The proposal ignores the reality of hiring in America.**

Based on my professional experience in the U.S. data science and investment industries, recruiting highly skilled professionals often requires multiple rounds of interviews, technical assessments, management approvals, and background checks. This process frequently takes several weeks or months.

Even the existing 60-day grace period is a challenging timeline. Eliminating it would make it nearly impossible for many qualified professionals affected by unexpected layoffs to transition to another American employer.

More importantly, American companies could lose access to highly qualified candidates simply because their hiring processes cannot be completed immediately. This creates unnecessary obstacles for U.S. businesses.

**2. Eliminating the grace period would impose unnecessary costs on American employers.**

American businesses invest substantial resources in recruiting and retaining talent. When qualified professionals are already living and working in the United States, employers can often hire them more efficiently than candidates who must relocate internationally.

Without the grace period, companies may face additional immigration expenses, delayed start dates, prolonged vacancies, and disruptions to business operations. Smaller companies and startups would be particularly vulnerable.

A policy intended to reduce administrative burdens on USCIS should not create significantly greater costs for American businesses.

**3. This proposal could weaken America's economic competitiveness.**

Highly skilled professionals contribute to American innovation, productivity, and business growth. Their work supports broader teams, including American workers, and strengthens the global competitiveness of U.S. companies.

When an employee is laid off due to restructuring or economic conditions, their skills and experience do not suddenly lose value to the American economy.

Forcing these professionals to leave the country before another American employer can reasonably complete its hiring process risks wasting valuable human capital.

Furthermore, eliminating the grace period does not guarantee additional employment opportunities for American workers. Instead, businesses may experience hiring difficulties, project delays, higher costs, or increased incentives to move certain operations overseas.

**4. The economic consequences deserve greater consideration.**

The proposed rule acknowledges potential productivity losses for employers but does not comprehensively quantify the resulting economic costs.

Before eliminating an established policy, DHS should carefully evaluate its impact on American businesses, including recruitment expenses, operational disruptions, lost productivity, and reduced labor market flexibility.

Administrative efficiency should not come at the expense of broader economic efficiency.

**5. The existing 60-day grace period is reasonable and balanced.**

The current policy is temporary and discretionary. It does not independently authorize employment or exempt anyone from existing immigration requirements.

It simply provides a reasonable transition period that reflects how the American labor market actually operates.

Unexpected layoffs are a normal part of a dynamic economy. American employers should have a fair opportunity to recruit qualified professionals already in the country without being constrained by an immediate immigration deadline.

**Conclusion**

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing 60-day grace period.

America should pursue policies that strengthen domestic businesses, promote innovation, and maintain an efficient and competitive labor market.

Eliminating this grace period risks increasing costs for American employers, disrupting business operations, and driving valuable talent and economic activity away from the United States.

The fundamental question should not simply be whether eliminating the grace period makes immigration administration easier, but whether it makes the American economy stronger.

I firmly believe it does not.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they strongly oppose eliminating the grace period and urge DHS to retain it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Lenard Richardson
comments.commentText:
DHS's proposal raises a fundamental question concerning its interpretation of the statutory framework governing the affected nonimmigrant classifications.

The Department adopted the discretionary grace period in 2016 under the same general statutory framework it now invokes to justify eliminating the provision. The relevant statutory provisions did not become newly enacted in 2026. The Department therefore must explain why the interpretation underlying the 2016 final rule is now considered inconsistent with the governing statute.

The 2016 final rule did not overlook the employment-related nature of the affected classifications. Rather, DHS expressly recognized that these workers' eligibility was connected to qualifying employment or activity and adopted a limited discretionary transition mechanism to address the practical consequences of employment cessation.

The 2026 NPRM now characterizes the grace period as creating a misalignment between nonimmigrant status and the statutory basis for admission. But the Department has not sufficiently explained why the same statutory structure could support the 2016 regulatory framework for nearly a decade but now requires the elimination of that framework.

DHS is not prohibited from changing its interpretation or regulatory policy merely because it previously adopted a different approach. However, the Department must acknowledge the change and provide a reasoned explanation. Fox Television, 556 U.S. at 515–16; State Farm, 463 U.S. at 42–43.

In particular, DHS should explain whether its present position is based on:

1. A newly identified statutory provision or controlling judicial decision.
2. New evidence demonstrating that the 2016 framework is inconsistent with the operation of the affected nonimmigrant classifications.
3. Administrative experience showing that the grace period has produced consequences that could not reasonably have been anticipated in 2016.
4. A change in the Department's policy priorities, rather than a conclusion that the prior rule was legally impermissible.

These explanations are materially different. If the Department is asserting that the 2016 rule was inconsistent with the statute from the beginning, it should identify the precise statutory language and explain why its prior interpretation was legally deficient. If the Department is instead making a policy choice based on administrative experience, it should provide the relevant evidence and explain why the benefits of the original framework no longer outweigh the costs.

DHS should also avoid relying on the phrase "restore its previous and long-standing policy" as a substitute for analyzing the legal and practical consequences of the proposed change. The 2016 final rule became effective on January 17, 2017, and has governed the relevant regulatory framework for nearly a decade. The fact that a different policy existed before 2017 does not eliminate the reliance interests and operational consequences created by the subsequent regulatory framework.

The Department must evaluate the policy that has actually been in force, not simply characterize the proposed action as a restoration of an earlier approach.

The Supreme Court's decision in Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), reinforces the importance of considering serious reliance interests when an agency rescinds an established policy. Although the precise regulatory context differs, the governing principle is relevant: an agency must consider important aspects of the problem, including significant reliance interests, when changing an established policy.

DHS should therefore provide a substantially more detailed explanation of why the 2016 framework is no longer appropriate, identify the evidence supporting its current interpretation, and explain how it has accounted for the consequences of reversing a regulatory framework that has operated for nearly ten years.

Without that explanation, the Department risks substituting a new policy preference for the reasoned statutory and factual analysis required by the Administrative Procedure Act.
comments.reason: The comment critiques the legal justification of the proposal without explicitly supporting or opposing the elimination.
