comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security's proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

While I understand the government's interest in maintaining immigration compliance and reducing administrative burdens, eliminating this grace period would create unnecessary hardships for workers, their families, and American businesses. Ultimately, it would also undermine the economic interests and global competitiveness of the United States.

1. Negative Impact on American Businesses

The 60-day grace period provides an essential transition period for workers who unexpectedly lose their jobs to seek new employment. Without it, American companies could lose access to highly qualified professionals who are already in the United States and have valuable industry experience.

Hiring and onboarding replacements takes time and resources. Losing qualified candidates simply because of immigration-related timing could delay projects, increase recruitment costs, and reduce productivity. This would create additional obstacles for American employers rather than helping them build stronger teams.

2. Disproportionate Impact on Families

Employment-based immigration affects entire families, not just the primary visa holder. Many workers have spouses and children who have established their lives in the United States, attending local schools, building friendships, and becoming part of their communities.

If a worker loses their job unexpectedly, eliminating the grace period could force the entire family to leave the country with little time to make arrangements. Children should not have their education and stability disrupted because of an employment decision made by their parent's company. Spouses should not have to abandon their careers and lives because of circumstances beyond their control.

Layoffs and corporate restructuring are common economic realities, not necessarily the result of any wrongdoing by employees. The consequences should not be disproportionately imposed on innocent family members.

3. Sixty Days Is Already a Limited Transition Period

Finding a new job is not instantaneous. Professional recruitment often involves multiple interview rounds, technical assessments, background checks, and internal approvals. Immigration procedures add further complexity and time.

Even highly qualified professionals may need several weeks or months to secure a suitable position, particularly during economic downturns when companies reduce hiring.

The existing 60-day grace period is not an unlimited right to remain in the country or work without authorization. It provides a reasonable opportunity to find new employment, pursue a lawful change of status, or arrange an orderly departure.

Eliminating this period entirely would turn an unexpected job loss into an immediate immigration crisis, creating unnecessary uncertainty for both workers and employers.

4. Damage to America's Global Competitiveness

The United States has long benefited from attracting talented professionals from around the world. International talent contributes significantly to American leadership in technology, science, engineering, medicine, and other critical industries.

However, professionals consider immigration stability and predictability when deciding where to build their careers and families. If an unexpected layoff could force an entire family to leave the country almost immediately, talented individuals may choose other countries with more predictable immigration policies.

The ability to retain qualified talent is just as important as the ability to recruit it. This proposal risks weakening America's long-term position in the global competition for skilled workers.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing discretionary 60-day grace period.

If the government seeks greater administrative efficiency, it should improve application procedures and clarify eligibility requirements rather than eliminate an important transition mechanism.

Losing a job should not automatically become a life-altering immigration crisis for an individual and their family, especially when they have complied with the law and contributed to the American economy.

Preserving the 60-day grace period is a reasonable policy that benefits workers, American businesses, and the United States as a whole.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing hardships for workers, families, and businesses.

The grace period allows employers to retain access to qualified professionals who are already in the United States and familiar with the American workplace. Without it, companies seeking to hire these individuals could face additional immigration-related delays, legal costs, and uncertainty.

A sudden job loss should not force children to abandon their education or families to leave their homes with little time to prepare. Spouses may also lose their ability to work or continue their studies.

3. Sixty Days Is a Reasonable Minimum Transition Period

Finding a new job is rarely immediate. Professional hiring processes often involve multiple interviews, technical assessments, background checks, and internal approvals. When immigration sponsorship is involved, additional legal and administrative procedures are required.

Even highly qualified professionals may need several weeks or months to secure another position, especially during economic downturns when hiring slows down.

Conclusion

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing 60-day grace period.

If the goal is to improve immigration administration, DHS should focus on streamlining procedures and clarifying requirements rather than eliminating a practical and important safeguard.

A fair and effective immigration system should recognize that job loss is sometimes unavoidable and that people who have followed the rules and contributed to the American economy deserve a reasonable opportunity to transition.

Preserving the 60-day grace period is not only fair to workers and their families; it is also in the best interests of American businesses and the long-term competitiveness of the United States.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Alok Kumar
comments.commentText:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services
DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364
Re: Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

Dear Department of Homeland Security:

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw its proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

As an H-1B professional with a spouse and a young U.S.-citizen child, I am deeply concerned about what this proposal would mean for families like mine who have built their lives in the United States.

Many H-1B workers have spent years living and working here. We have contributed our skills to American businesses, paid taxes, supported local economies, and built relationships in our communities. We have established homes, raised families, and come to consider the United States our home. Yet an unexpected job loss could leave us without a meaningful opportunity to find another employer or make arrangements for our families before having to leave.

My family and I have made long-term decisions with the expectation that we could continue building our lives here while following U.S. immigration rules. Our home, relationships, and community are here, and we are raising our young U.S.-citizen child here. If I unexpectedly lost my job, finding another eligible position, coordinating an employer’s immigration filing, and making decisions about our home and family would take time.

For a family with a young child, an immediate departure would mean much more than booking a flight. It could require finding housing abroad, arranging medical care, managing financial and housing obligations in the United States, and leaving behind friends and community ties—all while dealing with the loss of income. For children who are U.S. citizens, it could mean an abrupt disruption to the only home and community they have known.

It is difficult to understand why people who have followed the rules and spent many years contributing to the United States should be denied even a short opportunity to find another eligible job or arrange an orderly departure. The existing grace period recognizes that employment can end unexpectedly and that workers and their families need a reasonable amount of time to respond.

The current grace period is limited and discretionary. It does not guarantee a new job or an extension of status. It gives eligible workers and their families an opportunity to explore lawful options, including finding a new employer or preparing to depart.

I understand DHS’s concern about the administrative burden of determining when employment ended and whether the grace period applies. I urge DHS to consider simplifying the process rather than eliminating the grace period. For example, DHS could:

1. Establish a clear approach to the start date using a termination notice or other standard employment records.
2. Provide a checklist of acceptable evidence so workers and employers know what to submit.
3. Allow a worker’s signed statement when standard records are unavailable, subject to verification where appropriate.
4. Use the full eligible grace period as the ordinary default, while preserving DHS’s ability to review cases involving fraud, misrepresentation, or other specific concerns.

These measures could reduce uncertainty and make eligibility easier to assess. I ask DHS to evaluate their potential to reduce administrative burden and compare that with the consequences of eliminating the grace period.

DHS should consider the effects on workers’ ability to transition to another eligible job, employers’ ability to retain experienced talent, and families’ ability to manage an orderly transition. I also ask DHS to explain how it accounted for disruptions to children, housing, medical care, and community ties, as well as the reliance interests of people who made long-term decisions while this protection was in place.

The United States benefits when skilled professionals can continue contributing and employers can retain talent already in the country. A brief transition period supports those goals while treating workers and their families with fairness and dignity.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that DHS retain the existing 60-day grace period and pursue administrative improvements to make it clearer and easier to administer.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
An H-1B professional and parent of a U.S.-citizen child
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposal, arguing it harms H-1B workers and their families.

comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22: I oppose eliminating the 60-day grace period

I strongly oppose DHS's proposal to remove the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

1. It punishes workers for layoffs they didn't cause. Most people who lose an H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN or E job lose it through layoffs, restructuring or a business closing, not through anything they did. Under this rule they would fall out of status the day their job ends. Professionals who have followed every rule, paid taxes and contributed for years would have no fair chance to find a new sponsor.

2. It hurts families and U.S. communities. Spouses and children would lose status at the same moment. Children could be pulled out of school mid-year. Families would have to break leases, sell homes and leave their communities with almost no notice.

Please keep the 60-day grace period. At a minimum, keep it for workers whose employment ends involuntarily.

Respectfully,
Naresh Meda

Subject: Preserving the 60-Day Grace Period to Protect America’s Workforce and Economic Competitiveness

The United States has built its global leadership in technology and innovation by attracting talented professionals from around the world. Eliminating the 60-day grace period for employment-based visa holders could undermine this competitive advantage.

Job loss is not always a reflection of an individual’s skills or performance. Layoffs, corporate restructuring, and economic downturns can affect even the most talented professionals. Removing the grace period would force skilled workers to leave the country before they have a reasonable opportunity to find new employment.

This would not only harm foreign professionals but also American businesses. Companies would lose access to experienced talent already contributing to the U.S. economy. Instead of allowing these individuals to transition between employers and continue creating value, the policy could push them toward competing countries.

Furthermore, reducing employment flexibility could discourage talented individuals from choosing the United States as a place to build their careers. Over time, this could weaken innovation, slow technological progress, and reduce America’s ability to compete in critical industries such as artificial intelligence, software engineering, and advanced manufacturing.

The United States should focus on retaining talent, not creating unnecessary barriers that drive it away. A reasonable grace period strengthens the American economy by allowing skilled professionals to remain productive and American companies to retain access to global expertise.

I strongly urge policymakers to preserve the 60-day grace period and consider the long-term consequences that eliminating it could have on America’s economic growth, innovation, and global leadership.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposal because it does not adequately demonstrate that the benefits outweigh the significant costs it would impose on U.S. employers, families, communities, and government agencies.

Several aspects of the proposal appear insufficiently supported:

1. DHS argues that adjudicators spend time determining whether individuals qualify for the grace period. However, the proposal does not provide any estimate of the number of USCIS labor hours that would actually be saved by eliminating the grace period.

2. The proposal does not quantify any projected dollar savings to the government. Without a quantified estimate of benefits, it is difficult to evaluate whether the proposal is justified.

3. Rather than reducing administrative burden, the proposal appears to shift that burden from USCIS to other parts of the government, including immigration courts and enforcement agencies.

4. The proposal would reduce labor-market flexibility and could negatively affect U.S. employers that rely on highly skilled workers. Employers seeking to hire qualified workers who have recently experienced layoffs would face additional uncertainty and delays.

5. The proposal would likely increase the workload of immigration courts, ICE, and other government entities by requiring additional enforcement actions and proceedings. These resources could be more effectively devoted to addressing actual immigration fraud and other higher-priority enforcement matters.

6. A U.S. employer attempting to fill a critical position may lose access to an otherwise eligible worker solely because that worker would be required to depart the United States immediately following a layoff. This creates avoidable hiring risks and uncertainty for American businesses.

7. The proposal does not adequately consider the impact on families and local communities. Many affected individuals and families may have purchased homes, enrolled children in school, established businesses, and become active members of their communities. Requiring immediate departure could impose significant financial and emotional costs that extend beyond the affected worker.

8. DHS acknowledges limitations in its data but does not provide reliable information regarding how many individuals currently rely on the grace period. Without understanding the scope of current usage, it is difficult to accurately assess the proposal's economic and social impacts.

Overall, the proposal does not provide sufficient evidence that eliminating the grace period would produce meaningful benefits. Instead, it risks reducing U.S. competitiveness, increasing administrative burdens elsewhere in government, disrupting employers' ability to recruit qualified talent, and imposing significant hardships on families and communities. The proposal may ultimately create more problems than it solves while providing little measurable benefit to American workers.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposal due to costs for employers, families, and agencies, and lack of justification.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully and strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrants.

Lawful visa holders have followed the immigration system, maintained legal status, worked with authorization, and regularly paid federal, state, Social Security, Medicare, property, sales, and other applicable taxes. Many have contributed to the United States for years while waiting in extremely long employment-based green card backlogs through no fault of their own.

Job loss is often sudden and involuntary. It is neither reasonable nor humane to expect a worker and their family to leave the United States immediately after a layoff. Families may own homes, have mortgages, leases, vehicles, medical appointments, and children enrolled in school. They cannot withdraw or transfer their children, manage or sell their property, close their financial obligations, arrange international travel, and relocate their entire lives in a single day. Such a requirement would cause severe emotional, financial, and educational harm, especially to children who have no control over their parent’s employment situation.

Removing the grace period would also give excessive power to employers and could worsen abusive or unethical corporate practices. If termination immediately places a worker and their entire family out of status, some employers or managers may use that vulnerability to keep employees constantly fearful and under pressure. Workers may feel forced to accept unreasonable workloads, unpaid hours, unfair treatment, discrimination, wage violations, or unsafe working conditions because speaking up could result in immediate termination and displacement of their family.

This extreme imbalance of power could allow unethical employers to benefit from workers who are afraid to resign, report misconduct, request fair treatment, or change jobs. A system that effectively forces a person to choose between enduring workplace abuse and immediately uprooting their family conflicts with fundamental principles of human dignity, worker protection, and basic fairness.

The existing 60-day grace period offers an important safeguard against coercion and retaliation. It does not guarantee employment, permanent residence, or unrestricted work authorization. It simply provides a short and reasonable opportunity to find another sponsoring employer, file a lawful change of status, or arrange an orderly departure. Even 60 days can be difficult because hiring, interviews, background checks, legal review, and preparation of a transfer petition take time.

Eliminating the grace period would also harm responsible American employers by preventing them from recruiting experienced workers who are already lawfully present in the country. It could disrupt projects, increase hiring costs, weaken workforce mobility, and cause the United States to lose skilled professionals to competing countries.

A person who loses a job should not immediately lose the ability to protect their family and organize their life with dignity. Employment termination is already financially and emotionally devastating; it should not automatically become an immigration emergency the very next day.

I strongly urge DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period. At an absolute minimum, affected workers and their families must be given a reasonable transition period to pursue another lawful status or prepare for an orderly departure. Basic fairness, family stability, worker protection, human dignity, and practical reality all support keeping this essential safeguard.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing hardships to families and increased employer abuse.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by A B
comments.commentText:
I am submitting this comment in my personal capacity to ask DHS to withdraw this proposal and keep the 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

I manage a team at a U.S. technology company. Over my career, I have worked alongside many talented colleagues on work visas. I have seen how a reorganization can end a job with little warning, even for strong performers. For these colleagues, the 60-day grace period is the difference between a hard few weeks and a family crisis. It gives them a short window to find a new employer, sort out their status or plan an orderly move.

The grace period is already narrow. It lasts 60 days at most, or less if the I-94 expires sooner. Its main use is letting a skilled worker move to a new employer in the same classification. That is the kind of job mobility Congress supported through AC21 and H-1B portability. A short bridge between two qualifying jobs does not break the link between status and employment.

Without the grace period, someone laid off through no fault of their own would be out of status the next day. As the proposal itself explains, that can mean losing the ability to extend or change status, accruing unlawful presence that can lead to 3- or 10-year bars, and potential bars to a future green card. These are lasting consequences for an event the worker did not control.

The impact on families concerns me most. Spouses and children would lose status at the same moment. Spouses who are authorized to work, including E and L-2 spouses and certain H-4 spouses, could lose their own jobs. Children could have to leave school in the middle of the year. People who have built their lives here and contributed to their communities deserve more than a single day to respond.

Ending the grace period also hurts employers. When a skilled person already in the U.S. loses a job, other companies want to hire them. Without the grace period, that person would have to leave the country and wait abroad for an approval, a visa appointment and readmission before starting. In practice, H-1B portability would only help workers who line up a new job before their last day. Employers would also owe return transportation costs for terminated H-1B and O-1 workers more often. None of this makes U.S. employers more competitive.

I also do not believe the change meets its goal of reducing administrative burden. DHS's own proposal acknowledges that it would lead to Notices to Appear, more referrals to the immigration courts and more work for ICE. That moves the burden to a more costly part of the system rather than removing it. If the grace period is hard to administer, a clear, simple rule would fix that better than elimination.

Finally, workers, families and employers have relied on this policy since 2017 when making decisions about careers, homes, schools and hiring. DHS assessed the impact only qualitatively. Before taking this protection away, DHS should at least measure how many people would be affected and what it would cost them.

I respectfully ask DHS to:

Withdraw the proposal and keep the 60-day grace period.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly asks DHS to withdraw the proposal and keep the 60-day grace period.

A fairer system would weigh quantitative, job-related factors — salary, skills, experience, and contributions, including taxes paid over years of lawful work — rather than nationality alone.
Until that backlog is fixed, the grace period is one of the few humane safeguards in the system. It does not authorize work, and it does not excuse unlawful presence. Please withdraw this proposal and retain the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period.

As an H-1B worker, I understand that my immigration status is tied to my employment. However, expecting a worker and their family to leave the United States immediately after an unexpected termination is neither reasonable nor practical. Employment can end without advance notice for reasons entirely outside the worker’s control, including layoffs, restructuring, or business closures.

Many H-1B workers have established lives in the United States. They may have children attending school, a spouse with dependent status, a home or lease, financial commitments, medical needs, and other obligations. A family cannot realistically withdraw children from school, end housing arrangements, sell or move personal belongings, settle financial matters, and arrange international travel in a single day.

The current grace period does not guarantee continued employment or provide an unlimited stay. It simply offers a limited and reasonable amount of time for affected workers to find another qualifying employer, file the appropriate immigration paperwork, or make an orderly departure. We are not asking for the grace period to be extended. We are asking that the existing protection be retained so families have a fair opportunity to respond to an unexpected loss of employment.

Eliminating the grace period would create unnecessary instability and hardship for workers and their dependents while also making the United States less attractive to skilled professionals. Any reduction in administrative burden for the government should be weighed against the significant disruption imposed on law-abiding families.

I respectfully request that DHS retain the current discretionary 60-day grace period. At a minimum, the final rule should provide a clearly defined and reasonable transition period following termination so affected workers and their families can make appropriate legal and personal arrangements.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing hardship and the need for time to relocate.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Public Comment Opposing USCIS-2026-0364 – Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period

Dear DHS and USCIS Officials,

I respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B and other employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

The existing grace period provides a reasonable opportunity for legally employed professionals to find new employment, transfer their immigration sponsorship, or make arrangements following an unexpected job loss. Eliminating it would create unnecessary hardship for workers, their families, and American employers.

Many H-1B professionals have lived and worked legally in the United States for years, contributing to the economy, paying taxes, purchasing homes, and raising children. Sudden employment termination should not immediately jeopardize their families’ stability, children’s education, or lawful immigration status.

This proposal is particularly concerning for individuals with approved I-140 petitions who have already completed significant immigration requirements but face years of waiting due to employment-based green card backlogs.

American employers would also face additional recruitment challenges, increased immigration processing costs, and potential loss of experienced professionals.

The 60-day grace period does not provide unrestricted employment authorization or permanent immigration benefits. It simply offers a limited, practical transition period that supports immigration compliance and workforce stability.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the existing 60-day grace period. Administrative efficiency and immigration enforcement can be improved without imposing disproportionate hardship on law-abiding professionals and their families.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Respectfully,
A Concerned H-1B Professional
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

This change would create serious hardship for skilled immigrants who have built their careers and families in the United States. Their ability to remain in the country is tied to employment, yet layoffs and restructuring can happen through no fault of their own.

The current grace period gives workers a limited opportunity to find another employer, obtain sponsorship, and complete required immigration filings. A job search can involve interviews, offer negotiations, employer decisions, and legal paperwork. These steps often take weeks or months and are not entirely within the worker's control. Eliminating the grace period would force people to make major decisions under extreme time pressure.

The proposal would also increase the imbalance between employers and workers. Employment-based visa holders cannot change jobs as freely as U.S. citizens or permanent residents; a new job generally requires an employer willing to sponsor them and comply with immigration rules. Without a reasonable transition period, workers may feel pressured to accept unfavorable pay or working conditions rather than risk losing their ability to remain in the country.

The consequences extend to families. Many workers have spouses and children who depend on the primary visa holder's status. Sudden job loss could disrupt a spouse's employment, children's schooling, housing, and established community ties. Requiring an entire family to prepare to leave the United States on very short notice creates hardship far beyond the individual who lost a job.

Immigration processing also takes time. Finding a willing employer does not instantly complete a transfer. Employers need time to prepare and file petitions, and government processing is outside the worker's control. Workers should not face avoidable disruption because of administrative timelines they cannot control.

The existing rule already provides discretion: it allows up to 60 days, not an automatic or unconditional extension in every case. USCIS can assess individual circumstances and shorten or deny the grace period where appropriate. If DHS has concerns about misuse, it should clarify eligibility or improve administration rather than eliminate this important safeguard for everyone.

Finally, the proposal could make the United States less attractive to skilled professionals. Immigrants contribute to American businesses, innovation, taxes, and local communities. Greater uncertainty about whether a temporary job loss could force a family to leave may discourage talented people from building their futures here.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposal and preserve the discretionary grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). The existing framework balances immigration compliance with the realities of employment transitions. Losing a job should not automatically put a worker's family stability and future in the United States at risk.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that removing the grace period causes hardship, pressure, and disadvantage for workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my sincere opposition to proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary up to 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant visa classifications. Eliminating this critical safe harbor is highly impractical, structurally destabilizing to the American economy, and punitive to high-skilled professionals who contribute significantly to U.S. innovation.

Request this proposal should be withdrawn based on the following critical points:
1. Severely Harms U.S. Business Competitiveness: High-skilled layoffs often occur unexpectedly due to macroeconomic shifts or corporate restructuring. Forcing international experts to leave the country the day after employment ends deprives U.S. companies of a readily available, pre-vetted talent pool. Competitor nations with agile immigration frameworks will absorb this talent, directly undermining American technological and economic leadership.

2. Creates Unrealistic Administrative Demands: It is logistically impossible for a professional to wrap up their life, terminate housing leases, close financial accounts, and arrange international relocation for a family within 24 hours. The current 60-day window provides a necessary, humane period to execute an orderly departure or secure new employment, preventing immediate, involuntary unlawful presence.

3. Undermines the H-1B Portability Framework: Congress explicitly intended for high-skilled nonimmigrants to have job mobility. By erasing the grace period, DHS functionally renders H-1B portability useless for terminated workers, as they would have no lawful status remaining to bridge the gap during the filing of a change of employer petition.

4.Exacerbates Backlogs and Processing Burdens: Stripping the automatic grace period will force thousands of individuals to file costly, defensive Applications to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status (Form I-539) simply to bridge a multi-week gap between jobs. This will needlessly flood U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) with paperwork, worsening existing agency backlogs and increasing administrative friction.

For above reasons, the discretionary 60-day grace period remains an indispensable tool for balancing program integrity with economic stability and human dignity. I urge DHS to preserve the current regulation and withdraw this proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period" (docket USCIS-2026-0364) and to urge DHS to keep 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) in place.

The grace period was added in 2016 for good reason: it lets highly skilled workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own, usually because of layoffs or restructuring, take an orderly next step. In that window they can find a new employer, file for a change of status, or prepare to leave the country. Without it, a worker who is laid off without notice would be out of status the same day, with no time to sell a home, end a lease, pull children out of school, or settle their affairs.

DHS's own analysis estimates that about 3,795 people each year, nearly all of them H-1B workers, have a new employer petition filed during the grace period. These are people who were successfully rehired by U.S. employers who needed their skills. Removing the grace period would push many of them, and their spouses and children, to leave the country abruptly even though a new employer is ready to hire them. That harms U.S. businesses that rely on this talent and wastes the investment those workers and employers have already made.

The grace period is already discretionary and capped at 60 days or the end of the authorized stay, whichever comes first, so DHS keeps the ability to shorten or deny it in individual cases. Eliminating it entirely does not meaningfully reduce administrative burden, but it does create serious hardship for law-abiding families and for the employers who depend on them.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal and keep the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to keep the current 60-day grace period in place.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jayakumar S
comments.commentText:
Subject: Request to Retain the 60-Day H-1B Grace Period and Consider Extending It to 90 Days

I have been working in the United States for the past eight years on an H-1B visa and have an approved I-140. I have two school-going children, one in high school and the other in elementary school. Removing the existing 60-day grace period would create severe hardships for my family and other H-1B visa holders and their dependents. An unexpected departure from the United States would significantly affect my children’s education, emotional well-being, and overall family stability. I would like to highlight the following concerns based on my family’s circumstances.

1. Mental and Emotional Impact on School-Age Children

* Sudden relocation would force children to leave their friends, teachers, school environment, and familiar surroundings.
* Abrupt changes in their daily routines and social circles can cause significant emotional distress, anxiety, and insecurity.
* Children may struggle to adjust to an entirely new environment and lifestyle in another country.
* A 60- or 90-day grace period would give children valuable time to mentally and emotionally prepare for a potential relocation, say goodbye to friends and teachers, and gradually adjust to the possibility of a new lifestyle and environment.

2. Disruption to Children’s Education

* Relocating in the middle of an academic year would interrupt children’s education and academic progress.
* Both my high-school child and elementary-school child would be forced to leave their schools unexpectedly.
* Transitioning to a different country’s educational system, curriculum, and teaching methods could create additional academic challenges.
* Such disruptions could negatively affect their academic performance and long-term educational opportunities.

3. Severe Financial Hardship for H-1B Families

* Most H-1B families have significant financial commitments, including apartment leases, car payments, insurance, and household expenses.
* Sudden departure would force families to terminate rental leases early and incur substantial penalties.
* Families may have to sell their cars and household belongings, including furniture, televisions, and other essential items, at significant financial losses.
* Last-minute international flight bookings can be extremely expensive.
* After returning to their home country, the primary visa holder may need two or more months to secure new employment and housing, creating additional financial instability. So the grace period help me to find new job in India before leave from USA.

4. Mental Stress and Health Impact on the Entire Family

* The uncertainty of losing employment and immigration status creates enormous mental stress for both the primary H-1B visa holder and H-4 dependents.
* The pressure of finding a new job, arranging international relocation, and managing financial commitments within a very limited timeframe can cause severe anxiety and emotional distress.
* Spouses and children also experience uncertainty about their future, employment opportunities, education, and family stability.
* Sudden relocation could interrupt ongoing medical treatments, regular doctor consultations, specialist appointments, and follow-up care for both children and adults, potentially affecting their health and continuity of care.
* Prolonged stress and uncertainty can negatively affect the mental and physical health of the entire family.

Recommendation

I respectfully request USCIS to retain the existing 60-day grace period and consider extending it to at least 90 days.

An additional 30 days would provide H-1B families with a reasonable opportunity to:

* Secure alternative employment and complete immigration formalities.
* Manage financial obligations and existing commitments.
* Make necessary travel and relocation arrangements without excessive financial losses.
* Minimize disruption to children’s education and protect the family’s mental and physical well-being.
* Give children sufficient time to mentally and emotionally prepare for changes in their education, social relationships, and lifestyle, rather than forcing an abrupt transition.
* Arrange appropriate medical records, consultations, prescriptions, and continuity of care before relocating.

H-1B workers and their families have invested years of their lives contributing to the U.S. economy and communities. Immigration policies should also consider the well-being of dependent family members, particularly minor children.

A reasonable transition period is essential to prevent unnecessary hardship, protect family health, and ensure stability during an already difficult transition.

Thank you for considering the impact of this proposed change on H-1B families.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that removing the grace period causes severe hardship and asks to retain or extend it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This comment is submitted anonymously. I oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers who lose their employment. I write about the people the proposal never counts: the nearly-adult children of backlogged families, whose immigration future turns on a birthday.

Under the Child Status Protection Act, a child keeps derivative status only if their CSPA age — their biological age minus the time the immigrant petition was pending — is under 21 when a visa number becomes available. For families from India in the EB-2 and EB-3 categories, that wait is measured in years, often a decade or more. A child who was 10 when the petition was filed can be 20 by the time the priority date approaches. The margin between keeping derivative status and aging out is often measured in months.

The 60-day grace period is the only buffer protecting that margin. If an H-1B parent loses their job, the grace period is what lets the family stay, find a new employer, and file a transfer petition — keeping the parent's status, the child's H-4 status, and the family's place in the green-card queue intact. Eliminate it, and a layoff becomes an immediate departure order. The family must leave, the transfer never happens, and the child's CSPA clock — which does not pause for the family's misfortune — keeps running while the family is outside the country, scrambling to re-establish status from abroad. A child who was months from preserving derivative status can age out in the gap, permanently.

Aging out is not a delay. A child who loses derivative status cannot simply rejoin the parent's adjustment application later. They fall out of the family-based queue entirely and must find an independent status — an F-1 student visa with its own costs and constraints, or a separate employment-based petition with its own decades-long wait. The proposal converts a parent's job loss into a child's permanent separation from the family's immigration path, for reasons that have nothing to do with the child's conduct or eligibility.

DHS offers no analysis of this harm. The proposal discusses the grace period as though the only affected person is the worker, and the only cost is the worker's inconvenience. It never counts the derivative children, never estimates how many sit within a year of aging out, and never explains why a child who has lived in the United States for most of their life — attended American schools, with no other home — should lose their place in line because their parent's employer had a layoff. The agency's own data show the India EB-2 backlog stretches years beyond a child's 21st birthday; the grace period is the narrow bridge that keeps some of those children from falling through.

If the goal is program integrity, the existing framework already serves it: a worker who finds no new employer within 60 days must depart, and a worker who commits fraud loses status entirely. Eliminating the grace period adds no integrity. It adds a trapdoor under children whose only offense is approaching their 21st birthday while their parents wait in a queue the government itself created. USCIS should withdraw the proposal and retain the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period to protect families and children from status loss.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Dinesh S
comments.commentText:
I am writing to voice my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary up to 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant visa classifications. As a high-skilled foreign professional working in the United States and a parent, I urge the agency to consider the severe, impractical, and counterproductive consequences of this rule.

Losing a job is a normal economic occurrence, often driven by corporate restructuring or market shifts entirely outside of an employee's control. A normal career transition should not instantly transform law-abiding professionals into individuals facing involuntary unlawful presence.

The elimination of this grace period is entirely impractical and will actively work against the agency's stated goals for the following reasons

1) Actively Increases Administrative and Backlog Burdens: DHS cites a need to reduce administrative burdens, but this proposal will achieve the exact opposite intent. Stripping the automatic grace period will force thousands of suddenly unemployed, compliant professionals to immediately file costly, defensive Applications to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status simply to buy a few weeks to wrap up their lives. This will needlessly flood USCIS with a massive surge of paperwork, worsening existing agency backlogs, stretching administrative resources thin, and increasing the overall regulatory burden.

2) Inhumane Disruptions to Children's Education: I have two children currently enrolled in the U.S. school system—one in their junior year of high school and another in the sixth grade. Forcing a family to abruptly pull children out of school mid-term with zero notice is devastating to their academic progression, mental health, and social stability. A high school junior, in particular, faces critical milestones for college preparation that cannot simply be paused or seamlessly transferred overseas overnight.

3) Logistical Impossibility of Immediate Relocation: It is humanly impossible to wind down a life in the United States within 24 hours. Breaking housing leases, selling vehicles, closing bank accounts, and coordinating the international shipment of household goods takes weeks of planning. Expecting a family to execute this instantly without a grace period is a logistical absurdity that forces otherwise compliant individuals to technically violate the law.

4) Negation of Congress's Intent for Job Portability: Congress designed the immigration framework to allow for job mobility and portability. By erasing the 60-day window, a professional who loses their job has no legal bridge to file a change-of-employer petition. This effectively eliminates the ability to look for a new role, forcing vital talent to leave the U.S. workforce entirely.

The current 60-day grace period is not a loophole; it is a humane and necessary administrative cushion that balances program integrity with economic reality, agency efficiency, and family welfare. I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and maintain the current grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jaikumar Murjani
comments.commentText:
I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to any proposal that would eliminate the current 60-day grace period available to H-1B workers following the termination of employment.

The existing grace period serves a critical purpose by providing a reasonable transition period for highly skilled professionals who are legally present in the United States and have complied with all applicable immigration laws. These individuals contribute significantly to the U.S. economy through their work, tax payments, investments, and participation in local communities. Removing this safeguard would impose substantial financial, emotional, and practical hardships on thousands of workers and their families.

A job loss is already a challenging and stressful event. Eliminating the grace period would transform an employment setback into an immediate immigration crisis. Individuals and families would be forced to make life-altering decisions with little or no time to evaluate their options, seek new employment, transfer to another lawful status, or arrange an orderly departure from the country.

The financial consequences would be severe. Many H-1B professionals have established long-term roots in the United States after years of employment. They may have purchased homes, entered into lease agreements, financed vehicles, invested in retirement accounts, enrolled children in schools, and undertaken other significant financial commitments. Without a reasonable transition period, these individuals could be forced to sell homes under distressed conditions, terminate leases with penalties, dispose of personal property at a loss, or default on financial obligations that cannot be resolved immediately. The resulting economic disruption would affect not only the workers themselves but also their families, lenders, landlords, local businesses, and communities.

The emotional and psychological impact should also not be underestimated. The uncertainty associated with job loss is difficult under any circumstances. When combined with the potential loss of lawful status, families may experience heightened stress, anxiety, and fear about their future. Spouses may be required to abandon careers, children may face disruptions to their education, and families may be separated from their support networks with little notice. Such instability is inconsistent with the treatment that should be afforded to individuals who have followed the law, contributed to the economy, and integrated into American society.

The current grace period also helps address the unequal impact of corporate workforce reductions. In many cases, layoffs occur as part of broader restructuring initiatives, cost-reduction efforts, or measures intended to improve financial performance and shareholder value. While employers often have the flexibility and resources to plan such actions, affected employees have far less ability to prepare for the immediate consequences. The grace period provides a modest but essential safeguard that allows workers a fair opportunity to respond to circumstances beyond their control.

Furthermore, H-1B workers contribute billions of dollars to federal, state, and local tax revenues and participate in programs such as Social Security and Medicare throughout their employment. They make long-term investments in the United States with the expectation that they will be treated fairly and provided reasonable time to navigate unexpected life events such as job loss.

For these reasons, the 60-day grace period should be preserved. It represents a balanced and humane policy that supports compliance with immigration laws while recognizing the realities faced by skilled professionals and their families. Eliminating the grace period would create unnecessary hardship, financial instability, and emotional distress without providing a corresponding public benefit.

I respectfully urge the agency to retain the current 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and their dependents.
comments.reason: The commenter argues against eliminating the 60-day grace period, stating it harms workers and families.

**Subject: Opposition to the Proposed Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period for Nonimmigrant Workers**

I respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers.

I am a highly skilled professional who has worked lawfully in the United States for several years under H-1B status. I have contributed to the U.S. economy through my work, paid taxes, and followed the employment-based immigration process, including obtaining an approved I-140 immigrant petition.

The existing 60-day grace period provides an essential, limited safeguard for workers who unexpectedly lose their jobs through layoffs, restructuring, or other circumstances beyond their control. Eliminating this protection would create significant uncertainty for workers, their families, and American employers.

I urge DHS to consider the following concerns:

**1. Job loss should not immediately jeopardize lawful immigration status.**

Layoffs are often business decisions unrelated to an employee's performance or compliance with immigration laws. Workers who have maintained lawful status for years should have a reasonable opportunity to secure new qualifying employment following an involuntary termination. The current 60-day period is already relatively short, particularly given the time required for interviews, hiring decisions, and immigration filings.

**2. Eliminating the grace period could harm American businesses.**

U.S. employers invest significant resources in recruiting highly skilled workers. The current grace period allows employers to hire qualified individuals who have recently experienced job loss without requiring them to immediately leave the country. Removing this flexibility could increase recruitment difficulties, disrupt ongoing projects, and cause the United States to lose experienced professionals to competing countries.

**3. The proposal disproportionately affects workers facing lengthy employment-based immigration backlogs.**

Many employment-based immigrants, particularly those from countries with substantial visa backlogs, remain in temporary nonimmigrant status for years despite having approved immigrant petitions. These individuals have complied with immigration requirements and established careers and families in the United States. Eliminating the grace period would expose them to severe consequences from a single unexpected employment disruption.

**4. Less disruptive alternatives are available.**

If DHS believes the existing grace period creates administrative challenges, I encourage the agency to consider narrower alternatives, such as retaining the grace period for involuntary terminations, rather than eliminating it entirely.

I also urge DHS to evaluate whether the anticipated administrative benefits outweigh the potential economic costs, loss of skilled workers, increased disruption to employers, and hardship imposed on families.

The 60-day grace period does not provide unrestricted employment authorization or permanent immigration benefits. It is a temporary, limited measure that allows workers to pursue lawful options following unexpected job loss.

I respectfully request that DHS retain the existing 60-day grace period or adopt an alternative that preserves reasonable protections for workers who lose employment through no fault of their own.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Charles Hampton
comments.commentText:
To: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS)

Re: Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364

Dear USCIS:

I am a Technical Product Manager based in Oakland, California. I am commenting on DHS's proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(1)(2). I have the following concerns about the proposal based on my experience in the technology labor market.

In June 2023, I was laid off from my position at Best Buy. I had worked in Product Management for 12 years at that time. Since then, I have applied for approximately 1,000 positions, interviewed for dozens of positions, and been unemployed for 26 months. The effect on my employment or earnings has been in the hundreds of thousands of dollars.

My observations about employer hiring are as follows: 1) Employers prefer H1B candidates because they can pay them less, and they can’t leave. Just a couple months ago, an Indian friend of mine at my current job who is on H1B shared with me over lunch that her manager (also Indian) openly brags about paying her and her team less because they are on H1B. He also makes inappropriate comments about her appearance because, as he puts it “what [is she] going to do about it?” This is only the most recent example of this; I could detail dozens of such instances. 2) Employees on H1B almost always find jobs within 60 days after losing them, even in truly abysmal job markets when American citizens like myself search for months or years to land jobs. For example, in about October of 2020, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, a classmate of mine on H1B lost his job. Within a matter of weeks, he had another one. At this time, I had been looking for a new job for almost a year, without any success. Companies were furloughing and laying off employees by the thousands. When I looked my classmate up on LinkedIn, it was clear that his national origin, ethnicity, and visa status were directly responsible for the quick hiring decision. Both his new and old hiring manager were of the same national origin and caste as him. 3) There is clear hiring bias on the basis of national origin within this 60-day grace period. Specifically, Indian nationals overwhelmingly, almost exclusively hire Indian nationals. There are special Facebook, Whatsapp, and Telegram channels dedicated solely to helping laid-off Indian nationals find jobs before their grace period expires. I personally witnessed a student, presumably on F1, desperately scramble to find a job or anything to stop or pause the clock on his grace period in March of 2026.. He petitioned me and others relentlessly, even though I told him that my company was on a hiring freeze and there was nothing I could do. Eventually he found something completely unrelated to his field of study, and shared with me that he was being paid an absurdly low rate for the Bay Area, and indicated that his employer also did not have to pay payroll taxes, so he was “quite a bargain for them.” Again, he was an Indian national, and so was the hiring manager.

I understand that the 60-day grace period does not itself authorize employment, and I cannot say that it directly caused my layoff or the loss of a particular job. Still, my experience illustrates that there is no true shortage of local technology workers, that there is widespread fraud and discrimination in this system, and therefore there is no need for this grace period. It directly harms the wages, employment prospects, and working conditions of American workers.

DHS should consider evidence from U.S. workers when assessing the effects of allowing qualifying nonimmigrant workers to remain in status after their prior employment ends.

I ask DHS to finalize the repeal of this 60-day grace period, make it effectively zero days, and to explain in its final rule how it evaluated evidence concerning layoffs, opportunities for U.S. workers, and any labor-market effects. My comment is based on my personal experience and that of my friends, colleagues and classmates that they have shared with me over approximately the last 20 years.

Thank you for considering my experience.
Respectfully,

Charles Ryan Hampton

Oakland, CA

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed removal of the 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Today, I lead engineering teams building enterprise software that major businesses rely on daily. My wife, who also earned her Master’s degree at a top U.S. research university, leads software teams developing virtualization infrastructure critical to American hospitals and banks. For over a decade, we have followed every law down to never getting a single speeding or parking ticket. We earn our living here, pay significant taxes, and spend our money in our local community. We have a mortgage, car payments, and an American born child.

Removing the 60 day grace period ignores the basic reality of human life. It is physically and legally impossible for a family on an H1B visa to sell a house, close out car loans, pull a child out of their routine, and liquidate ten years of life overnight if a layoff happens. Without a 60 day buffer, law-abiding families like mine would be forced into an impossible choice: abandon our property and financial obligations overnight, or stay for a few weeks to wrap up our affairs and accrue unlawful presence. Anyone who goes through that kind of shock treatment, or triggers reentry bars just for taking a month to pack up their home, will never return to the United States.

While I agree that American workers should always be prioritized whenever they are available, companies already prioritize domestic hiring because sponsoring an H-1B worker is expensive, slow, and uncertain. Skilled immigrants are hired to fill genuine talent gaps in critical industries, just as immigrants in past generations helped build America's railroads, skyscrapers, and manufacturing base. Stripping away the 60day grace period will not create jobs for Americans. Instead, it will cause sudden staffing disruptions at U.S. companies, trigger local mortgage and lease defaults when families are forced to flee overnight, and push top global tech talent to competing nations ultimately hurting American tech leadership and shrinking the tax base, which only worsens the fiscal deficit. Furthermore, eliminating this clear 60day window will actually increase the administrative burden on USCIS by flooding the agency with emergency B2 change of status filings and reinstatement requests from people simply trying to buy time to pack their lives.

If DHS is concerned about people staying in the country without actively looking for work or preparing to leave, the solution is not to eliminate the grace period altogether. A more reasonable alternative would be to keep the 60day rule in place, or require workers to submit a simple online attestation at the 30day mark confirming they are either in active job interviews or finalizing departure logistics. comments.title: MM155 Comment Submitted by That Ton
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (91 FR 57807)

I am writing in strong opposition to this proposed rule as someone whose lawful status in the United States depends directly on it. I am in E-3 status in New York. I have lived in the United States for 1 year. I work in Technology. My household includes a spouse whose work authorization depends on this status.

I want to address the administrative burden rationale directly, because the rule appears to produce the opposite of what DHS predicts. Today a worker whose job ends is covered by a grace period that requires no application and no adjudication. Under this proposal, remaining lawfully requires a filing: Form I-129 from a new employer, or Form I-539 from the worker to change to another status, and a separate Form I-539 from every dependent whose status falls with theirs. DHS's own figures describe roughly 65,752 affected workers a year and more than 208,000 dependents. Form I-539 receipts already exceed 400,000 annually, with published processing times averaging nine to twelve months and backlogs reaching eighteen at some service centers, and since the Edakunni settlement expired on January 18, 2025, USCIS is no longer obliged to adjudicate dependent applications alongside the principal's petition. Adding tens of thousands of filings a year to that queue is not a reduction in agency workload, and the proposal neither estimates the increase nor explains why it is outweighed.

DHS characterizes this as restoring a prior policy, but that framing skips the most important question: what has been built in the years since. Nearly a decade of workers, employers, landlords and schools have arranged their affairs around a predictable 60-day window. Those reliance interests are legally relevant, and the proposal neither identifies nor weighs them. DHS should address this before it goes any further.

Speaking as an employer, the grace period is what makes it possible to pick up good people when another company lets them go. Remove it and the sequence simply does not fit together. A Labor Condition Application takes roughly a week before a petition can be filed, by which point the worker is already out of status. DHS should recognize that this rule does not just affect workers; it takes an option away from American businesses trying to fill roles they cannot otherwise fill.

I would like to see the numbers. DHS's own filing identifies roughly 65,752 affected workers a year and over 208,000 dependents, but stops short of quantifying what happens to them. Meanwhile the claimed benefit, less adjudicative work in determining whether the grace period applies, is never sized. Without a genuine comparison, the conclusion that this change is warranted is an assertion rather than a finding.

The effects of this rule do not stop at the household. These are tenants with leases, borrowers with mortgages, and customers of local businesses. Forcing an overnight departure converts an orderly wind-down into an abrupt default, and the landlord, lender or small business on the other side absorbs the loss. Research from the Economic Innovation Group finds the average H-1B household contributes roughly $30,050 a year net to public budgets, about 2.6 times a typical U.S. household, and produces a net fiscal gain for state and local government in 49 states. That revenue funds schools and emergency services in the communities these families live in, and this proposal writes it off without comment.

There is a middle path here that the proposal does not appear to have considered. The stated problem is administrative: working out whether the discretionary grace period applies during later adjudications. That is solvable by making the period automatic and fixed rather than discretionary, or by adding a simple notification requirement, or by shortening the window. Outright elimination is the most damaging option available and DHS has not shown why the less drastic ones were rejected.

To put a concrete case behind that, here is my own situation:

I moved here a year ago with my spouse who is a dependent on my E-3 visa. I work in tech so losing my job would give me and my spouse no time to properly move nor to find a new job.

I urge DHS not to finalize this rule and to retain the existing grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). The record as it stands does not support the change: the benefits are asserted rather than measured, the costs fall on tens of thousands of families a year, and less drastic alternatives have not been addressed. Thank you for taking this comment into account.

comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to retain the existing grace period of up to 60 days for H-1B workers who unexpectedly lose their employment.

The 60-day grace period serves an important and practical purpose. It provides a reasonable amount of time for individuals and their families to responsibly conclude their affairs in the United States following an unexpected loss of employment. It is not an authorization to work without proper employment authorization or a guarantee of continued immigration status. Rather, it provides a limited transition period to make necessary arrangements and depart the country in an orderly and lawful manner.

Losing a job unexpectedly is already a significant personal and financial hardship. However, leaving the United States is not something that can realistically be accomplished overnight. Individuals and families need time to vacate apartments or terminate leases, arrange the sale or shipment of personal belongings, close utility accounts, settle financial obligations, coordinate school transitions for children, and make international travel arrangements. These responsibilities require time, planning, and coordination, particularly for families with children.

International travel arrangements can also be complicated and expensive, especially when an entire family must relocate on short notice. Securing affordable flights, coordinating travel schedules, arranging transportation of belongings, and addressing outstanding contractual and financial commitments cannot always be completed within a few days.

The existing grace period also serves an important purpose in helping individuals avoid unintentionally accumulating unlawful presence or falling into an immigration compliance issue simply because they were unable to arrange their departure immediately after losing employment. Providing a clearly defined and limited transition period encourages individuals to remain compliant with U.S. immigration laws and make an orderly departure rather than face circumstances that could lead to unintended immigration violations.

Furthermore, the impact of an unexpected job loss extends beyond the individual H-1B worker. Families may have children enrolled in local schools, ongoing rental or mortgage obligations, vehicles, household possessions, health insurance arrangements, and other commitments established over several years of living and working in the United States. These families deserve a reasonable opportunity to responsibly close these obligations and transition to life outside the country.

The current up-to-60-day grace period is a modest and reasonable safeguard. It does not provide an indefinite extension of stay or permit unauthorized employment. It simply recognizes the practical realities of relocating an individual or an entire family internationally and provides sufficient time to comply with immigration requirements.

I respectfully request that DHS and USCIS retain the existing up-to-60-day grace period for H-1B workers following involuntary job loss. Eliminating or substantially reducing this period would create unnecessary hardship and could make it more difficult for otherwise law-abiding individuals and families to depart the United States in an orderly and compliant manner.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sudip Paul
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period"

I oppose this rule and ask DHS to withdraw it.

I have lived in the United States for 16 years, in H-1B status since 2015, and have changed employers four times under H-1B portability. I own my home in San Jose, California, and my wife and I are raising our daughter, a U.S. citizen, here. For most of those years, a layoff under this rule would have ended my status and my wife's the following day. We could not have sold a house or withdrawn a child from school in a day, and our daughter would have left the only country she is a citizen of. Few employers will hire into a role that requires a consular petition, weeks abroad and a six-figure fee if the $100,000 payment returns. Today I have a pending adjustment of status application that is likely to remain pending for years. The rule still reaches me: my H-1B status is the only fallback if that application is denied, and a layoff would strip it the same day. Sixteen years of work and community would turn on the timing of a layoff notice, not on any decision of mine.

My objections, each tied to a section of the NPRM:

1. Statute (Sections IV.A-B). INA 214(n) lets an H-1B worker start new employment once a nonfrivolous petition is filed "before the date of expiration of the period of stay authorized," the I-94 date. Congress did not require the worker to be employed on the day of filing. The grace period is what makes that provision usable after a layoff: a Labor Condition Application alone takes about seven working days (20 CFR 655.730(b)) and a filed petition takes weeks, so a zero-day window makes every involuntary termination a mandatory departure. That is not alignment; it is a condition the statute does not contain.

2. The regulatory impact analysis (RIA) (Section V.A) cannot support the "not economically significant" finding. DHS monetizes one cost, $204-$301 per court visit; everything else is "Not Estimated."
(a) Population. DHS proxies job loss with revoked I-129s (65,752 per year), admits it cannot separate voluntary moves from layoffs, and counts only petitions filed within 60 days after the old employer's withdrawal rather than after termination, excluding those who ported fastest. The resulting 3,795 is called an "upper bound"; it is a lower bound, omitting I-539 filers (2,733 in FY2025) and working H-4, L-2 and E spouses.
(b) Wages. DHS found a $131,000 median wage for grace-period porters and never multiplied. 3,795 x $131,000 = $497 million in annual wages at stake; departure and consular re-entry plausibly adds 8-16 weeks of absence, or $76-$153 million per year from this undercounted group alone, before dependents, employers or removal proceedings. That crosses the $100 million threshold of E.O. 12866 section 3(f)(1).
(c) NTAs. DHS expects NTAs to rise only marginally from 37 in FY2025. But under the rule every post-termination filer is out of status, and under USCIS's February 2025 NTA policy a denied I-539 (2,733 workers in FY2025, plus every dependent) produces an NTA; I-129 beneficiaries are spared only by a revocable policy exception. The $204-$301 per hearing also omits counsel, repeat hearings and the 3/10-year bars.

3. Burden (Section IV.C). The "over 1.9 million" filings since FY2018 is the whole caseload; Table 3 shows about 5,300 post-termination filings per year, roughly 45,000 over the same period, under 3 percent of that. Burden likely rises: the filings do not disappear; each becomes a request to excuse a status violation under 8 CFR 214.1(c)(4), the same kind of individualized discretionary review DHS calls burdensome, now in every case, plus the NTAs and EOIR referrals DHS admits.

4. Reliance (Section IV.D). DHS calls reliance "misplaced" because the period is discretionary. DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), rejected that reasoning for DACA. USCIS's own December 2022 guidance told workers they could remain for up to 60 days. Workers maintaining H-1B status as the fallback for a pending adjustment of status application relied on it most.

5. Footnote 19 strikes the grace-period reference from 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i), so compelling-circumstances EAD eligibility ends the day a job does, for a benefit designed for job loss. It receives no analysis. Withdraw it, or add an express 60-day filing window.

6. Alternatives (Section IV.E). It rejects every alternative for the same reason: it would still let a worker remain after employment ends. That is the proposal restated as its own justification. DHS should analyze a fixed, non-discretionary 60-day period from an employer-documented last day of employment, retaining the period for involuntary terminations, or at a minimum treating I-129, I-539 and I-765 filings within 60 days of cessation as timely.

Request: withdraw the rule; failing that, adopt a fixed non-discretionary period and publish a revised RIA with monetized ranges for re-comment.

Sudip Paul, San Jose, California
